defn: Wall painting of Ethiopian churches, on plaster and on canvas glued to walls: Debre Berhan Selassie ceiling of winged faces, Lake Tana monastery murals, Lalibela paintings.
note: attest is the general Ethiopian art article ('painting on walls')

label: Litema
defn: Incised and painted mud-wall decoration of Basotho homesteads in Lesotho and the Free State, renewed by women.

label: Ndebele House Painting
defn: Geometric mural painting of the Southern Ndebele of South Africa on homestead walls, by women (Esther Mahlangu).

label: Imigongo
defn: Rwandan relief panels of cow dung in black, white and red spirals and zigzags, from house walls to boards.

label: African Scarification
defn: Cicatrisation and keloid scarification as body art across Africa, with named regional marks: Yoruba facial marks (ila), Nuba and Dinka marks.
note: culture names are tags

label: Sona
defn: Sand drawings (lusona, pl. sona) of the Chokwe and neighbouring peoples of eastern Angola: continuous lines around a grid of dots, illustrating stories.

label: Byzantine Illuminated Manuscripts
defn: Painted miniatures in Greek manuscripts of the Byzantine empire, 4th–15th century, from late antique codices to the classicising Macedonian Renaissance and Palaiologan books: Vienna Dioscurides, Rossano Gospels, Paris Psalter, Menologion of Basil II.
note: period rows (Early, Middle, Palaiologan, Post-Byzantine) are tags; pool QID Q1400430 on the Middle row

label: Byzantine Icons
defn: Devotional images painted in encaustic or egg tempera on wooden panels in the Byzantine empire and its orbit, 6th–15th century: Sinai Christ Pantokrator, Theotokos of Vladimir, Hodegetria and Deesis icons.
note: QID from the pool row

label: Cretan School
defn: Post-Byzantine icon painting of Venetian Crete, 15th–17th century, joining the Palaiologan manner with Italian elements: icons of Andreas Ritzos and Michael Damaskinos, Theophanes the Cretan's Athonite murals.
note: in situ row is the school's mural work; leaf sits in A3 where most of its works are

label: Fayum Mummy Portraits
defn: Portraits painted in encaustic or tempera on wooden panels and bound over the faces of mummies in Roman Egypt, 1st–3rd century: Hawara and Er-Rubayat portraits, Tomb of Aline, portraits from Antinoöpolis.
note: no pool row of its own; evidenced by Roman Period Egypt and Roman, Egyptian rows; A5 is the nearest panel-painting sub-family

label: Book of the Dead
defn: Illustrated Egyptian funerary papyri of spells for the afterlife, with painted vignettes, New Kingdom to Ptolemaic: Papyrus of Ani, Papyrus of Hunefer, Greenfield Papyrus.
aliases: Egyptian funerary papyri;Coming Forth by Day
note: attested by the Ancient Egyptian papyri row (art-historical core of the row)

label: Assyrian Palace Reliefs
defn: Carved gypsum orthostat reliefs from Neo-Assyrian palaces, 9th–7th century BC, with lamassu gateway figures: Ashurnasirpal II at Nimrud, Sennacherib's Lachish reliefs, Ashurbanipal's lion hunt.
note: Assyrian palace reliefs redirects to Assyrian sculpture

label: Nimrud Ivories
defn: Carved, gilded and inlaid ivory plaques and figures of the 9th–7th century BC found at the Assyrian capital Nimrud, made in Assyrian, Phoenician and North Syrian styles: Lioness attacking a Nubian, Woman at the Window, furniture plaques.

label: Byzantine Ivories
defn: Ivory carving of the Byzantine empire, 5th–12th century: consular diptychs, Barberini Ivory, Romanos group icons, Veroli Casket.

label: Cylinder Seals
defn: Engraved stone cylinders rolled on clay to leave a continuous image, the glyptic art of Mesopotamia, Iran, Syria and Anatolia from the Uruk period to the Achaemenids: Uruk and Jemdet Nasr seals, Akkadian contest scenes, Old Syrian and Mitanni seals, Neo-Assyrian ritual scenes.
note: period rows (Late Uruk, Jemdet Nasr, Akkadian, Old Syrian, Mitanni, Kassite) carry stone/seal shares and become tags on its kinds

label: Minoan Seals
defn: Engraved sealstones of hardstone, bone and gold made on Bronze Age Crete and adopted on the Mycenaean mainland, 3rd–2nd millennium BC: lentoid and amygdaloid seals, Pylos Combat Agate, gold signet rings.
note: evidenced by Minoan (gems 345), Middle and Late Minoan rows

label: Engraved Gems
defn: Intaglios and cameos cut in hardstone in the Greek, Etruscan and Roman world, 6th century BC – 4th century AD: Graeco-Persian gems, Etruscan scarabs, Roman Republican ringstones, Gemma Augustea.
note: evidenced by Roman (gems 797), Late Republican (gems 189), Italic (gems 33) rows

label: Ancient Egyptian Sculpture
defn: Statuary and relief of pharaonic Egypt in stone, wood and metal, from the Old Kingdom to the Ptolemies: Menkaure triad, Middle Kingdom block statues and tomb models, Amarna reliefs, sunk temple relief.
note: the title Ancient Egyptian sculpture exists only as a redirect; period rows (Old, Middle, New Kingdom, Late Period) are tags

label: Cycladic Figures
defn: Marble figures, mostly folded-arm female figures, made in the Cyclades in the Early Bronze Age, 3rd millennium BC: Spedos and Dokathismata types, harp player from Keros, marble vessels.
note: P13: archaeological culture known for one dominant medium

label: Ancient Greek Sculpture
defn: Stone and bronze sculpture of the Greek world from the Archaic to the Hellenistic period: kouroi and korai, Parthenon marbles, Riace bronzes, Pergamon Altar.
note: no pool row of its own; Greek culture row and Archaic/Classical/Hellenistic period rows evidence it

label: Greek Terracotta Figurines
defn: Mould-made and painted clay figurines of the Greek world, votive and decorative, Archaic to Hellenistic: Tanagra figurines, Tarentine votive figures, Myrina figurines, Boeotian figures.
note: Tanagra figurine (wiki) placed as a kind

label: Etruscan Sculpture
defn: Sculpture of Etruria in terracotta, bronze, stone and alabaster, 7th–1st century BC: Sarcophagus of the Spouses, Apollo of Veii, Chimera of Arezzo, Volterran cinerary urns.
note: evidenced by Etruscan (bronzes 360) and Italic (bronzes 111) rows

label: Roman Portraiture
defn: Portrait sculpture of ancient Rome in marble and bronze, from veristic Republican heads to imperial portraits: Patrician Torlonia, Augustus of Prima Porta, Severan and Tetrarchic portraits.
note: imperial period rows (Julio-Claudian, Flavian, Trajanic, Hadrianic, Antonine, Severan) are tags

label: Roman Sculpture
defn: Roman sculpture other than portraits: historical relief, ideal statuary and copies after Greek works, and carved sarcophagi: Ara Pacis, Trajan's Column, Ludovisi sarcophagus.
note: evidenced by Mid-Imperial and Augustan sculpture shares

label: Luristan Bronzes
defn: Cast bronze horse-bits, finials, standards, pins and weapons from the Zagros mountains of western Iran, early 1st millennium BC: master-of-animals finials, cheekpieces with winged creatures, votive pins.
note: evidenced by excluded rows Iranian, From Luristan and Iranian, Lorestan, and Iron Age metalwork share

label: Achaemenid Metalwork
defn: Gold and silver vessels and ornaments of the Persian empire, 6th–4th century BC: gold fluted bowls and rhyta, Oxus Treasure, griffin-handled amphorae.
note: Met essay names the gold fluted bowl; label not a Wikipedia title

label: Sasanian Silver
defn: Silver and silver-gilt vessels of Sasanian Iran, 3rd–7th century, hammered and chased with royal hunts and Dionysiac scenes: royal hunting plates, ewers with dancing figures, high-footed bowls.

label: Etruscan Mirrors
defn: Bronze hand mirrors of Etruria and Latium with mythological scenes engraved on the back, 6th–2nd century BC, together with the engraved cistae of Praeneste: mirror with Minerva and Hercules, Ficoroni Cista.
note: Etruscan mirror redirects to Etruscan art; Praenestine cistae (wiki:Cista) placed as a kind

label: Geometric Pottery
defn: Greek painted pottery of c. 900–700 BC with banded meanders and, in its late phase, figural funeral and battle scenes: Dipylon amphora, Hirschfeld Krater, Protogeometric amphorae.
note: Geometric period row is a tag that evidences it

label: Corinthian Vase Painting
defn: Painted pottery of Corinth, 725–550 BC, where black-figure was invented: miniature Protocorinthian aryballoi such as the Chigi olpe, and Corinthian animal-frieze kraters and alabastra.
note: no English Wikipedia article (red link); Britannica entry is for the Proto-Corinthian phase

label: Black-Figure Pottery
defn: Greek vase painting with figures painted in black slip and incised on the red clay, above all in Attica, c. 620–480 BC: François Vase, Exekias's Achilles and Ajax amphora, Panathenaic prize amphorae.
note: named painters are kinds but the pool carries no maker evidence

label: Red-Figure Pottery
defn: Greek vase painting with figures reserved in the red clay on a black ground, invented in Athens c. 530 BC and carried to South Italy: Euphronios Krater, Berlin Painter's amphorae, Niobid Krater.

label: Laconian Vase Painting
defn: Black-figure and earlier painted pottery of Sparta and Laconia, 7th–6th century BC: Arkesilas Cup, cups of the Hunt and Naucratis Painters.

label: East Greek Vase Painting
defn: Painted pottery of the Ionian coast and East Aegean islands, 7th–6th century BC: Wild Goat Style oinochoai, Fikellura amphorae, Klazomenian sarcophagi and vases, Chian chalices.

label: South Italian Vase Painting
defn: Red-figure pottery made by Greek workshops of Magna Graecia and Sicily, late 5th–3rd century BC, in its Apulian, Lucanian, Campanian, Paestan and Sicilian fabrics: Darius Vase, Asteas's phlyax kraters.
aliases: South Italian ancient Greek pottery;Italiote vase painting
note: Apulian, Lucanian, Campanian and Paestan each have Wikipedia articles; kept as kinds

label: Gnathia Vases
defn: Black-glazed pottery of Apulia painted over the glaze in white, yellow and red, c. 370–250 BC: Gnathia skyphoi and oinochoai with vines, masks and garlands.

label: Centuripe Ware
defn: Hellenistic Sicilian pottery painted in tempera after firing, with pink grounds and figures in relief, 3rd–2nd century BC: lebetes and lekanides from Centuripe and Morgantina.

label: Etruscan Vase Painting
defn: Painted pottery of Etruria, 7th–3rd century BC, from Etrusco-Corinthian and black-figure to red-figure workshops at Vulci and Falerii: Pontic Group amphorae, Caeretan hydriae, Genucilia plates.

label: Bucchero
defn: The black, burnished, reduction-fired pottery of the Etruscans, 7th–5th century BC, from thin-walled bucchero sottile to moulded heavy bucchero: kantharoi, stamped oinochoai, rhyta.
note: no pool row; evidenced by the Etruscan vases share (607)

label: Minoan Pottery
defn: Painted pottery of Bronze Age Crete, from Vasiliki ware through polychrome Kamares ware to the Marine and Floral Styles: Kamares cups, Octopus flask from Palaikastro, Palace Style jars.
note: Minoan row is a culture tag that evidences it

label: Mycenaean Pottery
defn: Painted pottery of Late Bronze Age mainland Greece, c. 1600–1100 BC, traded across the Mediterranean: stirrup jars, pictorial chariot kraters, Warrior Vase.
note: Late Helladic rows are period tags

label: Terra Sigillata
defn: The glossy red-slipped Roman tableware, plain and mould-decorated, made in Arezzo, Gaul, Germany and North Africa, 1st century BC – 3rd century AD: Arretine ware, South Gaulish samian bowls, African red slip ware.
note: Roman, Gaul row (vases 74) evidences it

label: Hadra Vases
defn: Hellenistic cinerary hydriae painted on a light slip, used for burials at the Hadra cemetery of Alexandria, 3rd century BC: Laurel Group and Dolphin Group hydriae.
note: evidenced by the excluded row Greek, Alexandria-Hadra (21)

label: Kerma Ware
defn: The thin, polished, black-topped red pottery of the Kerma kingdom of Upper Nubia, c. 2500–1500 BC: Classic Kerma bell-shaped beakers with a grey band.
note: P13: archaeological culture known for its pottery

label: Meroitic Pottery
defn: Wheel-made fine ware of the Meroitic kingdom of Kush, 1st century BC – 4th century AD, painted with religious emblems, plants and animals: painted jars and cups from Karanog and Faras.
note: attestation weaker than others; owner check

label: Nabataean Pottery
defn: The eggshell-thin painted fine ware of the Nabataeans of Petra, 1st century BC – 2nd century AD, decorated with leaves and palmettes: Nabataean painted bowls.
note: Nabataean pottery redirects to Nabataean art

label: Egyptian Faience
defn: Glazed sintered-quartz ware of ancient Egypt, blue and green, used for small sculpture, amulets, vessels and inlay: scarabs, ushabti figures, blue hippopotamus figurines, lotus chalices.
note: placed in E2: a quartz-frit body like stonepaste

label: Roman Glass
defn: Blown, mould-blown, cast and cut glass of the Roman empire, 1st century BC – 5th century AD, made in Syria, Italy, Egypt and the Rhineland: Ennion's mould-blown cups, Portland Vase, Lycurgus cage cup.
note: glass (2321) is the leading Roman class in the pool

label: Hellenistic Glass
defn: Core-formed, cast and mosaic glass of the Greek world and the Eastern Mediterranean, 6th–1st century BC: core-formed alabastra and amphoriskoi, cast bowls, gold-sandwich glass.

label: Coptic Textiles
defn: Tapestry-woven linen and wool textiles of late antique and early Islamic Egypt, 3rd–8th century, from burial grounds: tunic clavi and roundels, hangings with Dionysiac and Nilotic scenes, weft-loop wall hangings.
note: Coptic textiles redirects to Coptic art; evidenced by Egyptian (textiles 1868)

label: Sasanian Rock Reliefs
defn: Royal reliefs carved on cliff faces in Fars and western Iran by the Sasanian kings, 3rd–7th century, following Achaemenid precedent: Naqsh-e Rostam investitures, Bishapur triumph of Shapur I, Taq-e Bostan.
note: pool QID Q20110463

label: Hittite Rock Reliefs
defn: Reliefs of gods and kings carved on rock in Hittite Anatolia, 14th–13th century BC: Yazılıkaya, Fraktin, Hanyeri, Taşçı.

label: Gobustan Rock Art
defn: Petroglyphs of hunters, dancers, animals and reed boats pecked into the rocks of Gobustan in Azerbaijan from the late Upper Palaeolithic onward (UNESCO 2007).
note: pool exemplar Q4313909

label: Rock Art in the Hail Region
defn: Petroglyphs of humans, animals and inscriptions at Jubbah and Shuwaymis in the Ha'il region of Saudi Arabia, spanning some 10,000 years (UNESCO 2015).
aliases: Hail rock art;Jubbah and Shuwaymis petroglyphs
note: UNESCO title Rock Art in the Hail Region of Saudi Arabia; Bir Hima and Wadi Rum kept as kinds

label: Egyptian Tomb Painting
defn: Wall painting in the tombs and temples of pharaonic Egypt, in tempera on plaster: Meidum Geese, Tomb of Nebamun, Tomb of Nefertari, Theban nobles' tombs.

label: Minoan Wall Painting
defn: Fresco painting of Bronze Age Crete and the Minoanised Aegean, c. 1700–1450 BC: Bull-Leaping Fresco from Knossos, Akrotiri Spring Fresco, Fisherman of Thera.
aliases: Minoan frescoes;Aegean wall painting;Wall Paintings of Thera
note: pool QID Q7962606 on the row

label: Etruscan Tomb Painting
defn: Painted chamber tombs of Etruria, 7th–2nd century BC, chiefly at Tarquinia and Cerveteri: Tomb of the Leopards, Tomb of the Triclinium, François Tomb at Vulci.

label: Ancient Greek Painting
defn: Surviving Greek wall painting, mostly from tombs of the 5th–3rd century BC in Macedonia, Thrace and Magna Graecia: Tomb of Philip II at Vergina, Thracian Tomb of Kazanlak, Tomb of the Diver at Paestum.
note: Ancient Greek painting redirects to Ancient Greek art

label: Pompeian Wall Painting
defn: Roman wall painting of the Vesuvian cities and Rome, classed by August Mau in four Pompeian Styles, 2nd century BC – AD 79: Villa of the Mysteries, Villa of Poppaea at Oplontis, House of the Vettii.
note: pool QID Q740856

label: Catacomb Painting
defn: Early Christian and Jewish funerary and devotional wall painting of the 2nd–5th century, above all in the catacombs of Rome and at Dura-Europos: Catacomb of Priscilla, Via Latina catacomb, Dura-Europos synagogue.
note: pool QID Q18390991; row also carries provincial Roman murals (Syria, France, Britain)

label: Byzantine Wall Painting
defn: Fresco programmes of Byzantine and post-Byzantine churches, 6th–15th century: Cappadocian rock-cut churches, painted churches of Troödos, Panselinos at the Protaton, Mystras.
note: no dedicated English Wikipedia article; owner check

label: Faras Wall Paintings
defn: Wall paintings of the cathedral of Faras in the Nubian kingdom of Makuria, 8th–14th century, removed in 1961–64 to Warsaw and Khartoum: Bishop Petros with St Peter, Saint Anne, Nativity.
attest: wiki:Faras Gallery at the National Museum in Warsaw

label: Hellenistic Mosaics
defn: Greek floor mosaics from the 5th to the 1st century BC, from pebble mosaics to tessellated opus vermiculatum: Pella stag hunt, Alexander Mosaic, Sosos's unswept floor.
note: pool QID Q3827470; Hellenistic mosaics redirects to Hellenistic art

label: Roman Mosaics
defn: Floor and wall mosaics of the Roman world, 1st century BC – 5th century AD, with strong regional schools in North Africa, Antioch and Sicily: Nile mosaic of Palestrina, Antioch mosaics, Villa Romana del Casale, Bardo mosaics.
note: pool QID Q1253440

label: Byzantine Mosaics
defn: Glass and stone wall mosaics of Byzantine churches and of the workshops they trained, 5th–14th century: San Vitale, Ravenna, Hagia Sophia, Daphni and Hosios Loukas, Monreale, San Marco.
note: pool QID Q3324686

label: Borgia Group
defn: The pre-Hispanic ritual and divinatory screenfold codices painted on deerskin in the Mixteca-Puebla style of central Mexico, 14th–early 16th century: Codex Borgia, Codex Laud, Codex Fejérváry-Mayer, Codex Cospi.
see: A1-18 Mixtec Codices;A1-19 Aztec Codices;C2-16 Maya Codices
note: placed in A1 by P1: the painted pictures are the text

label: Mixtec Codices
defn: Genealogical and historical screenfold codices painted on deerskin by Mixtec (Ñudzavui) tlacuiloque of Oaxaca, 14th–16th century: Codex Zouche-Nuttall, Codex Vindobonensis Mexicanus I, Codex Bodley, Codex Colombino.
note: label is the field's term; no stand-alone article, attested in the Mixtec writing article

label: Aztec Codices
defn: Pictorial manuscripts of the Nahua of central Mexico, from the few pre-Hispanic and early colonial ritual books to the colonial histories, tribute rolls and encyclopedias painted by indigenous tlacuiloque: Codex Borbonicus, Codex Mendoza, Florentine Codex, Codex Azcatitlan.

label: New Spanish Baroque
defn: The painting of the Viceroyalty of New Spain in the Baroque idiom, 17th–18th century, from the large altarpieces and sacristy canvases of Mexico City to devotional and civic pictures: Villalpando's Puebla cathedral dome, Juan Correa's sacristy canvases, Miguel Cabrera's Virgins of Guadalupe.
see: A5-6 Casta Painting;A5-7 Enconchado;A5-8 Biombo;A5-9 Cusco School
note: defined here for painting; New Spanish Baroque architecture belongs to K5

label: Casta Painting
defn: Sets of paintings made in 18th-century New Spain (and occasionally Peru) depicting the hierarchy of racial mixtures as family groups with their dress and produce: Miguel Cabrera's casta series (1763), José de Páez series.
note: a genre that the field treats as its own tradition

label: Enconchado
defn: Paintings of late 17th- and early 18th-century New Spain in oil on panel with inlaid fragments of mother-of-pearl under translucent glazes, influenced by Japanese namban lacquer: González family Conquest of Mexico series, Virgin of Guadalupe (1698).
see: A5-5 New Spanish Baroque;A5-8 Biombo;I2-15 Mexican Lacquerware
note: pool QID Q135448181 not verified; Met object record names the technique

label: Biombo
defn: Painted folding screens made in New Spain from the early 17th century after Japanese byōbu, with views of Mexico City, the Conquest and festivities: Biombo of the Conquest and View of Mexico City, Indian wedding and flying pole screen.
note: attested in the colonial section of Mexican art; pool QID Q42187367 (Biombo) not checked

label: Cusco School
defn: The school of religious painting centred on Cusco in the Viceroyalty of Peru, 16th–18th century, with Andean painters working from Flemish prints and adding brocade gold (brocateado) and local flora: Corpus Christi series, archangel arquebusiers, Diego Quispe Tito's zodiac series.
see: A5-10 Potosí School;A5-11 Quito School;A5-5 New Spanish Baroque

label: Potosí School
defn: The school of painting of the silver city of Potosí in Upper Peru (Bolivia), 17th–18th century, led by Melchor Pérez de Holguín: Entry of Viceroy Morcillo into Potosí, Virgin of the Cerro.

label: Quito School
defn: The painting and polychrome sculpture of the Audiencia of Quito, 16th–18th century, known for its realist carved and estofado images and its painting workshops: Miguel de Santiago's Augustinian series, Legarda's winged Virgin of Quito, Caspicara's sculptural groups.
note: spans painting and sculpture; its sculptors are kinds here with a see to Estofado (seam)

label: Retablo
defn: Small devotional paintings of saints in oil on tin (lámina) made by popular painters in Mexico in the 19th century, with the related ex-voto paintings giving thanks for a miracle: Santo Niño de Atocha láminas, ex-votos of San Juan de los Lagos.
note: ex-voto paintings kept as a kind

label: Amate Painting
defn: Painting in bright colours on amate bark paper by Nahua artists of the Alto Balsas in Guerrero since the 1960s, with Otomí paper cut-figures from San Pablito: village fiesta scenes, birds and flowers.

label: Tablas de Sarhua
defn: Painted boards of Sarhua (Ayacucho), originally genealogical beams given at house-raisings, later sold as narrative paintings of village life: house-beam tablas, Piraq Causa series.

label: Tigua Painting
defn: Painting on stretched sheepskin by Kichwa artists of Tigua in Ecuador's central highlands, begun by Julio Toaquiza in the 1970s, depicting fiestas and Andean landscapes: Corpus Christi dancers, Cotopaxi landscapes.
note: weak attestation (collection record only); see problems

label: Fileteado
defn: The decorative painting of Buenos Aires carts, buses and shop signs with scrolls, flowers and lettering, inscribed by UNESCO in 2015: colectivo panels, filete signboards.

label: Cordel Literature
defn: The chapbooks of north-eastern Brazil sold hung on strings, whose covers are woodcuts (xilogravura) by popular printmakers: J. Borges woodcuts, cordel covers of Caruaru and Juazeiro.
note: placed in B2 for the woodcut covers

label: Maya Codices
defn: The surviving bark-paper screenfold books of the Postclassic Maya, written in hieroglyphs with painted almanacs: Dresden Codex, Madrid Codex, Paris Codex, Maya Codex of Mexico.
see: A1-17 Borgia Group;L2-36 Maya Mural Painting
note: C2 not A1: studied as hieroglyphic books (P1); seam with the A1 codex leaves

label: Papel Picado
defn: Mexican cut tissue paper banners chiselled through stacked sheets with designs for the Day of the Dead and fiestas.

label: Mesoamerican Jade
defn: Jadeite and greenstone carved by the peoples of Mesoamerica and Costa Rica from the Olmec to the Aztec, as masks, figures, celts, earspools and pendants: Olmec votive axes, Maya jade mosaic masks of Palenque and Calakmul, Costa Rican axe-god pendants.

label: Olmec Sculpture
defn: The stone sculpture of the Olmec of the Gulf Coast, c. 1500–400 BCE, from monumental basalt carving to small greenstone figures and ceramic hollow babies: colossal heads of San Lorenzo and La Venta, La Venta Altar 4, Las Limas Monument 1.
see: D3-8 Mesoamerican Jade;D5-65 Classic Veracruz Sculpture
note: P13: Olmec carving as the dominant medium; Olmec colossal heads (wiki:Olmec colossal heads) is the core kind

label: Maya Sculpture
defn: The carved stone and stucco sculpture of the Classic and Postclassic Maya: dated stelae, altars, lintels and panels with rulers and glyphic texts: Copán stelae, Yaxchilan Lintel 24, Piedras Negras Panel 3, Palenque stuccos.
see: E1-43 Maya Ceramics;D3-8 Mesoamerican Jade;L2-36 Maya Mural Painting

label: Aztec Sculpture
defn: The stone sculpture of the Mexica of Tenochtitlan, 14th–16th century, from colossal cult images and calendrical monuments to small household deities: Coatlicue statue, Sun Stone, Stone of Tizoc, Coyolxauhqui Stone.

label: Classic Veracruz Sculpture
defn: The sculpture of the Classic-period Gulf Coast (c. 100–1000 CE): carved stone ballgame yokes, hachas and palmas with scrollwork, and hollow ceramic figures: El Tajín ballcourt panels, Remojadas smiling figures, stone yokes.

label: West Mexican Shaft-Tomb Figures
defn: Hollow and solid ceramic figures and village tableaux placed in shaft tombs of Jalisco, Nayarit and Colima, c. 300 BCE–400 CE: Colima dogs, Nayarit house and ballgame models, Jalisco Ameca figures.
note: ceramic sculpture placed in D5 (images, not vessels)

label: Chavín Sculpture
defn: The carved granite of Chavín de Huántar and the Chavín horizon, c. 900–200 BCE, with fanged composite deities in contour-rivalry: Lanzón, Raimondi Stele, Tello Obelisk, tenon heads.
note: Chavín goldwork and Cupisnique pottery as kinds (P13)

label: Valdivia Figurines
defn: Small fired-clay female figures of the Valdivia culture of coastal Ecuador (c. 3500–1500 BCE), among the earliest ceramics of the Americas: Venus of Valdivia.

label: Estofado
defn: Polychrome wooden sculpture of Spain and Spanish America in which gilded surfaces are painted and scratched to imitate brocade, the technique of viceregal image-makers (imagineros) of Mexico, Guatemala and Quito: Antigua Guatemala saints, Quito sculptural groups.
see: A5-11 Quito School;D5-70 Brazilian Baroque;D5-71 Santos
note: technique-named leaf; seam with Quito School and the European slices' polychrome sculpture

label: Brazilian Baroque
defn: The sculpture and church decoration of colonial Brazil, 17th–early 19th century, culminating in the Rococo of Minas Gerais: Aleijadinho's soapstone prophets at Congonhas, Mestre Ataíde's ceilings, Bahia gilded talha.
note: placed in D5 for sculpture; ceiling painting is L2, churches are K5 (see problems)

label: Santos
defn: Carved and painted devotional images of saints made by santeros in the Hispanic Caribbean and New Mexico: bultos in the round and painted retablo panels: New Mexican bultos, Puerto Rican santos de palo, Three Kings figures.
see: A6-13 Retablo;D5-69 Estofado;southeast_asia D5-68 Philippine Santos
note: the wiki article also covers Philippine santos, built as a separate leaf by the southeast_asia slice (seam)

label: Alebrije
defn: Brightly painted fantastic creatures, first made in papier-mâché by Pedro Linares in Mexico City and from the 1980s carved in copal wood by Zapotec carvers of Oaxaca: Arrazola carvings, San Martín Tilcajete tonas.

label: Cartonería
defn: Mexican papier-mâché sculpture for festivals: Judas figures burned on Holy Saturday, skeletons for the Day of the Dead and mojigangas: Judas figures, Linares calaveras.

label: Caruaru Clay Figures
defn: Small painted clay figures of north-eastern rural life made at Alto do Moura, Caruaru (Pernambuco), after Mestre Vitalino: bands of zabumba players, retirantes, cangaceiros.
note: label not a stand-alone article; attested via the Caruaru article (see problems)

label: Haitian Metal Art
defn: Sculpture cut and hammered from flattened oil drums by the smiths of Croix-des-Bouquets after Georges Liautaud: vodou lwa figures, trees of life, mermaids.
note: attested in the town article

label: Taíno Zemís
defn: Sculptural objects of the Taíno of the Greater Antilles that housed deities and ancestral spirits, in stone, wood, shell and cotton, with the ritual seats and cohoba stands of the same cult: three-pointer stones, Vere zemís of Jamaica, duhos.

label: Peruvian Retablo
defn: Portable box altars of Ayacucho (Huamanga) filled with painted plaster and potato-paste figures, from the cajón de San Marcos to scenes of village life: cajón de San Marcos, Joaquín López Antay retablos.

label: Maya Ceramics
defn: The painted and carved pottery of the Classic Maya, above all the polychrome and codex-style cylinder vases and plates with courtly and mythological scenes and glyphic texts: codex-style vases of the Mirador Basin, Ik'-style vases of Motul de San José, Jaina figurines.

label: Teotihuacan Ceramics
defn: The pottery of Teotihuacan (c. 100–650 CE): cylindrical tripod vessels with painted stucco, Thin Orange ware and composite theatre-type censers: stuccoed tripod vases, Thin Orange effigy vessels, theatre censers.
note: attested via the site article; see problems

label: Gran Coclé Pottery
defn: The polychrome pottery of central Panama (c. 200–1500 CE) in its named styles, painted with stylised crocodiles, birds and rays: Conté style plates from Sitio Conte, Macaracas pedestal dishes, Parita style.

label: Nicoya Polychrome
defn: The white-slipped polychrome pottery of Greater Nicoya (north-western Costa Rica and Nicaragua), c. 800–1500 CE, with Mexican-derived feathered-serpent motifs: Papagayo polychrome vessels, effigy jars.
note: attested in the Nicoya article; see problems

label: Moche Ceramics
defn: Mould-made and painted stirrup-spout vessels of the Moche of Peru's north coast (c. 100–800 CE): naturalistic portrait heads, effigy vessels and fineline painted narrative scenes: portrait vessels, Presentation Theme fineline vessels.
see: G1-26 Moche Metalwork;L2-39 Moche Murals;E1-48 Nazca Pottery

label: Nazca Pottery
defn: Slip-painted polychrome pottery of the Nazca of Peru's south coast (c. 100 BCE–700 CE) in up to twelve colours, with mythical beings and trophy heads: double-spout and bridge bottles, Anthropomorphic Mythical Being bowls.

label: Chimú Blackware
defn: The burnished reduction-fired black pottery of the Chimú kingdom of Peru's north coast (c. 900–1470 CE), mould-made in stirrup-spout and effigy forms: stirrup-spout bottles with monkey adornos, double-chambered whistling vessels.

label: Shipibo-Conibo Pottery
defn: Pottery painted by Shipibo-Conibo women of the Peruvian Amazon with the maze-like kené designs that also cover their textiles and bodies: chomo jars, quenti cooking pots.
note: kené is the design system; the leaf is the pottery

label: Talavera Poblana
defn: Tin-glazed earthenware of Puebla and Tlaxcala made since the 16th century by guild potters after Spanish maiolica, in blue-and-white and polychrome: tibores, lebrillos, azulejos of Puebla façades.
note: UNESCO 2019 jointly with Talavera de la Reina (routed to Europe)

label: Barro Negro Pottery
defn: Black burnished pottery of San Bartolo Coyotepec (Oaxaca), reduction-fired and polished to a metallic sheen since Doña Rosa in the 1950s: cántaros, openwork vessels.

label: Tonalá Pottery
defn: The burnished and painted pottery of Tonalá and Tlaquepaque in Jalisco, in its colonial and modern styles: bruñido, petatillo, bandera, canelo.

label: Mata Ortiz Pottery
defn: Fine-walled painted pottery of Juan Mata Ortiz (Chihuahua) revived by Juan Quezada from the 1970s after Casas Grandes (Paquimé) wares.

label: Tree of Life
defn: Multi-branched painted clay candelabra-sculptures of Metepec and Izúcar de Matamoros depicting Eden and other narratives: Adam and Eve trees, Soteno family trees.

label: Pucará Bulls
defn: Paired glazed clay bulls of Pucará and Santiago de Pupuja (Puno) set on house roofs for protection and fertility.
see: E1-55 Tree of Life;D5-74 Caruaru Clay Figures
note: museum exhibition page

label: Chulucanas Pottery
defn: Burnished and smoke-resist decorated pottery of Chulucanas (Piura), revived from Vicús and Tallán techniques, with a denomination of origin.

label: Quinchamalí Pottery
defn: Black burnished pottery with white incised inlay made by women potters of Quinchamalí and Santa Cruz de Cuca in central Chile (UNESCO urgent safeguarding 2022): guitarrera figure, chanchito alcancía.
aliases: Quinchamalí and Santa Cruz de Cuca pottery

label: Awajún Pottery
defn: Pottery made by Awajún women of the Peruvian Amazon with its knowledge and ritual, inscribed by UNESCO in 2021.

label: Goiabeiras Clay Pots
defn: Black clay cooking pots (panelas) of the paneleiras of Goiabeiras in Vitória (Espírito Santo), smoke-blackened with tannin, the first Brazilian intangible heritage registered by IPHAN (2002).
aliases: panelas de barro de Goiabeiras;craft of the clay pot makers of Goiabeiras

label: Moche Metalwork
defn: Gold, silver and gilded-copper objects of the Moche, worked by depletion gilding and inlaid with turquoise and shell: Sipán ear ornaments, backflaps, nose ornaments.

label: Sicán Metalwork
defn: Gold and tumbaga objects of the Sicán (Lambayeque) culture of Peru's north coast (c. 900–1100 CE): Sicán funerary masks, tumi knives, beakers.

label: Chimú Metalwork
defn: Hammered and repoussé silver and gold of the Chimú kingdom (c. 900–1470 CE): beakers, ear spools, feathered tunics with plaques.
see: E1-49 Chimú Blackware;G1-27 Sicán Metalwork;G1-29 Inca Metalwork

label: Inca Metalwork
defn: Gold and silver of the Inca empire (c. 1400–1532): cast and hammered figurines from capacocha offerings, keros and ornaments: silver llamas, gold female figurines.

label: Muisca Goldwork
defn: Lost-wax tumbaga castings of the Muisca of the Colombian highlands (c. 600–1600 CE), above all the votive tunjos: Muisca raft, tunjo figures.

label: Colonial Andean Silverwork
defn: The silver of the Viceroyalty of Peru (16th–19th century) from Potosí, Cusco and Lima: church plate, sahumadores, and the domestic and equestrian silver that continued in the Río de la Plata: incense burners in animal form, mate cups, altar frontals.
see: G3-14 Mapuche Silverwork;H2-6 Colonial Andean Tapestry
note: gaucho silver kept as a kind (seam)

label: Tairona Goldwork
defn: Cast gold and tumbaga ornaments of the Tairona of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta (c. 900–1600 CE): bat-man and eagle pendants, nose ornaments, labrets.

label: Quimbaya Goldwork
defn: The gold of the Quimbaya of the Middle Cauca valley, with its ceramics: Quimbaya Treasure poporos, seated figures, helmets.

label: Calima Goldwork
defn: Hammered and cast gold of the Calima region of south-western Colombia in its Ilama, Yotoco and Malagana phases: diadems, nose rings, pectorals with faces.
note: no stand-alone article; see problems

label: Tolima Goldwork
defn: Flat cast gold pendants of the Tolima region of the Magdalena valley, with anchor-shaped human-bat figures.
note: no stand-alone article; see problems

label: Isthmian Goldwork
defn: Cast and hammered gold and tumbaga ornaments of the chiefdoms of Panama and Costa Rica (c. 200–1500 CE) in the Coclé, Veraguas, Chiriquí and Diquís styles: Sitio Conte plaques, eagle pendants, crocodile deity figures.
see: E1-45 Gran Coclé Pottery;G3-8 Tairona Goldwork
note: label is the field's umbrella for these styles

label: Mixtec Goldwork
defn: Lost-wax cast gold ornaments of the Postclassic Mixtec of Oaxaca, with filigree-effect wax threads: Monte Albán Tomb 7 pectorals, labrets, bell pendants.

label: Mapuche Silverwork
defn: The silver jewellery of Mapuche women in Chile and Argentina, flourishing from the 18th century: trapelacucha pectorals, tupu pins, trarilonco headbands.

label: Inca Textiles
defn: The tapestry-woven cumbi cloth of the Inca state, woven by aqllakuna and cumbicamayoc, with tocapu tunics as the highest rank: Dumbarton Oaks tocapu tunic, checkerboard military tunics.
see: H2-5 Wari Textiles;H2-6 Colonial Andean Tapestry;H2-7 Andean Textiles

label: Wari Textiles
defn: The interlocking tapestry tunics of the Wari state (c. 600–1000 CE) with abstracted staff-god profiles expanded and compressed across the field.

label: Colonial Andean Tapestry
defn: Tapestry-woven textiles of the Viceroyalty of Peru (16th–19th century) in which cumbi weavers combined Inca, Spanish and Asian designs: colonial uncus with tocapu, tapices with coats of arms.
see: H2-4 Inca Textiles;G1-31 Colonial Andean Silverwork

label: Andean Textiles
defn: The living warp-faced and complementary-warp weaving of Quechua and Aymara communities of Peru, Bolivia and Ecuador, with named regional styles: Jalq'a and Tarabuco axsus, Chinchero lliclla, Otavalo weaving.
see: H2-8 Taquile Textile Art;H2-4 Inca Textiles
note: defined here for the post-colonial traditions; pre-Hispanic cultures have their own leaves

label: Taquile Textile Art
defn: The weaving and knitting of Taquile Island in Lake Titicaca, where men knit chullos and women weave belts (chumpi) recording the agricultural calendar, inscribed by UNESCO in 2008.
note: knitted and woven; placed with the flatweaves

label: Saltillo Serape
defn: Tapestry-woven wool blankets of Saltillo and northern Mexico (18th–19th century) with a central diamond medallion and serrated fields.

label: Maya Textiles
defn: The backstrap-woven and brocaded cotton cloth of the Maya of Guatemala and Chiapas, whose huipiles, sashes and headcloths are distinct by town and community: Chichicastenango huipiles, Santiago Atitlán tzutes, Chamula wool.
note: community kinds come from the NMAI rows

label: Chancay Textiles
defn: Cotton and camelid cloth of the Chancay culture of Peru's central coast (c. 1000–1470 CE): gauze and openwork, painted cloth and woven dolls: gauze panels, painted cloths.
note: Chancay cuchimilco figures noted but not a leaf

label: Paracas Textiles
defn: Camelid-wool embroidered mantles from the Paracas Necropolis on Peru's south coast (c. 300 BCE–200 CE), stem-stitched with repeating flying figures: Paracas Necropolis mantles.

label: Mola
defn: Reverse-appliqué cotton panels made by Guna women of Panama and Colombia for the front and back of their blouses.

label: Arpillera
defn: Appliqué and embroidered burlap-backed pictures made by women's workshops in Chile under the Pinochet dictatorship and later in Peru.

label: Drapo Vodou
defn: Sequinned and beaded ritual flags of Haitian Vodou, carried to salute the lwa: vèvè flags, Myrlande Constant tapestries.

label: Ñandutí
defn: Paraguayan needle lace of radiating spider-web suns, made in Itauguá.

label: Divina Pastora Irish Lace
defn: The needle lace (renda irlandesa) made with cord and buttonhole stitches in Divina Pastora, Sergipe, registered by IPHAN.

label: Rebozo
defn: The Mexican woman's shawl, at its finest in warp-ikat (jaspe) cotton and silk with knotted fringe from Santa María del Río and Tenancingo.
note: garment type treated as a tradition by the field (ikat rebozo); P10 seam

label: Panama Hat
defn: Hats plaited from toquilla palm straw in Ecuador (Montecristi, Cuenca), inscribed by UNESCO in 2012.

label: Mexican Featherwork
defn: Feather mosaic of Mesoamerica and colonial New Spain (amanteca), from Aztec shields and headdresses to Christian feather paintings: Moctezuma's headdress, Mass of Saint Gregory (1539).

label: Mate Burilado
defn: Engraved and pyrographed gourds of the central Peruvian Andes (Huanta, Cochas Chico), with dense narrative scenes.
note: gourd placed in I1 with carved plant material

label: Mexican Lacquerware
defn: Lacquer (maque) of Mexico made with insect and seed-oil lacquers on gourds and wood, by inlay or painting, in its regional centres: Olinalá boxes, Pátzcuaro gilded trays, Chiapa de Corzo gourds.

label: Barniz de Pasto
defn: Decoration of wood with sheets of mopa-mopa resin cut and applied in colour, practised in Pasto (Nariño) since the colonial period (UNESCO urgent safeguarding 2020).

label: Cueva de las Manos
defn: Stencilled hands and hunting scenes of guanacos painted in the Río Pinturas caves of Patagonia from c. 9300 BP (UNESCO 1999).
see: L1-17 Serra da Capivara Rock Art

label: Serra da Capivara Rock Art
defn: The painted rock shelters of Serra da Capivara (Piauí), with Nordeste-tradition hunting, dancing and sexual scenes (UNESCO 1991): Pedra Furada, Toca do Boqueirão.
see: L1-16 Cueva de las Manos;L1-19 Chiribiquete Rock Paintings

label: Toro Muerto Petroglyphs
defn: Thousands of petroglyphs pecked on volcanic boulders at Toro Muerto (Arequipa) with dancers, camelids and birds, with related Andean sites: Toro Muerto, Toquepala Caves, Miculla.
note: the pool row is a regional bucket named for its chief site

label: Chiribiquete Rock Paintings
defn: Red-ochre paintings of jaguars, hunters and dancers on the tepuis of Chiribiquete in the Colombian Amazon (UNESCO 2018).
see: L1-17 Serra da Capivara Rock Art

label: Maya Mural Painting
defn: The wall paintings of the Maya from the Preclassic to the Postclassic: San Bartolo murals, Bonampak Room 2 battle, Calakmul market murals.

label: Teotihuacan Mural Painting
defn: The fresco painting of the apartment compounds of Teotihuacan (c. 200–650 CE): Tepantitla Great Goddess, Tetitla, Atetelco.

label: Cacaxtla Murals
defn: The Epiclassic murals of Cacaxtla (Tlaxcala, c. 650–900 CE), mixing Maya and central Mexican styles: Battle Mural, Bird Man.
see: L2-36 Maya Mural Painting;L2-37 Teotihuacan Mural Painting

label: Moche Murals
defn: Painted and modelled mud-plaster friezes of Moche temples: Huaca de la Luna Ai Apaec friezes, El Brujo.

label: Mexican Muralism
defn: The public mural movement of post-revolutionary Mexico (1920s–1970s) led by Rivera, Orozco and Siqueiros: Rivera's National Palace murals, Orozco's Hospicio Cabañas, Siqueiros' Polyforum.
see: L2-41 Chilean Muralism;L2-42 Murals of Revolutionary Nicaragua
note: artists route to artist-led cells as makers

label: Chilean Muralism
defn: Chilean public mural painting from the 1940s, from Siqueiros' Chillán murals to the brigade painting of the Brigada Ramona Parra.
note: pool QID, not independently verified

label: Murals of Revolutionary Nicaragua
defn: Public murals painted in Sandinista Nicaragua (1979–1990) by Nicaraguan and international brigades.

label: Nazca Lines
defn: Geoglyphs scraped into the desert of the Nazca and Palpa pampas (c. 500 BCE–500 CE), with straight lines and animal figures (UNESCO 1994): Hummingbird, Monkey, Condor, Palpa figures.

label: Pintados Geoglyphs
defn: Hillside geoglyphs of the Atacama made by removing or piling stones (c. 600–1500 CE): Cerro Pintados panels, Atacama Giant, Chug-Chug.
note: pool row is a bucket; leaf named for its principal site

label: Acre Geoglyphs
defn: Geometric ditched enclosures of the south-western Amazon (Acre, Brazil), c. 0–1300 CE.

label: Plains Hide Painting
defn: Painting on tanned or raw hide by the peoples of the Great Plains: men's figurative war-exploit and calendar painting and women's geometric designs, on painted buffalo robes, tipi covers and liners, parfleches and winter counts.
note: evidence: rawhide/paint parfleches in Siksika and Shoshone rows; winter counts are kinds

label: Ledger Art
defn: Plains narrative drawing in pencil, crayon and ink on the pages of account ledgers and on muslin, from the 1860s, continuing hide painting on paper: the Fort Marion drawings, Cheyenne and Kiowa warrior ledgers, Lakota ledger books.
note: Cheyenne, Kiowa, Lakota and Arapaho are kinds; contemporary ledger artists go artist-led

label: Inuit Printmaking
defn: Stonecut, stencil and lithographic printmaking of Inuit community co-operatives in Canada since 1957, issued in annual collections: Kinngait (Cape Dorset) annual print collections, Baker Lake prints, Kenojuak Ashevak's The Enchanted Owl.

label: Alaska Native Ivory Carving
defn: Carving and engraving of walrus ivory and bone by the Iñupiat, Yupik and St Lawrence Island peoples of the Bering Strait, from ancient engraved hunting gear to figures, cribbage boards and engraved tusks for the curio trade.
aliases: walrus ivory carving;Bering Strait ivory carving;Eskimo ivory
note: centres (King Island, Diomede, Point Hope, Point Barrow, St Lawrence Island) are place tags on the culture rows; Old Bering Sea / Ipiutak archaeological ivories not in pool

label: Mississippian Shell Gorgets
defn: Engraved discs of marine-shell worn at the neck in the Mississippian Southeast (c. 1000–1600), cut with Southeastern Ceremonial Complex imagery: Spiro and Etowah gorgets, rattlesnake and cross-in-circle gorgets, mask gorgets.
note: shell is placed in D2 with ivory and bone (organic hard material); Mississippian copper plates have no pool evidence

label: Northwest Coast Masks
defn: Carved and painted wooden masks of the Northwest Coast peoples, danced at winter ceremonials and potlatches: Kwakwaka'wakw transformation masks, Hamat'sa bird masks, Nuu-chah-nulth and Heiltsuk masks, Tlingit shaman's masks.
note: wiki:Transformation mask exists for the sub-type

label: Yup'ik Masks
defn: Shamanic dance masks of driftwood, feathers and paint carved by the Yup'ik and Cup'ik of south-western Alaska, made in pairs and destroyed after use, from finger masks to large hanging masks.

label: Totem Poles
defn: Monumental carved cedar poles of the Northwest Coast in formline style — memorial, mortuary, house-frontal and welcome poles carrying crests: Haida poles of SGang Gwaay, Tlingit and Tsimshian crest poles, Kwakwaka'wakw poles.
see: D4-24 Northwest Coast Masks;I1-14 Bentwood Boxes
note: no pool row names it; culture rows Haida, Tlingit, Kwakwaka'wakw evidence NWC carving

label: Inuit Sculpture
defn: Figurative carving of the Canadian and Greenlandic Inuit in soapstone, serpentine, ivory and bone, above all the stone sculpture made for sale through co-operatives since the late 1940s.
see: B2-6 Inuit Printmaking;D2-9 Alaska Native Ivory Carving

label: Kachina Dolls
defn: Carved and painted cottonwood-root figures of the katsinam given to Hopi (and Zuni) children at ceremonies, from flat cradle dolls to the action figures of the 20th-century market.
note: Hopi Pueblo row: Sculpture/Carving/Figures 904 of 3052

label: Zuni Fetishes
defn: Small carved stone, shell and antler animal figures of Zuni Pueblo, made for ritual and since the 20th century for collectors, often with inlaid eyes and bundled offerings.
note: A:shiwi (Zuni) row: Sculpture/Carving/Figures 440

label: Storyteller Figures
defn: Painted clay figures of a seated storyteller covered with listening children, created by Helen Cordero at Cochiti Pueblo in 1964 and taken up across the Rio Grande pueblos.
note: modelled clay figures go to D5 by the tab key

label: Ceremonial Pipes
defn: Carved stone pipes of Native North America made for ceremony and diplomacy: Hopewell platform pipes, Adena tubular pipes, Mississippian figural pipes, Iroquoian effigy pipes, catlinite (pipestone) pipes of the Plains.
note: archaeological pipe-dominated rows are kinds

label: Ancestral Puebloan Pottery
defn: Pottery of the Ancestral Puebloans of the Four Corners (c. 500–1300), above all the painted black-on-white wares and corrugated grey wares: Mesa Verde black-on-white mugs, Chaco cylinder jars, Kayenta and Tusayan wares.
note: branch rows (Cibola, Chaco, Kayenta, Rio Grande) are kinds; Cibola White Ware and Rio Grande White Ware have Wikipedia articles

label: Mimbres Pottery
defn: Black-on-white bowls of the Mimbres branch of the Mogollon in south-western New Mexico (c. 1000–1130), painted with figural and geometric designs and buried, 'killed', with the dead.
see: E1-61 Ancestral Puebloan Pottery;E1-65 Casas Grandes Pottery

label: Hohokam Red-on-Buff Ware
defn: Buff-bodied pottery of the Hohokam of the Sonoran Desert (c. 300–1450) painted in iron-red with geometric, animal and human figures: Sacaton Red-on-buff, Santa Cruz Red-on-buff, Casa Grande Red-on-buff.

label: Salado Polychrome
defn: Red, white and black painted pottery of the Classic period southern Southwest (c. 1275–1450): Pinto Polychrome, Gila Polychrome, Tonto Polychrome.
see: E1-63 Hohokam Red-on-Buff Ware;E1-65 Casas Grandes Pottery

label: Casas Grandes Pottery
defn: Polychrome pottery of the Casas Grandes (Paquimé) culture of Chihuahua in its Medio period (c. 1200–1450), with macaws, plumed serpents and effigy forms: Ramos Polychrome, Babícora Polychrome.
see: mesoamerica_south_america H8-20 Mata Ortiz Pottery;E1-62 Mimbres Pottery
note: the modern Mata Ortiz revival is the Mesoamerica slice's L47

label: Pueblo Pottery
defn: Hand-coiled, slipped and painted pottery of the Pueblo peoples of New Mexico and Arizona from the Pueblo IV period to the present, made by women potters of each pueblo in its own ware: Zuni owls and water jars, Zia and Santo Domingo polychromes, Taos micaceous ware, Tesuque rain gods.
see: E1-61 Ancestral Puebloan Pottery;E1-67 Acoma Pottery;E1-68 Hopi Pottery;E1-69 Black-on-Black Ware
note: the broad Pueblo leaf; each pueblo is a kind except the wares the field names apart (Acoma, Hopi, black-on-black)

label: Acoma Pottery
defn: Thin-walled white-slipped pottery of Acoma Pueblo painted in black and orange, from historic water jars with parrots and rainbows to the fine-line revival of Lucy Lewis and Marie Chino.

label: Hopi Pottery
defn: Yellow-firing pottery of the Hopi mesas, from Jeddito and Sikyátki Polychrome (c. 1400–1625) to the Sikyátki Revival begun by Nampeyo of Hano at First Mesa around 1895 and carried on by Hopi-Tewa potters.

label: Black-on-Black Ware
defn: Burnished reduction-fired blackware with matte black designs developed by Maria and Julian Martinez at San Ildefonso Pueblo around 1918, and the polished and carved blackware of Santa Clara Pueblo.
note: San Ildefonso rows were routed here by the Mesoamerica slice but are not in this pool

label: Mississippian Pottery
defn: Shell-tempered pottery of the Mississippian cultures of the Eastern Woodlands (c. 800–1600): Cahokia and Moundville engraved bottles, head pots and effigy vessels, Caddo engraved bottles, Lamar complicated-stamped jars.
see: D2-10 Mississippian Shell Gorgets;E1-71 Swift Creek Pottery

label: Swift Creek Pottery
defn: Woodland-period pottery of Georgia and northern Florida (c. 100–800) paddle-stamped with curvilinear 'complicated stamped' designs carved on wooden paddles.

label: Weeden Island Pottery
defn: Pottery of the Weeden Island culture of Florida and the Gulf coast (c. 200–900): incised and punctated wares and the pierced animal-effigy vessels made for burial mounds (McKeithen effigy vessels).

label: Catawba Pottery
defn: Coil-built, burnished and pit-fired earthenware of the Catawba Nation of South Carolina, the oldest continuously practised Native pottery tradition east of the Mississippi.
note: Pamunkey pottery noted as a neighbouring tradition (tag only)

label: Navajo Silverwork
defn: Silver jewellery and horse gear of Diné smiths since the 1850s, hammered, cast in tufa and stamped, set with turquoise from the 1880s: concho belts, squash blossom necklaces, ketohs, cuff bracelets.
note: article section Navajo; maker Kenneth Begay from evidence

label: Zuni Jewelry
defn: Lapidary jewellery of Zuni Pueblo, silver set with small cut stones since the 1920s: needlepoint and petit point, channel inlay, mosaic inlay.
note: article section Zuni

label: Heishe
defn: Fine disc beads ground from shell, turquoise and stone and strung in necklaces, above all at Kewa (Santo Domingo) Pueblo.
note: Kewa row is mixed pottery/jewellery

label: Trade Silver
defn: Silver and later German-silver ornaments of the fur trade and of Native smiths of the Northeast, Great Lakes and Prairies (18th–19th century): ring and luckenbooth brooches, gorgets, armbands and hair plates.
note: attestation weak (trade journal): see problems

label: Navajo Weaving
defn: Tapestry-woven blankets and rugs of Diné women on the upright loom: chief's blankets (first to third phase), eye-dazzlers, Two Grey Hills and Ganado rugs, Yeibichai rugs.

label: Chilkat Weaving
defn: Twined mountain-goat-wool and cedar-bark robes, tunics and aprons of the Tlingit and Haida, woven from painted pattern boards in formline designs.
see: H2-12 Coast Salish Weaving;H8-14 Spruce-Root Basketry

label: Coast Salish Weaving
defn: Twill and twined blankets of mountain-goat and dog wool woven by Coast Salish women on two-bar looms, revived since the 1960s.
note: Cowichan row: weaving tools 52

label: Chimayó Weaving
defn: Hispano wool weaving of the upper Rio Grande valley, New Mexico, from colonial Rio Grande blankets to the Chimayó blankets and vests woven by families such as the Ortegas and Trujillos.
see: H2-10 Navajo Weaving;mesoamerica_south_america L72 Saltillo Serape
note: a settler (Hispano) folk tradition; attestation is a state cultural page

label: Seminole Patchwork
defn: Machine-pieced bands of cotton strips sewn into skirts, jackets and shirts by Seminole and Miccosukee women of Florida since the early 20th century.

label: Ribbonwork
defn: Silk-ribbon appliqué cut and layered in negative and positive designs on skirts, leggings and blankets by Great Lakes and Prairie peoples (Menominee, Ho-Chunk, Meskwaki, Potawatomi, Osage) since the late 18th century.

label: Moosehair Embroidery
defn: Embroidery in dyed moosehair on birchbark and black cloth by Wendat (Huron) women of Wendake (Lorette) and other Northeastern peoples, learned from Ursuline nuns: floral moccasins, calling-card boxes, cigar cases.

label: Star Quilts
defn: Pieced quilts centred on a single eight-pointed star of diamond patches, made by Lakota, Dakota and other Plains women since the reservation era and given at honouring and memorial giveaways.

label: Pomo Basketry
defn: Coiled and twined baskets of the Pomo of northern California, among them the feathered and beaded gift baskets and the art baskets made for sale by named weavers.

label: California Indian Basketry
defn: Twined and coiled basketry of the Native peoples of California and the adjoining Great Basin edge other than the Pomo: Hupa, Karuk and Yurok overlay-twined caps, Yokuts bottleneck baskets, Cahuilla coiled baskets, Washoe degikup.
note: tribal sub-traditions are kinds

label: Spruce-Root Basketry
defn: Fine twined baskets and hats of split spruce root with false-embroidery grass designs, made by Tlingit and Haida women of the northern Northwest Coast.
see: H2-11 Chilkat Weaving;H8-15 Unangan Grass Basketry

label: Unangan Grass Basketry
defn: Very finely twined wild-rye-grass baskets, wallets and lidded jars of the Unangan (Aleut), above all the Attu baskets with silk false embroidery made for sale after 1867.

label: Plateau Cornhusk Bags
defn: Flat twined bags of Indian hemp with cornhusk false embroidery made by Nez Perce, Yakama, Umatilla and other Columbia Plateau women for root storage and exchange.

label: Plateau Imbricated Basketry
defn: Coiled cedar-root baskets imbricated with bear grass and cherry bark made by Klickitat, Nlaka'pamux and other Interior Salish weavers: berry baskets, lidded trunks.

label: Apache Basketry
defn: Coiled willow and devil's-claw ollas and trays and pitched twined water jars of the Western, Jicarilla and Mescalero Apache, with figures of people and animals.

label: Pima Basketry
defn: Coiled willow, cattail and devil's-claw baskets of the Akimel O'odham (Pima) and Tohono O'odham (Papago), the latter also in yucca and bear grass, with fret and squash-blossom designs.

label: Hopi Basketry
defn: Basketry of the Hopi mesas: coiled galleta-grass and yucca plaques of Second Mesa and wicker plaques of rabbitbrush of Third Mesa, often with katsina figures.

label: Rivercane Basketry
defn: Plaited baskets of split rivercane dyed with walnut and bloodroot, made by Cherokee, Chitimacha, Choctaw and Koasati weavers of the Southeast, including the double-woven baskets.

label: Wabanaki Basketry
defn: Woven brown-ash splint and braided sweetgrass baskets of the Wabanaki (Passamaquoddy, Penobscot, Maliseet, Mi'kmaq) of Maine and the Maritimes, from work baskets to fancy 'curly' baskets.

label: Birchbark Biting
defn: Designs bitten into thin folded sheets of birchbark by Anishinaabe, Cree and Algonquin women, used as patterns for quill and bead embroidery and as works in themselves.
note: birchbark containers themselves have no attested leaf: see problems

label: Porcupine Quillwork
defn: Embroidery with flattened dyed porcupine quills on hide and birchbark across the Plains, Subarctic and Northeast: Lakota quilled robes and shirts, Mi'kmaq and Odawa quilled birchbark boxes, Dene quilled bands.

label: Plains Beadwork
defn: Glass-bead embroidery of the peoples of the Great Plains and Plateau in lane-stitch and overlay techniques, in tribal styles: Lakota fully beaded vests and cradleboards, Crow (Apsáalooke) horse gear, Blackfeet and Cree floral beadwork.
see: H9-5 Porcupine Quillwork;H9-7 Haudenosaunee Raised Beadwork
note: attestation is a collection page; see problems

label: Haudenosaunee Raised Beadwork
defn: Raised (embossed) glass beadwork on velvet by Mohawk, Tuscarora and Seneca women, above all the 'whimsies' (pincushions, frames, purses) sold at Niagara Falls from the mid-19th century.

label: Wampum
defn: Tubular beads of white whelk and purple quahog shell strung and woven into belts and strings by the Haudenosaunee and Algonquian peoples of the Northeast to record treaties and council business: Hiawatha Belt, Two Row Wampum.
note: archaeological Seneca and Cayuga shell-bead rows are tagged, not kinds

label: Bentwood Boxes
defn: Kerfed, steamed and bent cedar boxes and chests of the Northwest Coast, carved and painted in formline: storage and grease boxes, bentwood chests, bent-corner bowls.

label: Pecos River Style
defn: Large polychrome pictographs of shamanic figures painted in the rock shelters of the Lower Pecos Canyonlands of Texas and Coahuila (c. 2700 BCE onward): White Shaman Shelter, Fate Bell Shelter, Panther Cave.

label: Barrier Canyon Style
defn: Archaic pictographs of tall tapering ghost-like figures on the Colorado Plateau of Utah: Great Gallery, Horseshoe Canyon, Sego Canyon.

label: Chumash Rock Painting
defn: Polychrome pictographs of circles, wheels and beings painted in caves of the Chumash territory of southern California (c. 1000–1800): Painted Cave, Painted Rock (Carrizo Plain), Burro Flats.

label: Coso Rock Art
defn: Petroglyphs of bighorn sheep, hunters and patterned-body figures in the Coso Range of the Mojave Desert, the largest concentration in North America.
note: attested through the Coso Rock Art District

label: Writing-on-Stone Rock Art
defn: Petroglyphs and pictographs of the Plains, incised in the sandstone of the Milk River valley, Alberta, including biographic warrior scenes (Áísínai'pi, UNESCO 2019).
note: attested through the site (Writing-on-Stone Provincial Park)

label: Rock Paintings of the Sierra de San Francisco
defn: The Great Murals of Baja California: life-size red and black human and animal figures painted in the rock shelters of the Sierra de San Francisco and Sierra de Guadalupe (UNESCO 1993).
note: Baja California is outside Mesoamerica: kept here

label: Effigy Mounds
defn: Earthen mounds raised in the shapes of animals and serpents in the Eastern Woodlands: Serpent Mound, the bear and bird mounds of Effigy Mounds National Monument.
note: no pool row of its own; Serpent Mound from row 574 exemplars

label: Blythe Intaglios
defn: Giant human and animal figures scraped into the desert pavement near Blythe on the lower Colorado River.

label: Kakiniit
defn: Inuit women's facial and body tattooing, sewn or pricked with soot-blackened sinew, revived in Nunavut and Greenland since the 2000s.

label: Navajo Sandpainting
defn: Dry paintings of coloured sands, pollen and charcoal made by Diné medicine men for healing chants and erased after use, and their permanent versions glued on board for sale since the 1930s.

label: Western Desert Painting
defn: The acrylic painting movement of the Central and Western Desert begun at Papunya in 1971, in which Dreaming (Tjukurrpa/Jukurrpa) designs once made in sand, body paint and ceremony are painted on canvas and board in dotted and concentric-circle fields, carried on by community art centres: Papunya Tula boards, Warlukurlangu Jukurrpa canvases, Utopia and APY Lands painting.
aliases: Western Desert art movement;dot painting;Papunya Tula painting;acrylic desert painting
note: Western Desert art movement and Dot painting both redirect to Papunya Tula; art centres are kinds; Utopia (Anmatyerre/Alyawarr, Arandic) is placed here by convention as Central Desert painting

label: Contemporary Indigenous Australian Art
defn: Painting by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander artists from the 1970s onward outside the Western Desert and bark-painting lineages, in ochre and acrylic on canvas, worked through community art centres: Warmun (Turkey Creek) ochre paintings, Mangkaja and Ngukurr acrylics, Mornington Island painting, Mowanjum Wandjina paintings.
note: kept narrow in use: holds the painting centres that have no leaf of their own; the article title is the movement umbrella (see problems)

label: Hermannsburg School
defn: The Western Arrernte watercolour landscape school of the Hermannsburg mission (from 1934), founded by Albert Namatjira after lessons with Rex Battarbee and carried on by his family and followers: MacDonnell Ranges landscapes, ghost gums.
note: artists (Namatjira, Pannka) are artist-led

label: Bark Painting
defn: Painting in natural ochres on prepared stringybark sheets, the classic medium of Arnhem Land, with clan designs in fine cross-hatching (rarrk) in the east and figurative and x-ray figures in the west: Yolŋu miny'tji clan paintings, Kunwinjku x-ray figures, Groote Eylandt black-ground barks.
note: art centres and regional schools are kinds; Tiwi painted bark baskets (tunga) see L18

label: Torres Strait Islander Printmaking
defn: The linocut and etching movement of the Torres Strait (Zenadth Kes) from the 1990s, cutting island cosmology, totems and turtle-shell mask forms into large black-and-white prints: Badu and Moa linocuts, Mabuiag etchings.
note: printmakers (Tipoti, Nona, Bosun, Missi) are artist-led

label: Torres Strait Turtle-Shell Masks
defn: Masks of the Torres Strait Islands built from heated and stitched turtle-shell plates, worn in initiation, funerary and increase ceremonies, with composite human-animal forms in the west and human faces in the east: krar (western islands), le op (Mer, Erub), crocodile-head masks.
note: dhari (feather headdress) and wooden mawa masks of Saibai are kinds

label: Whakairo
defn: Māori wood carving: the carved figures, panels, gateways and canoe prows of meeting houses (wharenui), storehouses and canoes, cut in regional and tribal schools with manaia, spiral and figure motifs: poupou wall panels, pātaka storehouse carvings, tauihu canoe prows, waka huia treasure boxes.
note: iwi schools and named carvers are kinds; the meeting house as a building is K12

label: Malagan
defn: The carved and painted funerary sculpture of northern New Ireland, made for malagan memorial ceremonies and discarded after display: openwork friezes, figures and masks of softwood with opercula eyes: vavara friezes, totok poles, tatanua masks.

label: Uli
defn: The massive hermaphroditic ancestor figures of central New Ireland (Mandak and Barak), displayed in the long ceremonies of skull reburial: uli figures with raised arms and crested headdresses.

label: Asmat Woodcarving
defn: The wood carving of the Asmat of south-west New Guinea (Papua, Indonesia), carvers (wowipits) working in the tradition of the culture hero Fumeripits: bisj ancestor poles, carved shields, canoe prows, ancestor figures.

label: Sepik Carving
defn: The figure sculpture, masks and ceremonial-house carving of the peoples of the Sepik River basin of Papua New Guinea: Iatmul orator's stools and ancestor figures, Sawos malu boards, Abelam yam masks and ancestor figures.
note: Abelam sago-spathe ceiling painting and Sawos/Aibom pottery are not under this leaf (see problems)

label: Massim Carving
defn: The curvilinear carving of the Massim region (Milne Bay, PNG), above all the Trobriand Islands, in hardwood incised and filled with lime: tabuya and lagim canoe prow boards for kula voyages, lime spatulas, dance shields.

label: Nguzu Nguzu
defn: The blackened wood canoe-prow figureheads of New Georgia in the western Solomon Islands, inlaid with nautilus shell, the emblem of the Solomon Islands shell-inlay tradition: nguzu nguzu figureheads, shell-inlaid bowls.
note: label is the field's object name; it stands for the shell-inlay carving of New Georgia (see problems)

label: Marquesan Carving
defn: The carving of the Marquesas Islands (Te Henua ʻEnana) in wood, bone and stone, dense with the eye-and-face (mata) motifs shared with Marquesan tattoo: uʻu clubs, tiki figures, carved bowls and fan handles, bone ear ornaments (taiana).

label: Moai Kavakava
defn: The small wooden figures of Rapa Nui (Easter Island) carved in toromiro, emaciated male ancestor images worn at feasts, with their companion carvings: moai kavakava, moai paepae, rei miro pectorals.
note: label is an object type standing for Rapa Nui wood carving (see problems); stone moai are K/D monumental

label: Aurukun Sculpture
defn: The ochre-painted softwood sculpture of the Wik and Kugu peoples of Aurukun on Cape York, made for ceremony and since the 1990s through the art centre: Ku' (camp dog) figures, ancestral beings.

label: Hei-tiki
defn: Māori ornaments carved from pounamu (New Zealand nephrite and bowenite) with stone tools, worn as heirlooms (taonga): hei-tiki human figure pendants, hei matau hook pendants, kuru ear pendants, mere pounamu clubs.
note: label per the field; the leaf covers pounamu ornament carving

label: Pukumani Poles
defn: The carved and ochre-painted ironwood grave posts (tutini) of the Tiwi Islands, erected round the grave at the Pukumani mourning ceremony and crowned with painted bark baskets: tutini, tunga bark baskets, carved figures.
note: Tiwi ochre painting on canvas sits under L2 as a kind

label: Toas
defn: Small painted direction-markers of gypsum, wood and found materials made by the Diyari and neighbouring peoples of the Lake Eyre basin about 1904, left to show where a group had gone.

label: Riji
defn: Pearl-shell pendants and pubic coverings of the Kimberley, engraved with interlocking meanders and filled with ochre, worn in ceremony and traded far inland: riji, jakoli, longkalongka.
note: shell ornament filed in G3 for want of a non-metal ornament sub-family (see problems)

label: Māori Weaving
defn: The fibre arts of the Māori in harakeke (New Zealand flax) and muka (its fibre): finger-twined (whatu) cloaks with tāniko borders and plaited (raranga) baskets and mats: kaitaka and korowai cloaks, piupiu, kete, whāriki.
note: plaited raranga (kete, whāriki) sits under this leaf, not H8, to keep the culture's weaving in one place

label: Tivaevae
defn: The appliqué and piecework quilts of the Cook Islands (and tīfaifai of Tahiti), sewn communally by women's groups (vainetini) and given at weddings, birthdays and funerals: tivaevae manu, tivaevae taorei, tivaevae tataura.

label: Possum-Skin Cloak
defn: Cloaks of sewn possum pelts incised on the skin side with clan and Country designs, worn by the Aboriginal peoples of south-eastern Australia and revived since the 1990s: Lake Condah and Maiden's Punt cloaks, revival cloaks.
note: SE Australian carved shields and clubs in the same row have no leaf (see problems)

label: Tapa Cloth
defn: Barkcloth beaten from paper-mulberry and other inner bark across the Pacific and painted, stencilled, rubbed or printed with designs: Samoan siapo, Tongan ngatu, Fijian masi, Hawaiian kapa, Niuean hiapo, Omie and Maisin barkcloth.
note: island traditions are kinds

label: ʻIe Tōga
defn: The finely plaited pandanus fine mats of Samoa, and the fine mats of Tonga and Tuvalu, exchanged as the highest valuables at life-crisis ceremonies: ʻie tōga, Tongan kie and taʻovala.

label: Aboriginal Fibre Art
defn: The coiled, looped, twined and plaited fibre work of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women and men, from string bags and baskets to contemporary fibre sculpture: dillybags, Arnhem Land pandanus baskets, rainforest bicornual baskets, Tjanpi grass sculpture, ghost-net sculpture.

label: Lalava
defn: Decorative coconut-fibre (sennit, magimagi) lashing of Tonga, Fiji and Samoa, binding the beams of houses and the hulls of canoes in red and black geometric patterns, now also made as freestanding works.

label: Hawaiian Featherwork
defn: The featherwork of the Hawaiian chiefs: red and yellow honeyeater and ʻiʻiwi feathers knotted to olonā netting as emblems of rank and divinity: ʻahu ʻula cloaks and capes, mahiole helmets, lei hulu, feathered god images.

label: Kahu Huruhuru
defn: Māori feather cloaks: muka cloaks finger-woven (whatu) with feathers of kiwi, kererū, kākā and other birds set in the weft, the highest-ranking cloaks of the 19th century onward: kahu kiwi, kahu kererū.
note: attest by the redirect Kahu huruhuru to its section

label: Fijian Clubs
defn: The carved hardwood war clubs (i-wau) of Fiji, made by specialist carvers in named forms and often finely incised: totokia (pineapple club), gata (gunstock club), i-ula throwing clubs, kinikini paddle clubs.
note: Tongan clubs (ʻakau tau) are a see-also gap

label: Vanuatu Slit Gongs
defn: The upright slit gongs of northern Vanuatu (Ambrym, Malakula), breadfruit trunks hollowed and carved with ancestral faces and raised in dancing grounds of the grade societies: atingting kon (Ambrym), Malakula slit gongs; tree-fern grade figures as a kind.

label: Hermannsburg Potters
defn: The hand-built, painted terracotta of the Western Arrernte women of Hermannsburg (Ntaria) since 1990, with modelled animal lids and landscapes painted in underglaze: lidded pots.
note: an art-centre ware

label: Arnhem Land Rock Art
defn: The painted rock shelters of the western Arnhem Land plateau and Kakadu, from Dynamic figures to the recent x-ray and contact paintings: Ubirr, Burrungkuy (Nourlangie), Nanguluwur, Injalak Hill.

label: Gwion Gwion Rock Paintings
defn: The fine-line figure paintings of the north-west Kimberley, slender tasselled human figures of great age.
note: Wandjina rock paintings of the same region are a kind (see problems)

label: Murujuga Rock Art
defn: The petroglyphs of the Burrup Peninsula and Dampier Archipelago (Murujuga), over a million engravings made across tens of thousands of years.

label: Sydney Rock Engravings
defn: The outline engravings on Hawkesbury sandstone in the Sydney basin: animals, ancestral beings and people: Ku-ring-gai Chase sites.

label: Quinkan Rock Art
defn: The painted shelters around Laura on Cape York with the Quinkan spirit figures.

label: Panaramitee Style
defn: The widespread Australian engraving style of tracks, circles and dots ('track and circle'), among the oldest rock art of the continent: Ewaninga, Panaramitee.

label: Māori Rock Art
defn: The charcoal and red-ochre drawings in limestone shelters of South Canterbury and North Otago: Takiroa, Awamoko.
note: Māori rock art redirects to Māori culture#Painting

label: Tā Moko
defn: Māori tattooing, chiselled (uhi) into the skin in curvilinear designs that mark descent and rank: moko on men's faces, moko kauae for women.

label: Polynesian Tattooing
defn: The tattoo traditions of Polynesia worked with toothed combs and a mallet: Samoan peʻa and malu, Marquesan full-body tattoo, Tahitian tatau, Fijian veiqia.
note: Peʻa attests the Samoan core; Polynesian tattoo redirects to History of tattooing#Polynesia

label: Armenian Manuscript Illumination
defn: Painting and ornament of Armenian Gospel books and service books from the 10th to the 18th century, taught in monastic schools named after their regions: Etchmiadzin Gospels, Mugni Gospels, Toros Roslin's Gospels, Glajor Gospels.
note: enwiki Armenian manuscript illumination redirects to Armenian illuminated manuscripts; schools (Cilician, Vaspurakan, Glajor, Tatev, Crimean, New Julfa) are kinds; routed europe_folk_east rows attach here

label: Georgian Icon Painting
defn: Painted panel icons of medieval and early modern Georgia, from the 10th century, often set in chased silver revetments: icons of Svaneti, Gelati iconostasis, Georgian icons at Sinai.
note: no English Wikipedia article; attested by art-historical article (N. Chichinadze); leaf made for the routed europe_folk_east row 'Georgian / icon painting'

label: Theorem Painting
defn: American stencilled still lifes of fruit and flowers painted on velvet or paper with cut stencils (theorems), a schoolgirl and amateur art of c. 1810–1860: fruit baskets on velvet, bowls of flowers.
note: Theorem painting redirects to Theorem stencil

label: Georgian Calligraphy
defn: Writing of the Georgian scripts (asomtavruli, nuskhuri, mkhedruli) as an art, in manuscripts and inscriptions.
note: leaf made for the routed europe_folk_east row 'Georgian calligraphy'

label: Late Antique Illumination
defn: Illustrated and decorated Latin books of late antiquity, 4th–7th century, in rustic capitals and uncial: Vergilius Vaticanus, St Augustine Gospels, Codex Argenteus.
note: Wikidata 'art of Late Antique illumination'; no English Wikipedia article

label: Insular Illumination
defn: Manuscript art of Ireland and Britain, c. 600–900, joining Celtic, Germanic and Mediterranean ornament in carpet pages and great initials: Book of Durrow, Lindisfarne Gospels, Book of Kells, Book of Armagh.
note: pool QIDs Q612118 Q13522717; ornament-led, so C2 not A1 (P1)

label: Merovingian Illumination
defn: Book decoration of Frankish Gaul, 7th–8th century, with zoomorphic initials of fish and birds: Gellone Sacramentary, Gelasian Sacramentary.
note: pool QID Q1776421; attested by the manuscripts section of the article

label: Carolingian Illumination
defn: Manuscript painting of the Frankish empire, c. 780–900, in its court and monastic schools: Godescalc Evangelistary, Coronation Gospels, Utrecht Psalter, Codex Aureus of St. Emmeram.
note: pool QIDs Q614082 Q1734271; Ada, Palace, Reims, Tours and Metz schools are kinds by the field

label: Ottonian Illumination
defn: Manuscript painting of the Ottonian empire, c. 950–1050, at Reichenau, Trier, Echternach, Cologne and Regensburg: Gospels of Otto III, Pericopes of Henry II, Registrum Gregorii, Bamberg Apocalypse.
note: Ottonian illumination redirects to Ottonian art#Manuscripts

label: Anglo-Saxon Illumination
defn: Late Anglo-Saxon manuscript art, 10th–11th century, in the acanthus-bordered Winchester style and in outline drawing: Benedictional of St Æthelwold, Harley Psalter, Ramsey Psalter.
note: Wikidata 'art of Anglo-Saxon illumination'

label: Mozarabic Illumination
defn: Manuscript painting of early medieval Christian Iberia, 10th–11th century, in flat banded colour, above all the illustrated commentaries of Beatus of Liébana: Morgan Beatus, Gerona Beatus, León Bible of 960.
aliases: Spanish illumination of the Early Middle Ages;Visigothic illumination
attest: wiki:Spanish illumination of the Early Middle Ages
note: pool QIDs Q1951304 Q18214676

label: Romanesque Illumination
defn: Manuscript painting of Latin Europe c. 1050–1200, with large-format Bibles and monumental figure style: Bury Bible, Winchester Bible, St Albans Psalter, Hortus deliciarum.
see: T134 Gothic Book Illustration (artist);T157 Mosan Art (artist);L2-43
note: Wikidata 'art of Romanesque illumination'; no dedicated English article

label: Renaissance Illumination
defn: Manuscript illumination of the 15th–16th century influenced by Renaissance painting, in Italy, France and the courts that collected it: Farnese Hours, Bible of Borso d'Este, Hours of Étienne Chevalier, Corvinian manuscripts.
see: T134 Gothic Book Illustration (artist);T135 Ghent-Bruges School (artist)
note: pool QID Q998631

label: Hebrew Illuminated Manuscripts
defn: Decorated and illustrated Hebrew books of the Middle Ages and early modern period — Bibles, haggadot and mahzorim — with micrography and painted cycles: Sarajevo Haggadah, Golden Haggadah, Birds' Head Haggadah, Rothschild Miscellany.
note: Wikidata 'art of Jewish illumination'; Ashkenazi, Sephardi, Italian and French-Provençal rows are kinds

label: Russian Illuminated Manuscripts
defn: Gospel books, chronicles and service books of Kievan Rus' and Muscovy, 11th–17th century, with Byzantine-derived miniatures and teratological headpieces and initials: Ostromir Gospels, Khitrovo Gospels, Radziwiłł Chronicle.
note: label after O. Popova, Russian Illuminated Manuscripts (1984); see also nlr.ru Old Russian Manuscripts; routed europe_folk_east rows (Old Russian illumination, Old Believer Vyg/Pomor book painting) attach here

label: Fraktur
defn: Illuminated folk documents of the Pennsylvania Germans, 18th–19th century, lettered in a broken script and painted with birds, hearts and tulips: Taufschein (birth and baptismal certificates), Vorschrift (writing samples).
note: settler North American folk tradition (see problems)

label: Gothic Ivories
defn: Elephant-ivory carving of Gothic Europe, c. 1200–1530, led by Parisian workshops: devotional diptychs and polyptychs, statuettes of the Virgin, mirror cases and caskets with romance scenes.
note: attested by the Courtauld Gothic Ivories Project; evidence: met/aic 'North French' (ivories 27) and 'North French, Upper Rhenish'

label: Scrimshaw
defn: Engraving and carving on whale teeth, whalebone and walrus ivory by sailors of the whaling fleets, 18th–19th century: engraved sperm-whale teeth, busks, jagging wheels.

label: Neapolitan Nativity Scene
defn: Elaborate crèches of 18th-century Naples, with articulated figures of terracotta heads on tow bodies, dressed in silk, set among angels, Magi's retinues and street life: Met Neapolitan Baroque Crèche, Presepe Cuciniello.
note: also https://www.metmuseum.org/exhibitions/christmas-tree-and-neapolitan-baroque-creche

label: Wildfowl Decoys
defn: Carved and painted wooden decoys of ducks, geese and shorebirds made by North American hunters and carvers, 19th–20th century, collected as folk sculpture: Shang Wheeler's black duck, Elmer Crowell's shorebirds.
note: American Folk Art Museum collection category 'Wildfowl Decoys'; also MoMA 1932 catalogue American Folk Art

label: Weathervanes
defn: American weathervanes of carved wood and moulded sheet copper, 18th–19th century, and the related whirligigs, collected as folk sculpture: Ames and Dexter heart-and-hand vane, J. W. Fiske and Cushing copper horses.
note: whirligigs a kind; placed in D5 as images, whatever the metal or wood

label: Maiolica
defn: Tin-glazed earthenware of Renaissance Italy, painted in high-temperature colours, from Florentine and Faentine wares to the istoriato of Urbino and the lustre of Deruta and Gubbio: Deruta lustre dishes, Urbino istoriato plates, albarelli.
note: routed europe_folk_west rows 'maiolica' and 'Deruta maiolica' attach here

label: Faience
defn: Tin-glazed earthenware of France and its neighbours from the 16th century, made in named centres: Nevers blue-ground wares, Rouen lambrequin dishes, Moustiers grotesques.
note: French centres are kinds

label: Delftware
defn: Tin-glazed earthenware of Delft and the Netherlands, 17th–18th century, painted in blue in imitation of Chinese porcelain, and its English counterpart: tulip vases, tile pictures, blue-and-white chargers.
note: routed europe_folk_west row 'delftware' attaches here

label: Saint-Porchaire Ware
defn: Rare French lead-glazed white earthenware of the mid-16th century, inlaid with coloured clays and modelled in Mannerist forms: salts, ewers, candlesticks.

label: Staffordshire Pottery
defn: The pottery of the Staffordshire Potteries, 17th–19th century: slipware, salt-glazed and creamware tablewares, Wedgwood's jasper and basalt, transfer-printed pearlware and Staffordshire figures: Toft slipware chargers, Wedgwood jasper vases, flatback figures.
note: bodies are mixed (earthenware dominant; jasper and basalt are stoneware): owner check; routed europe_folk_west row 'Jasperware' attaches here as a kind

label: Pennsylvania German Redware
defn: Lead-glazed red earthenware of the Pennsylvania Germans, 18th–19th century, slip-trailed or sgraffito-decorated with tulips and birds: sgraffito plates, slip-decorated pie dishes.
