note: row also names painted dower chests (an I3 seam; kind here pending a furniture leaf)

label: Limoges Porcelain
defn: Hard-paste porcelain made at Limoges from the discovery of kaolin nearby (1768) to the industrial factories of the 19th–20th century (Haviland).
note: leaf made for the routed europe_folk_west row 'Limoges porcelain'; no pool row here

label: Venetian Glass
defn: The glass of Venice and Murano from the 15th century: clear cristallo, enamelled and gilded wares, filigrana (latticino), ice glass and chandeliers: Barovier wedding cup, filigrana goblets, façon de Venise.
note: Murano glass redirects here

label: Bohemian Glass
defn: Glass of Bohemia from the late 17th century, potash-lime crystal decorated by wheel-engraving and cutting, later with coloured and cased glass: engraved goblets, Zwischengoldglas, Biedermeier cased glass.

label: La Tène Art
defn: The curvilinear art of the Iron Age Celts, c. 450 BC to the Roman conquest, chiefly in bronze and gold metalwork: Basse-Yutz flagons, Waldalgesheim style torcs, Battersea Shield.
note: attested in the art section of the culture article; label is the field's style name (Jacobsthal)

label: Migration Period Art
defn: The metalwork of the Germanic peoples, c. 300–800, in polychrome garnet cloisonné and the interlaced animal styles I and II: brooches and fibulae, Lombard gold-foil crosses, Visigothic votive crowns of Guarrazar.
note: Frankish, Lombard, Visigothic and East Germanic rows are kinds; routed ancient_world rows (Migration, East Germanic or nomadic, East German Byzantine, Langobardic Roman, Ottonian Byzantine) attach here

label: Anglo-Saxon Metalwork
defn: Metalwork of Anglo-Saxon England, 5th–11th century, from garnet-cloisonné and filigree gold to Trewhiddle-style silver: Sutton Hoo great buckle, Staffordshire Hoard, Fuller Brooch.
note: Anglo-Saxon metalwork redirects to Anglo-Saxon art#Metalwork

label: Viking Art
defn: The animal-ornament art of Scandinavia and its settlements, c. 750–1100, in its succession of styles named after finds (Oseberg, Borre, Jelling, Mammen, Ringerike, Urnes), chiefly in metal and wood: Oseberg ship carvings, Mammen axe, Urnes stave church portal.
note: routed europe_folk_west row 'Viking art' attaches here; style phases are kinds by the field, not seeded (no evidence rows)

label: South Staffordshire Enamels
defn: English painted enamel on copper of c. 1750–1800 from Bilston, Wednesbury, Birmingham and London (popularly 'Battersea enamels'): snuffboxes, étuis, patch boxes, cassolettes.
note: Met culture term 'British, South Staffordshire'

label: Ormolu
defn: Fire-gilt bronze of 17th–19th-century France and its imitators, cast and chased for furniture mounts, clocks and candelabra, and for mounting Chinese and Japanese porcelain: mounted porcelain vases, Gouthière candelabra.
note: leaf made for routed east_asia rows (Chinese porcelain with French and London mounts); no pool row here

label: Milanese Armour
defn: Plate armour of Milan, the leading European centre from c. 1400 to the 16th century (the Missaglia and Negroli families), from smooth white harness to embossed parade armour all'antica: Avant armour, Negroli burgonets.
note: no English Wikipedia article; attested by Met catalogue text

label: Fabergé
defn: The jewellery and objets de luxe of the House of Fabergé in St Petersburg and Moscow, 1842–1918, in guilloché enamel, gold and hardstone: Imperial Easter eggs, cigarette cases, hardstone animals.
note: leaf made for the routed europe_folk_east row 'Fabergé egg'; workmasters are kinds by P9

label: Ceinture Fléchée
defn: The finger-woven wool sash of French Canada and the Métis, with its arrow (flèche) and lightning patterns, an element of Quebec's intangible heritage: Assomption sashes.
note: pool QID Q56551063

label: Flemish Tapestry
defn: Tapestry woven in the Southern Netherlands, 14th–17th century, at Arras, Tournai, Brussels, Oudenaarde and Antwerp, after cartoons by leading painters: Apocalypse of Angers, Unicorn tapestries, Acts of the Apostles after Raphael.
note: also wiki:Brussels tapestry for the Brussels kind

label: Aubusson Tapestry
defn: Tapestry and carpet weaving of Aubusson and Felletin in the Creuse, from the 16th century to its 20th-century revival (Lurçat), inscribed by UNESCO in 2009.
note: leaf made for the routed europe_folk_west row 'Aubusson tapestry'

label: Opus Anglicanum
defn: English medieval embroidery in silk and gold thread, c. 1200–1400, prized across Europe for vestments: Syon Cope, Butler-Bowdon Cope, Steeple Aston Cope.
note: leaf made for the routed europe_folk_west row 'Opus Anglicanum'

label: Bucks Point Lace
defn: English bobbin lace of Buckinghamshire and the East Midlands, 18th–19th century, a point-ground lace in the manner of Lille and Mechlin.
see: D2-11 Brussels Lace, D2-12 Mechlin Lace, D5-92 Honiton Lace (europe_folk_west)
note: bobbin lace sits in H4 for want of a lace sub-family (see problems)

label: Bedfordshire Lace
defn: English bobbin lace of the Midlands from the mid-19th century, a guipure lace of plaits and leaves influenced by Maltese lace.

label: Amish Quilts
defn: Pieced quilts of the Amish of Pennsylvania and the Midwest, c. 1870–1950, in solid dark colours and bold geometric fields with fine quilting: Center Diamond, Bars, Sunshine and Shadow.
see: T158 Quilts of Gee's Bend (artist);G3-20 Star Quilts (north_america_indigenous)
note: also americanart.si.edu Pattern and Paradox: The Quilts of Amish Women

label: Hooked Rugs
defn: Rugs and mats made by hooking strips of cloth or yarn through a backing, in New England and the Canadian Maritimes from the 19th century, including the Grenfell mats of Labrador and Newfoundland.
note: not needlework strictly; placed in H4 with the needle-based techniques

label: Sweetgrass Baskets
defn: Coiled baskets of sweetgrass, bulrush and pine needle sewn with palmetto by the Gullah Geechee of the South Carolina Lowcountry, a West African coiling tradition: fanner baskets, sewing baskets.

label: Tramp Art
defn: American and European woodwork of c. 1870–1940 built up from notch-carved layers of cigar-box and crate wood: boxes, frames, miniature furniture.
note: pool QID Q7833175

label: Franco-Cantabrian Cave Art
defn: Upper Palaeolithic painted and engraved cave art of south-western France and northern Spain, c. 40,000–11,000 BP: Chauvet, Lascaux, Altamira, Font-de-Gaume.
note: UNESCO Cave of Altamira and Paleolithic Cave Art of Northern Spain; Vézère Valley

label: Côa Valley and Siega Verde Rock Art
defn: Open-air Upper Palaeolithic engravings of animals on schist outcrops in the Côa valley (Portugal) and at Siega Verde (Spain), c. 25,000–10,000 BP: Canada do Inferno, Penascosa, Ribeira de Piscos.
attest: wiki:Prehistoric Rock Art Sites in the Côa Valley and Siega Verde

label: Levantine Rock Art
defn: Post-Palaeolithic naturalistic rock painting of eastern Spain, c. 8000–3500 BC, with hunting, warfare and gathering scenes in shelters: Cova dels Cavalls, Roca dels Moros (Cogul), Valltorta.
aliases: Rock Art of the Mediterranean Basin on the Iberian Peninsula;Levantine art
note: UNESCO 874

label: Iberian Schematic Art
defn: Schematic rock painting and engraving of the Iberian peninsula, c. 5000–1000 BC, associated with the first farming and metal-using cultures: anthropomorphs and idols, Galician petroglyphs of Os Mouchos and Portela da Laxe.
note: Galician (Atlantic) petroglyphs in the row are a seam with Cup and Ring Marks

label: Cup and Ring Marks
defn: Neolithic and Bronze Age carvings of cups and concentric rings on outcrops and standing stones of Atlantic Europe, above all Britain and Ireland: Cochno Stone, Achnabreck, Roughting Linn.
note: pool QID Q373661

label: Rock Carvings in Tanum
defn: Bronze Age rock carvings of Bohuslän in western Sweden, c. 1700–500 BC, with ships, warriors, ploughing scenes and weddings: Vitlycke panel, Aspeberget, Fossum.
note: Scandinavian rock carvings row is a place bucket (no attested umbrella)

label: Rock Carvings at Alta
defn: Rock carvings of hunter-fisher communities at Alta in Finnmark, c. 5000 BC – AD 0, with reindeer, elk, boats and bear hunts: Hjemmeluft, Bergbukten, Amtmannsnes.

label: Petroglyphs of Lake Onega and the White Sea
defn: Neolithic petroglyphs of Russian Karelia, c. 4000–2000 BC, on the shores of Lake Onega (swans, solar signs, the 'demon') and at Zalavruga on the White Sea (hunting and boat scenes).
attest: wiki:Petroglyphs of Lake Onega and the White Sea
note: UNESCO 2021

label: Ural Pictograms
defn: Red-ochre rock paintings (pisanitsy) on river cliffs of the Urals, Neolithic to Iron Age, with animals, figures and signs: Ignatievskaya Cave, Tagil pisanitsa.
note: pool QID Q4476738; Kapova (Shulgan-Tash) Cave in the row is Palaeolithic: a seam

label: Rock Drawings in Valcamonica
defn: Petroglyphs of the Camunni in the Val Camonica (Lombardy), from the Epipalaeolithic to the Iron Age and beyond: Bedolina Map, Camunian rose, Naquane.
note: UNESCO 94

label: Romanesque Wall Painting
defn: Fresco programmes of Romanesque churches, c. 1000–1200: Sant Climent de Taüll, Saint-Savin-sur-Gartempe, San Isidoro, León, Sant'Angelo in Formis.
note: Romanesque wall painting redirects to Romanesque art#Wall painting; routed in_situ row 'mural - United States (medieval)' (Spanish Romanesque frescoes in US museums) attaches here

label: Gothic Wall Painting
defn: Wall painting in Gothic churches and palaces, 13th–15th century, north of the Alps and in the Adriatic: Albi Cathedral, Saint-Sernin, Beram and Hrastovlje Danse macabre, Albertus Pictor's Swedish churches.
note: Wikidata 'Gothic mural'; Italian Trecento frescoes are artist-led

label: Painted Churches of Northern Moldavia
defn: The 15th–16th-century churches of Bukovina painted inside and out with Byzantine-derived cycles under Stephen the Great and Petru Rareș: Voroneț Last Judgement, Humor, Sucevița, Moldovița.
note: enwiki Painted churches of northern Moldavia redirects to Churches of Moldavia; UNESCO 598

label: Scottish Renaissance Painted Ceilings
defn: Tempera-painted timber ceilings of Scottish houses and castles, c. 1550–1650, with emblems, grotesques and heraldry: Prestongrange, Aberdour Castle, Culross Palace.
note: pool QID Q7437936

label: Murals in Northern Ireland
defn: Loyalist and republican political murals painted on gable walls in Northern Ireland since the early 20th century and above all from the 1970s: Falls Road murals, Bogside Artists, King Billy murals.
note: pool QID Q1144161

label: Azulejo
defn: Painted tin-glazed tile panels covering walls of churches, palaces and streets in Portugal, Spain and Brazil from the 16th century: Palace of the Marquises of Fronteira, São Bento station, Valencian ceramic retables.
note: P2: placed in L3 as a revetment studied on the wall; pool QID Q3179385; routed europe_folk_west row 'azulejo' attaches here

label: Trencadís
defn: Mosaic of broken tile and crockery shards laid on curved surfaces, the cladding of Catalan Modernisme (Gaudí, Jujol): Park Güell, Casa Batlló, Hospital de Sant Pau.
note: pool QID Q2476034; routed europe_folk_west row 'Catalan modernism' belongs to T168 Art Nouveau (Modernisme a kind), not here

label: Portuguese Pavement
defn: Patterned pavement of black basalt and white limestone setts laid by hand in Portugal and its former colonies since the 19th century: Rossio waves, Copacabana promenade.
note: pool QID Q616484

label: Soviet Mosaics
defn: Monumental mosaics on public buildings, metro stations and housing of the Soviet Union and its republics, 1920s–1991, a state programme of monumental art: Kyiv and Donetsk school mosaics, Yerevan facade mosaics.
note: no English Wikipedia article; modern and tradition-led (anonymous collective commissions)

label: Hill Figures
defn: Figures cut into hillsides to expose the chalk or limestone beneath, mainly in southern England, from the Bronze Age (Uffington) to the 18th–19th-century white horses: Uffington White Horse, Cerne Abbas Giant, Long Man of Wilmington.
note: pool QID Q2918952

label: Sailor Tattoos
defn: The Western tattoo tradition of sailors and its prison and street derivatives, which grew into the American traditional style of bold outlines and limited colour (Sailor Jerry): swallows, anchors, pin-ups.
note: exemplar QIDs Q613135 (American traditional), Q7400437, Q7245794

label: Reverse Glass Painting
defn: Folk pictures painted in reverse on the back of a glass pane, made in glassworks districts of Austria, Bavaria and Bohemia from the 18th century and sold at fairs and shrines: Sandl devotional pictures with the Sandl rose, saints and Madonnas for the home altar.
note: West slice holds the Alpine/Danubian folk tradition; eastern glass icons are a seam with europe_folk_east

label: Duodji
defn: The handicraft of the Sámi of Norway, Sweden, Finland and the Kola peninsula, divided into hard duodji (antler, bone and wood) and soft duodji (leather, textiles and pewter-thread embroidery): antler-handled knives, carved drinking cups (guksi), pewter-thread embroidered bags.
note: placed in D2 because carved antler and bone is its core; soft duodji is a kind group

label: Processional Giants
defn: Huge carried effigies of giants, animals and dragons, built of wicker, wood and papier-mâché and paraded at town festivals of the Low Countries, northern France and Iberia: gegants of Catalonia, giants of Flanders and Wallonia, Jas de Keistamper of Boxtel.

label: Estremoz Clay Figures
defn: Small modelled and painted clay figures of Estremoz in the Alentejo, made since the 17th century, first for nativity scenes and then of saints and rural types in regional dress: presépios, Primavera, Amor é cego.
aliases: Bonecos de Estremoz;figurado de barro de Estremoz
note: UNESCO 2017

label: Gákti
defn: The dress of the Sámi, a tunic of wool or reindeer skin trimmed with woven bands and coloured cloth whose cut and colours mark region and family: Kautokeino gákti, four-winds hat.

label: Bunad
defn: The regional folk costumes of Norway, revived and standardised from local dress since the late 19th century, with embroidered bodices, aprons and silver brooches (sølje): Vest-Telemark bunad, Hardanger bunad.
see: H7-6 Swedish Folk Costume;H7-7 Tracht;H4-49 Hardanger Embroidery

label: Swedish Folk Costume
defn: The parish costumes of Sweden, worn and revived as signs of local and national identity, with embroidered bodices, pockets and headdresses: Dalarna costumes, Leksand and Rättvik dress.
note: Dalarna and Nås costume rows were excluded below the inclusion rule

label: Tracht
defn: The regional folk dress of the German-speaking Alps and southern Germany, made and worn in local forms with their own headdresses, bodices and embroidery: Bregenzerwald Juppe, Lake Constance Radhaube, Gailtal costume.

label: Greek Island Embroidery
defn: The silk-on-linen embroidery of the Aegean and Ionian islands and Epirus (17th–19th century), each island with its own stitches and designs, used for bed curtains, cushions and dress: Cretan skirt borders, Rhodian bed tents, Naxos and Dodecanese hangings.
note: Met-collection study; Ashmolean "Aegean Legacies" also uses the term; lace is a kind group

label: Hardanger Embroidery
defn: Norwegian whitework of counted satin-stitch blocks (kloster) with cut and drawn threads, from the Hardanger district, used on bunad aprons and linens.

label: Mountmellick Embroidery
defn: Irish white embroidery of raised floral designs in thick cotton on white cotton satin, begun in Mountmellick, County Laois, about 1825 by Johanna Carter.

label: Arraiolos Rug
defn: Portuguese wool rugs embroidered in Slav (long-armed cross) stitch on linen or jute canvas, made in Arraiolos in the Alentejo since the 17th century.
note: needlework rug: H4 by technique, not H1

label: Bordados da Glória do Ribatejo
defn: The embroidery of Glória do Ribatejo (Salvaterra de Magos), worked mainly in cross stitch on household linens and local dress.
note: QID only; narrow

label: Alençon Lace
defn: French needle lace of Alençon in Normandy, developed in the 1660s under royal patronage and made into the 19th century, with fine réseau ground and corded outlines: flounces, lappets.
note: luxury lace industry (P10 urban); UNESCO 2010

label: Burano Lace
defn: Venetian needle lace of the island of Burano, revived in 1872 by the Burano lace school on the model of the old Venetian points.
note: enwiki redirect goes to Argentella; QID used

label: Lefkara Lace
defn: The drawn-thread and needle-lace embroidery of Pano Lefkara in Cyprus, worked on linen in geometric designs (UNESCO 2009).

label: Brussels Lace
defn: Pillow lace of Brussels and Brabant, its motifs made separately in bobbin or needle lace and joined to a droschel or bride ground (17th–19th century), including point de gaze and Brussels appliqué.

label: Mechlin Lace
defn: Flemish bobbin lace of Mechelen with a hexagonal ground and a flat thread outlining the motifs, the 18th century's favourite lace for ruffles.

label: Quill Embroidery
defn: Embroidery of leather with split quills of peacock tail feathers on belts, braces and shoes of Alpine dress, practised in Tyrol (Sarntal) and Austria.
note: Austrian ICH; https://www.unesco.at lists it

label: Honiton Lace
defn: English bobbin lace of east Devon whose motifs are made separately and joined, famed for Queen Victoria's wedding lace (1840).

label: Le Puy Lace
defn: Bobbin lace of Le Puy-en-Velay in the Auvergne, in linen, silk and wool guipures and Cluny-style laces made by cottage lacemakers.
note: no enwiki article; QID

label: Maltese Lace
defn: Bobbin lace of Malta and Gozo, above all the 19th-century silk guipure with the Maltese cross and wheatears.

label: Headford Lace
defn: The bobbin lace of Headford, County Galway, a cottage industry of the 18th–19th centuries revived today.
note: QID only; narrow

label: Carrickmacross Lace
defn: Irish appliqué lace of County Monaghan, cambric shapes cut and sewn on machine net, introduced about 1820 by Mrs Grey Porter.
see: H4-64 Limerick Lace;H4-65 Irish Crochet Lace

label: Limerick Lace
defn: Irish embroidered net lace of Limerick (from 1829), worked in tambour (chain stitch) or run (darning) stitch on machine net.

label: Irish Crochet Lace
defn: Crochet made in imitation of Venetian needle lace, spread as famine relief from the 1840s; motifs are worked separately and joined with a crocheted mesh: Clones lace, Youghal-area crochet.

label: Blaudruck
defn: Resist block printing and indigo dyeing of linen and cotton, carried on by family dye-works of Central Europe (UNESCO 2018, Austria, Czechia, Germany, Hungary, Slovakia): Burgenland blueprint, Mühlviertel indigo printing.
note: multinational; East slice may hold its centres as kinds

label: Staphorster Stipwerk
defn: Dot printing of Staphorst in Overijssel: coloured patterns stamped with pin-headed stamps on cloth for the village dress (kraplap, caps).
note: nl wiki Staphorster stipwerk

label: Freest Fisherman's Carpets
defn: Knotted carpets designed and made since the 1920s on the coast of the Bay of Greifswald (Freest, Western Pomerania), with motifs of fish, birds and sea.
note: German ICH; narrow

label: Panier de Mayun
defn: The willow and bramble baskets of Mayun in the Brière marshes (Loire-Atlantique).
note: French ICH; QID only

label: Bastabinne
defn: Swedish baskets plaited from strips of spruce bast.
note: Swedish ICH; QID only

label: Talavera de la Reina Pottery
defn: Tin-glazed earthenware of Talavera de la Reina and El Puente del Arzobispo in Castile from the 16th century, in blue-and-white and polychrome, for tableware, apothecary jars and tile panels (UNESCO 2019, with Puebla): serie tricolor, Puente del Arzobispo green-and-ochre ware.

label: Bisalhães Black Pottery
defn: Black earthenware of Bisalhães near Vila Real, burnished and fired in a smothered pit kiln (soenga), for cooking and decoration (UNESCO urgent safeguarding 2016).

label: Gmundner Keramik
defn: Earthenware of Gmunden on the Traunsee, made since the 15th century, best known for its 'flamed' (geflammt) slip decoration in green, blue or brown.

label: Émaux de Longwy
defn: Faience of Longwy in Lorraine decorated since the 1870s with coloured enamels filled into printed outlines in the manner of cloisonné.
note: French ICH

label: Rhenish Stoneware
defn: Salt-glazed stoneware of the Rhineland centres (Siegburg, Raeren, Frechen, Cologne, Westerwald), 15th–19th century, exported across Europe and its colonies: Bartmann (Bellarmine) jugs, Westerwald blue-and-grey tankards.
note: Met and V&A use the term; no enwiki article (Westerwald pottery has one)

label: Art of Glass Beads
defn: Venetian and French lampwork and drawn glass beadmaking (perle veneziane), inscribed by UNESCO in 2020 for Italy and France.
note: label is the UNESCO element name

label: Hairwork
defn: Jewellery and pictures worked from human hair, a 19th-century fashion carried on as a village craft in Vamhus, Dalarna.
note: in G3 by function (worn as ornament)

label: Petrykivka Painting
defn: Ornamental painting of the village of Petrykivka (Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Ukraine) with flowers, berries and birds brushed with fingers, cat-hair brushes and reeds on house walls, paper sheets and wooden objects (UNESCO 2013): painted malyovky sheets, painted chests and plates.

label: Tauric Painting
defn: Traditional decorative painting of Mykolaiv Oblast in southern Ukraine, inscribed on the National Inventory of Intangible Cultural Heritage of Ukraine.
note: recent Ukrainian ICH item; English label from Wikidata only

label: Gorodets Painting
defn: Painting of the Gorodets district on the Volga from the mid-19th century, first on distaff bottoms and later on boards, boxes and furniture, with horsemen, ladies, birds and roses in a quick brush style on bright grounds: distaff bottoms (donce), painted panels.

label: Mezen Painting
defn: Red-and-black painting on distaffs, boxes and ladles from the lower Mezen River (Arkhangelsk region), with rows of horses, deer and birds in a graphic, archaic style: Palashchelye distaffs.

label: Northern Dvina Painting
defn: The painting of distaffs, chests and utensils in the villages along the Northern Dvina (Arkhangelsk region), in local styles with red floral grounds, birds, sirins and scenes of sleighing: Borok distaffs, Permogorye distaffs, Rakulka distaffs.
note: kinds Permogorsk (Q4351485) and Borok (Q4093621) in kinds.csv

label: Ural-Siberian Painting
defn: Floral painting of the Old Believer and peasant households of the Urals and western Siberia (18th–19th century) on furniture, chests, walls and utensils, with large peonies and roses in a free brush.

label: Zhostovo Painting
defn: Oil painting of flower bouquets on black-lacquered iron trays made in Zhostovo near Moscow since the early 19th century, built up in layers and varnished: bouquet trays, gilded-rim trays.
see: Nizhny Tagil Tray Painting;I2 Russian lacquer miniatures
note: painted metal tray; placed with folk painting (A6) rather than G1

label: Nizhny Tagil Tray Painting
defn: Painted and lacquered iron trays made in Nizhny Tagil in the Urals from the 18th century, with flowers and genre scenes under a translucent varnish, the forerunner of Zhostovo.

label: Naïve Painting of Kovačica
defn: Naïve painting of the Slovak community of Kovačica in Vojvodina (Serbia) from the 1950s, in oil on canvas and on objects, with village life, harvests and weddings (UNESCO 2024).
aliases: Kovačica naive art;Slovak naive art painting

label: Pysanka
defn: Easter eggs decorated in the Slavic and East European wax-resist (batik) technique with layered dyes and symbolic patterns; regional schools and related types (krashanka, krapanka, drapanka) are kinds: Hutsul pysanky, Boyko pysanky.
note: no family fits eggshell; placed in A6 as painted folk work (see problems)

label: Lubok
defn: Russian popular prints from the 17th to the early 20th century, first woodcuts then copper engravings and lithographs, hand-coloured and sold at fairs, with saints, folk tales, satire and the Mice Burying the Cat: The Mice Burying the Cat, Baba Yaga.

label: Vytsinanka
defn: Belarusian folk paper cutting, symmetrical designs cut with scissors from folded paper for interiors and festivals (UNESCO 2024).
note: Polish wycinanki (Kurpie, Łowicz) are below inclusion in this pool

label: Slovenian Paper Flower Making
defn: The Slovenian craft of making crepe and tissue paper flowers for church feasts, processions and festive decoration.
note: label from the Register of the Intangible Cultural Heritage in Slovenia

label: Uelen Bone Carving
defn: Engraving and carving of walrus ivory by Chukchi and Yupik carvers at Uelen in Chukotka, institutionalised as a workshop in 1931: engraved walrus tusks with hunting scenes, small figures of walrus and bears.
note: also damuseum.ru (All-Russian Museum of Decorative Art) bone-carving catalogue

label: Tobolsk Bone Carving
defn: Bone and mammoth-ivory carving of Tobolsk in western Siberia from the 18th century, with small sculptures of northern life (reindeer sleds, hunters); a factory since 1929.
note: see also https://damuseum.ru/en/catalog/wood-and-bone/khudozhestvennaya-reznaya-kost-xvii-kontsa-khkh-vekov/

label: Yakut Bone Carving
defn: Mammoth-ivory carving of the Sakha (Yakutia), from 19th-century combs and caskets to Soviet-era sculptural compositions combined with silver and leather.

label: Matryoshka Doll
defn: Russian nesting dolls of turned and painted lime wood, first made at the Abramtsevo circle in 1890 (Malyutin, Zvyozdochkin) and then in Sergiev Posad, Semyonov and Polkhovsky Maidan.

label: Polkhovsky Maidan
defn: Turned and brightly painted wooden toys and matryoshkas of Polkhovsky Maidan (Nizhny Novgorod region), with large aniline-coloured flowers over ink outlines.

label: Bogorodskoye Carving
defn: Carved lime-wood toys and figures of the village of Bogorodskoye near Sergiev Posad, often with moving parts: the Blacksmiths (bear and peasant), pecking hens.

label: Dymkovo Toys
defn: Moulded, whitewashed and brightly painted clay figures of the Dymkovo settlement near Vyatka (Kirov): ladies in crinolines, turkeys, water-carriers.

label: Filimonovo Toys
defn: Clay whistles and figures of Filimonovo (Tula region) with elongated bodies painted in stripes of red, green and yellow.

label: Kargopol Toys
defn: Clay figures of the Kargopol district (Arkhangelsk region), squat and painted in earth colours: Polkan, bereginya, peasant figures (Babkin family).

label: Abashevo Toys
defn: Clay whistles of Abashevo (Penza region) shaped as goats, deer and rams with long necks and horns, glazed or painted.

label: Yavoriv Toy
defn: Turned and painted wooden toys of Yavoriv in Lviv Oblast (Ukraine): carts, horses and rattles painted in red, green and black.

label: Valky Whistle Toy
defn: Small ceramic whistle toys of the town of Valky (Kharkiv Oblast, Ukraine).

label: Wooden Toys of Hrvatsko Zagorje
defn: Hand-carved and painted willow and lime-wood toys of Hrvatsko Zagorje (Croatia), sold at pilgrimage fairs (UNESCO 2009).

label: Pauper Statues
defn: Carved and painted wooden figures of beggars holding alms boxes placed outside Lutheran churches in Finland and Sweden, 18th–19th century.

label: Khachkar
defn: Armenian carved memorial stones bearing a cross over a rosette or sun disc, surrounded by lace-like interlace, from the 9th century (Noratus, Julfa): Amenaprkich khachkar.
note: UNESCO 2010 (symbolism and craftsmanship of khachkars)

label: Lithuanian Cross Crafting
defn: Lithuanian making of wooden crosses, roofed poles and shrines with carved figures of saints (rūpintojėlis), set at roadsides and farms (UNESCO 2008).

label: Izraztsy
defn: Russian glazed and relief stove and wall tiles from the 16th to the 19th century — terracotta, polychrome 'peacock-eye' relief tiles and painted Dutch-style tiles — for tiled stoves and church façades.
note: attestation weak (commercial history page); Wikidata stove tile Q19921342 generic

label: Skopin Ceramics
defn: Glazed earthenware of Skopin (Ryazan region) since the 19th century, with fantastic sculptural vessels in the form of birds, beasts and dragons under green and brown glazes.

label: Balkhar Pottery
defn: Hand-built earthenware of the Lak village of Balkhar (Dagestan), made by women and painted in white engobe with free linear ornament.
note: attestation weak (news page); ru-wiki Балхарская керамика redirects to Balkhar

label: Opishnia Ceramics
defn: The pottery of Opishnia (Poltava Oblast, Ukraine) with painted engobe ornament and sculptural vessels and toys (barany, lions).

label: Kosiv Painted Ceramics
defn: Engobe-painted earthenware of Kosiv and the Hutsul region (Ukraine), with green, yellow and brown sgraffito-painted scenes of Hutsul life on a white ground (UNESCO 2019).

label: Sokal Ceramics
defn: Traditional painted ceramics of Sokal in Lviv Oblast (Ukraine).
note: recent Ukrainian ICH item

label: Bubnivka Ceramics
defn: Painted earthenware of Bubnivka (Vinnytsia Oblast, Ukraine), with dense floral ornament.

label: Oleshnia Pottery
defn: Traditional pottery of Oleshnia in Chernihiv Oblast (Ukraine).

label: Horezu Ceramics
defn: Slip-painted earthenware of Horezu in Oltenia (Romania), decorated with the cock, star and spiral in brown, red, green and blue on cream (UNESCO 2012).

label: Zlakusa Pottery
defn: Unglazed hand-wheel pottery of the village of Zlakusa in western Serbia, of clay mixed with calcite, for cooking pots (UNESCO 2020).

label: Gzhel
defn: Ceramics of the Gzhel district near Moscow, from 18th-century majolica and 19th-century semi-faience to the cobalt blue-and-white porcelain of the 20th century.
note: phases (majolica, faience, porcelain) span E1–E4; placed by the dominant modern porcelain

label: Czech Blown Glass Bead Christmas Decorations
defn: Christmas tree ornaments made by hand from blown glass beads in the Poniklá region of the Czech Republic, silvered, coloured and threaded (UNESCO 2020).
aliases: Rautis decorations;handmade production of Christmas tree decorations from blown glass beads

label: Līvāni Glassblowing
defn: The glassblowing craft of Līvāni in Latvia, centre of Latvian glassmaking since 1887.

label: Kubachi Silver
defn: Silver and metalwork of the Dargin village of Kubachi in Dagestan: engraved, niello and filigree vessels, arms and jewellery with dense floral ornament.
note: not to be confused with E2-9 Kubachi ware (Safavid fritware found at Kubachi)

label: Kasli Iron Casting
defn: Cast-iron sculpture and openwork made at the Kasli works in the Urals since the 19th century: Kasli cast-iron pavilion (Paris 1900), statuettes of horsemen and animals.

label: Finift
defn: Painted enamel on copper of Russia, above all of Rostov the Great from the 18th century: icons, medallions and jewellery painted in enamel colours.

label: Hutsul Metalwork
defn: The brass casting and metal inlay of the Hutsuls of the Carpathians: cast crosses, jewellery, pipes and toporets axes, and brass-inlaid wood (UNESCO-listed in the Ukrainian National Inventory).
aliases: metalworking traditions of the Hutsul region

label: Drotárstvo
defn: Slovak wire craft developed by itinerant tinkers who mended pottery with wire and later made wire objects and sculpture (UNESCO 2023).

label: Puukko
defn: The traditional Finnish belt knife with a wooden or birch-bark handle and leather sheath, made by named smiths (Kauhava, Fiskars).

label: Ryijy
defn: Finnish knotted-pile wall hangings and bed covers with a long shaggy pile, from 18th-century folk ryijys to modern artist-designed rugs.
note: seam with Swedish rya in europe_folk_west

label: Raanu
defn: Finnish weft-faced flatwoven wool coverlet and wall hanging in stripes and geometric patterns.

label: Chiprovtsi Kilim
defn: Tapestry-woven kilims of Chiprovtsi in north-western Bulgaria since the 17th century, with geometric and later floral designs (UNESCO 2014).

label: Pirot Kilim
defn: Double-sided tapestry-woven kilims of Pirot in south-eastern Serbia, with geometric motifs such as the turtle and the vine.

label: Sjenica-Pešter Kilim
defn: Kilims woven on the Pešter plateau around Sjenica in south-western Serbia.
note: label from Serbian ICH inventory

label: Stapar Rugs
defn: Rug-making in the village of Stapar in Vojvodina (Serbia), with floral rugs on dark grounds.

label: Kotsy
defn: Ukrainian woollen flatwoven carpets (kots, kylym) of the Left-Bank and Polissia regions.

label: Reshetylivka Carpets
defn: Handwoven floral carpets of Reshetylivka in Poltava Oblast (Ukraine).

label: Romanian and Moldovan Wall Carpets
defn: Woollen wall carpets (scoarțe, covoare) woven in Romania and the Republic of Moldova and hung in houses as dowry and decoration (UNESCO 2016).

label: Täkänä
defn: Finnish double-weave (Finn-pick) technique giving reversible two-colour cloth, used for coverlets and hangings.
note: attestation weak (Finlandia Foundation course page)

label: Northern Vidzeme Double-Weave Blankets
defn: Double-weave colour-gradient blanket weaving of Northern Vidzeme in Latvia.
note: label from Latvian ICH list

label: Sigulda Belts
defn: Patterned belts woven in Sigulda municipality (Latvia).

label: Bezdan Damask
defn: Damask linen woven in Bezdan (Vojvodina, Serbia) since the 1880s, with pictorial and floral designs.

label: Serpanok Weaving
defn: Weaving of serpanok, a fine gauze-like cloth, in Dubrovytsia hromada (Rivne Oblast, Ukraine).
note: recent Ukrainian ICH item

label: Hlyniany Textile
defn: Patterned woven textiles of Hlyniany (Lviv Oblast, Ukraine), long known for its kilims.
note: recent Ukrainian ICH item

label: Obukhovychi Weaving
defn: Traditional patterned weaving of the village of Obukhovychi (Kyiv Oblast, Ukraine).
note: recent Ukrainian ICH item

label: Ukrainian Embroidery
defn: The regional embroidery of Ukraine on shirts (vyshyvanka), rushnyky and household linen in cross, satin and counted stitches, distinct by region and village: Reshetylivka white-on-white, Borshchiv black shirts, Podillia nyz.

label: Rushnyk
defn: East Slavic ritual cloths of linen embroidered or woven with symbolic red and black ornament, used at weddings, funerals and to dress icons: Krolevets woven rushnyky.

label: Belarusian Embroidery
defn: Embroidery of Belarus on ritual towels, shirts and aprons in counted red geometric ornament, including the Vetka negliubka tradition.

label: Chuvash Embroidery
defn: Counted-thread embroidery of the Chuvash of the Volga in red, black and green on white linen, for headdresses, shirts and ritual cloths.

label: Mari Embroidery
defn: Embroidery of the Mari of the Volga-Kama region, dense red-and-black geometric patterns on shirts and headdresses (shurka, shymaksh).

label: Karelian Embroidery
defn: Embroidery of the Karelians of Finland and Russia, in red counted and drawn work on towels and shirts.

label: Krestets Stitch
defn: Drawn-thread whitework embroidery of Krestsy (Novgorod region) on linen, with geometric openwork grounds.

label: Mstyora Embroidery
defn: White satin-stitch and openwork embroidery of Mstyora (Vladimir region) on batiste and linen.

label: Muhu Embroidery
defn: Embroidery of the Estonian island of Muhu, with bold floral motifs and birds in bright pinks, greens and oranges on black wool.
note: attestation weak (TATTER workshop page)

label: Matyó Embroidery
defn: The embroidery of the Matyó community of Mezőkövesd in Hungary, with dense roses and peonies in bright satin stitch (UNESCO 2012).
aliases: Folk art of the Matyó;Mezőkövesd embroidery

label: Zmijanje Embroidery
defn: Dark-blue wool embroidery on women's dress and household linen of the Zmijanje villages near Banja Luka (UNESCO 2014).

label: Macedonian Embroidery
defn: Embroidery of North Macedonia on women's shirts and sleeves in dense red, black and gold geometric motifs.

label: Kosovo-Style Embroidery
defn: Serbian embroidery in the Kosovo style, inscribed in the Serbian ICH inventory.

label: Altiță
defn: Embroidery on the shoulder band (altiță) of the Romanian and Moldovan traditional blouse (ie), the defining ornament of the costume (UNESCO 2022).

label: Syrian-Armenian Embroidery
defn: The embroidery culture of the Syrian-Armenian community of Armenia (Marash and Aintab traditions), inscribed in Armenia's ICH list.
aliases: Embroidery culture of the Syrian-Armenian community

label: Armenian Needlelace
defn: Knotted needle lace of Armenia and the Armenian diaspora, made with a needle in rows of knots for collars and covers.

label: Tatar Leather Mosaic
defn: The Kazan Tatar technique (kayuly kün) of stitching coloured morocco pieces into mosaic patterns with gold thread, for boots (ichigi) and slippers.
note: leather has no family; placed with appliqué in H4

label: Orenburg Shawl
defn: Knitted lace shawls of goat down from the Orenburg region, including the fine gossamer 'web' shawl that passes through a ring.
note: knitted lace; no knitting sub-family

label: Vologda Lace
defn: Bobbin tape lace of Vologda with continuous tape patterns on a net ground (from the 19th century).
note: Russian lace kinds Vyatka, Mikhailov, Mtsensk are below inclusion

label: Yelets Lace
defn: Fine bobbin tape lace of Yelets (Lipetsk region), with small motifs on delicate grounds.

label: Rauma Lace
defn: Bobbin lace of the town of Rauma in Finland, made since the 18th century with fine linen thread.

label: Lace-Making in Heinämaa
defn: The bobbin lace tradition of the village of Heinämaa in Finland.
note: label from the Finnish National Inventory of Living Heritage

label: Knipelēšana
defn: Latvian bobbin lace-making tradition.

label: Idrija Lace
defn: Bobbin tape lace of Idrija (Slovenia), made since the 17th century with a continuous tape (UNESCO 2018).

label: Lacemaking in Croatia
defn: The lace traditions of Croatia — needle lace of Pag, bobbin lace of Lepoglava and Sveta Marija, aloe-thread lace of Hvar (UNESCO 2009).

label: Pavlovo Posad Shawl
defn: Printed woollen shawls of Pavlovo Posad (Moscow region) since the 1860s, with dense roses and borders, first block-printed then screen-printed.

label: Kelaghayi
defn: Silk headscarves of Azerbaijan (Sheki, Basqal) printed by wooden stamps with resist and natural dyes, with buta motifs (UNESCO 2014).

label: Traditional Albanian Clothing
defn: The regional folk costume of the Albanians, with distinct ensembles by region and community: xhubleta bell-shaped skirt, fustanella, xhamadan vests.

label: Croatian National Costume
defn: The regional folk costumes of Croatia, from Slavonian gold-embroidered dress to Dalmatian and Zagorje ensembles.

label: Macedonian Traditional Clothing
defn: The regional folk costumes of North Macedonia, with heavily embroidered women's shirts and sleeveless coats.

label: Erzya Costume
defn: The traditional dress of the Erzya (Mordvin) people, with embroidered white shirts (panar), pulai hip ornament and headdresses.

label: Birch-Bark Crafts
defn: Containers, boxes, footwear and objects of folded, woven, sewn and carved birch bark made across Finland, Karelia and Russia: tuohikontti backpacks, tuesok boxes, woven bast shoes.

label: Shemogodsk Carving
defn: Openwork carving of birch bark from the Shemoksa river near Veliky Ustyug since the early 19th century, called 'northern lace', on boxes and tuesoks.

label: Pärekori
defn: Finnish baskets plaited from pulled wood shingles (päre).
aliases: shingle basket;making of shingle baskets from pulled shingles

label: Clubrush Work of Kruunupyy
defn: Weaving of clubrush (bulrush) into mats and objects in Kruunupyy (Kronoby), Finland.
note: label from the Finnish wiki-inventory

label: Himmeli
defn: Geometric hanging mobiles of straw tubes threaded together, made at Christmas in Finland and the Baltic (Lithuanian sodai).

label: Straw Weaving in Belarus
defn: Belarusian straw weaving of ritual and decorative objects — figures, baskets, spiders (paŭki) and boxes (UNESCO 2025).

label: Turiisk Straw Plaiting
defn: Straw plaiting tradition of Turiisk hromada in Volyn Oblast (Ukraine).
note: recent Ukrainian ICH item

label: Iza Vine Weaving
defn: Willow-vine basket and furniture weaving of the village of Iza in Zakarpattia (Ukraine).

label: Shchitky Reed Weaving
defn: Reed weaving tradition of Shchitky and Pysarivka (Vinnytsia Oblast, Ukraine).
note: recent Ukrainian ICH item

label: Abramtsevo-Kudrino Carving
defn: Flat relief wood carving of curling floral ornament on boxes, ladles and furniture, created at the Abramtsevo estate workshop by Vasily Vornoskov of Kudrino (late 19th century) and continued at Khotkovo.

label: Untsukul Inlay
defn: Woodwork of the Avar village of Untsukul (Dagestan) inlaid with fine silver and cupronickel wire and plates in geometric patterns: walking sticks, boxes, vases.
note: attestation weak (news page)

label: Hutsul Wood Carving
defn: Carving and inlay of the Hutsuls of the Ukrainian Carpathians — chip carving, beadwork inlay and brass inlay on boxes, plates and crosses (Shkriblyak family).

label: Chernihiv Wood Carving
defn: Traditional artistic wood carving of Chernihiv Oblast (Ukraine).
aliases: artistic wood carving of Chernihiv Oblast
note: recent Ukrainian ICH item

label: Konjic Woodcarving
defn: Woodcarving of Konjic in Bosnia and Herzegovina, with dense floral and geometric relief on furniture and interiors (UNESCO 2017).

label: Kuksa
defn: Carved drinking cups of birch burl made by the Sámi and Finns.
note: seam with europe_folk_west (Sámi duodji)

label: Khokhloma
defn: Painted and varnished turned woodenware of the Nizhny Novgorod region (Semyonov, Khokhloma) since the 17th century, with red and black foliage over a gold-like ground produced by tin powder and oven-hardened varnish: bowls, spoons, ladles.

label: Palekh Miniature
defn: Lacquer miniature painting in egg tempera on black papier-mâché boxes from Palekh, created by former icon painters in 1923 (Golikov), with fairy-tale scenes in gold.

label: Fedoskino Miniature
defn: Lacquer miniature painting in oils on papier-mâché from Fedoskino near Moscow since 1795 (Lukutin factory), with genre scenes over mother-of-pearl and metal-leaf grounds.

label: Mstyora Miniature
defn: Lacquer miniature painting of Mstyora (Vladimir region) from 1923, with landscapes in warm tones and gold ornament on papier-mâché.

label: Kholuy Miniature
defn: Lacquer miniature painting of Kholuy (Ivanovo region) from 1934, by former icon painters, with dense narrative scenes in blue and green.

label: Samchyky Painting
defn: The decorative painting of the walls and interiors of houses in Samchyky village (Khmelnytskyi Oblast, Ukraine), with unique floral patterns.

label: Corpus Christi Flower Carpets
defn: Carpets of flowers laid on the streets of Polish villages (Spycimierz and others) for the Corpus Christi processions (UNESCO 2021).
aliases: Flower carpets tradition for Corpus Christi processions

label: Gothic Revival Architecture
defn: The revival of medieval Gothic forms from the mid-18th century to the early 20th, in churches, colleges, parliaments and houses: the Palace of Westminster, Cologne Cathedral's completion, St Patrick's Cathedral, New York.
see: T181 Gothic Architecture; K2-7 Tudor Revival Architecture
note: enwiki: Gothic Revival architecture; 11158 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Tudor Revival Architecture
defn: The revival of Tudor and Elizabethan domestic forms (half-timbering, tall chimneys, mullioned windows) in late 19th- and 20th-century houses: Jacobethan country houses, mock-Tudor suburban villas.
see: K5-1 Tudor Architecture; K2-6 Gothic Revival Architecture
note: enwiki: Tudor Revival architecture; 1112 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Romanesque Revival Architecture
defn: The 19th-century revival of round-arched Romanesque forms, from the German Rundbogenstil to Richardsonian Romanesque in America: Trinity Church, Boston, the Natural History Museum, London.
see: K4-10 Romanesque Architecture; K2-9 Neo-Byzantine Architecture
note: enwiki: Romanesque Revival architecture; 4598 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Neo-Byzantine Architecture
defn: The 19th–20th-century revival of Byzantine domes, arcades and banded masonry, in Orthodox and Catholic churches and public buildings: Sacré-Cœur, Paris, Westminster Cathedral, Saint Sava, Belgrade.
see: K4-2 Byzantine Architecture; K2-27 Russian Revival Architecture
note: enwiki: Neo-Byzantine architecture; 490 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Renaissance Revival Architecture
defn: The 19th-century revival of Italian, French and Northern Renaissance forms for palaces, banks, museums and civic buildings: the Vienna State Opera, the Reform Club, the Rijksmuseum.
see: T182 Renaissance Architecture; K2-11 Italianate Architecture; K2-12 Second Empire Style
note: enwiki: Renaissance Revival architecture; 5698 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Italianate Architecture
defn: The 19th-century picturesque revival of Italian villa and palazzo forms, with bracketed eaves and towers, popular in Britain and North America: Osborne House, Italianate row houses of San Francisco.
note: enwiki: Italianate architecture; 1828 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Second Empire Style
defn: The Napoleon III-era style of mansard roofs and rich Baroque-Renaissance ornament, spread from Paris to the Americas: the Palais Garnier, Philadelphia City Hall, the Eisenhower Executive Office Building.
aliases: Napoleon III style; Second Empire architecture
see: K2-10 Renaissance Revival Architecture; K2-16 Beaux-Arts Architecture
note: enwiki: Second Empire style; 375 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Baroque Revival Architecture
defn: The late 19th- and early 20th-century revival of Baroque massing and ornament for public buildings and theatres: the Berlin Cathedral, Edwardian Baroque town halls.
see: T183 Baroque Architecture; K2-16 Beaux-Arts Architecture
note: enwiki: Baroque Revival architecture; 1311 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Greek Revival Architecture
defn: The late 18th- and 19th-century revival of Greek temple forms and orders, dominant in the United States and northern Europe: the Second Bank of the United States, the Altes Museum, St George's Hall, Liverpool.
see: T184 Neoclassical Architecture; K3-8 Ancient Greek Architecture
note: enwiki: Greek Revival architecture; 5571 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Egyptian Revival Architecture
defn: The revival of ancient Egyptian pylons, obelisks and lotus columns after Napoleon's Egyptian campaign, in cemeteries, prisons, synagogues and cinemas: the Egyptian Hall, Piccadilly, the Tombs, New York.
note: enwiki: Egyptian Revival architecture; 96 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Beaux-Arts Architecture
defn: The academic classical architecture taught at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris (c. 1830–1920), symmetrical and richly sculpted, carried to the Americas: the Petit Palais, New York Public Library, Grand Central Terminal.
see: K2-12 Second Empire Style; K2-17 Eclecticism in Architecture
note: enwiki: Beaux-Arts architecture; 1175 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Eclecticism in Architecture
defn: Nineteenth- and early 20th-century architecture freely combining historical styles in one building: Gründerzeit apartment blocks, Stile Umbertino palaces of Rome, Russian eclectic mansions.
see: K2-16 Beaux-Arts Architecture; K2-18 Victorian Architecture
note: enwiki: Eclecticism in architecture; 7072 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Victorian Architecture
defn: The succession of revival and picturesque styles built in Britain and its empire and in North America during Victoria's reign (1837–1901): Stick style houses, Eastlake villas, Australian Victorian terraces.
see: K2-6 Gothic Revival Architecture; K2-19 Queen Anne Style Architecture; K2-33 Federation Architecture
note: enwiki: Victorian architecture; 1150 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Queen Anne Style Architecture
defn: The late 19th-century British and American domestic style of red brick or shingle, asymmetrical towers, bays and turrets: Norman Shaw's Swan House, the Carson Mansion.
see: K2-18 Victorian Architecture; K2-20 Shingle Style Architecture
note: enwiki: Queen Anne style architecture; 1078 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Shingle Style Architecture
defn: The American seaside and suburban house style of the 1880s wrapped in continuous wood shingles: the Isaac Bell House, the William Watts Sherman House.
see: K2-19 Queen Anne Style Architecture; K2-21 Colonial Revival Architecture
note: enwiki: Shingle style architecture; 428 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Colonial Revival Architecture
defn: The American (and Brazilian) revival from the 1876 Centennial of colonial Georgian and Dutch forms: Georgian Revival houses, Dutch Colonial Revival gambrel houses.
see: K5-15 American Colonial Architecture; K5-10 Georgian Architecture
note: enwiki: Colonial Revival architecture; 4439 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Spanish Colonial Revival Architecture
defn: The early 20th-century revival of Spanish colonial forms in California, Florida and the American Southwest, after the 1915 Panama–California Exposition: Santa Barbara County Courthouse, the California Building, San Diego.
see: K5-16 Spanish Colonial Architecture; K2-23 Mission Revival Architecture
note: enwiki: Spanish Colonial Revival architecture; 1013 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Mission Revival Architecture
defn: The Californian revival (1890–1920) of the Spanish missions' arcades, curved parapets and bell towers: the Mission Inn, Riverside, the Santa Fe Depot, San Diego.
note: enwiki: Mission Revival architecture; 318 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Pueblo Revival Architecture
defn: The 20th-century revival in New Mexico and Arizona of Pueblo and Spanish adobe forms: the New Mexico Museum of Art, La Fonda on the Plaza.
note: enwiki: Pueblo Revival architecture; 236 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Mayan Revival Architecture
defn: The 1920s–1930s American revival of Maya and Mesoamerican ornament: Frank Lloyd Wright's Hollyhock House, the Mayan Theater, Los Angeles.
note: enwiki: Mayan Revival architecture; 18 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Neo-Manueline
defn: The Portuguese and Brazilian revival (from the 1840s) of Manueline ornament: Pena Palace, Rossio Station, the Royal Portuguese Cabinet of Reading, Rio.
note: enwiki: Neo-Manueline; 15 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Russian Revival Architecture
defn: The 19th-century revival of medieval Muscovite and Byzantine-Russian forms in the Russian Empire: the State Historical Museum, the Church of the Savior on Blood, the Upper Trading Rows.
note: enwiki: Russian Revival architecture; 1509 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Russian Neoclassical Revival
defn: The revival of Russian Neoclassicism and Empire style in the Russian Empire c. 1900–1917 (retrospectivism): Fomin's Polovtsov Dacha, Zholtovsky's Tarasov House.
see: K5-11 Empire Style; T184 Neoclassical Architecture
note: enwiki: Russian Neoclassical Revival; 26 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Romanian Revival Architecture
defn: The Romanian national style (from the 1880s) reviving Brâncovenesc and Moldavian forms: Ion Mincu's Lahovari House, Mincu's Bufetul de la Șosea.
note: enwiki: Romanian Revival architecture; 39 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: National Romantic Style
defn: The Nordic and Baltic national architecture of c. 1890–1920 drawing on vernacular and medieval forms: Helsinki Central Station, Stockholm City Hall, Norwegian dragestil.
see: T185 Art Nouveau Architecture; K2-31 Zakopane Style
note: enwiki: National Romantic style; 161 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Zakopane Style
defn: The Polish national style created by Stanisław Witkiewicz (1890s) from Podhale highland timber building: Villa Koliba, the Chapel in Jaszczurówka.
note: enwiki: Zakopane Style; 37 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Swiss Chalet Style
defn: The 19th-century picturesque revival of the Alpine timber chalet, built across Europe and Scandinavia: Norwegian sveitserstil villas, spa pavilions.
note: enwiki: Swiss chalet style; 140 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Federation Architecture
defn: The Australian architecture of c. 1890–1915, combining Queen Anne, Arts and Crafts and Romanesque elements: Federation Queen Anne houses, the Queen Victoria Building.
see: K2-18 Victorian Architecture; K2-19 Queen Anne Style Architecture
note: enwiki: Federation architecture; 57 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Rustic Architecture
defn: The North American log-and-stone style of the Adirondack Great Camps and the national parks (1870s–1940s): Old Faithful Inn, Timberline Lodge.
note: enwiki: Rustic architecture; 1316 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Ancient Egyptian Architecture
defn: The stone architecture of pharaonic Egypt (c. 3000 BC – AD 300): pyramids, temples and rock-cut tombs: the Pyramids of Giza, Karnak, Abu Simbel.
note: enwiki: Ancient Egyptian architecture; 13 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Architecture of Mesopotamia
defn: The mud-brick architecture of Sumer, Babylonia and Assyria: ziggurats, temples, palaces and city walls: the Ziggurat of Ur, the Ishtar Gate, the palaces of Nimrud.
aliases: Mesopotamian architecture; Assyrian architecture; Babylonian architecture
note: enwiki Architecture of Mesopotamia checked (200); no pool row (gap leaf for K3 axis); Elamite a kind; 3 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Achaemenid Architecture
defn: The palace and tomb architecture of the Persian empire (550–330 BC): Persepolis, Pasargadae, Naqsh-e Rostam.
see: K3-2 Architecture of Mesopotamia; K3-4 Parthian Architecture
note: enwiki: Achaemenid architecture; 47 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Parthian Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Arsacid empire (247 BC – AD 224), with the first monumental iwans and Hellenistic ornament: Hatra, Nisa, Ashur's Parthian palace.
see: K3-3 Achaemenid Architecture; K3-5 Sasanian Architecture
note: enwiki title Parthian architecture checked: redirects to Parthian style (Pope); label attested by QID; 25 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Sasanian Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Sasanian empire (224–651): vaulted iwans, squinch domes and fire temples: Taq Kasra, Palace of Ardashir, Takht-e Soleyman.
note: enwiki: Sasanian architecture; 143 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Minoan Architecture
defn: The Bronze Age palace architecture of Crete (c. 2000–1450 BC): Knossos, Phaistos, Malia.
note: enwiki Minoan architecture checked: redirects to Minoan civilization#Architecture; 0 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Mycenaean Architecture
defn: The Late Bronze Age citadels, megara and tholos tombs of mainland Greece: the Lion Gate, Mycenae, the Treasury of Atreus, Tiryns.
see: K3-6 Minoan Architecture; K3-8 Ancient Greek Architecture
note: enwiki Mycenaean architecture checked: redirects to Mycenaean Greece#Architecture; 3 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Ancient Greek Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Greek world from the Archaic to the Hellenistic period, defined by the temple and the orders: the Parthenon, the Temple of Hephaestus, the Theatre of Epidaurus.
see: K3-10 Ancient Roman Architecture; K2-14 Greek Revival Architecture
note: enwiki: Ancient Greek architecture; 193 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Etruscan Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Etruscans (c. 900–27 BC): timber-and-terracotta temples, arched gates and rock-cut tombs: the Banditaccia necropolis, the Arch of Augustus, Perugia.
note: enwiki: Etruscan architecture; 2 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Ancient Roman Architecture
defn: The architecture of Rome and its empire (c. 500 BC – AD 400), of the arch, vault, dome and concrete: the Pantheon, the Colosseum, the Pont du Gard.
see: K3-8 Ancient Greek Architecture; K4-1 Early Christian Architecture
note: enwiki: Ancient Roman architecture; 258 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Nabataean Architecture
defn: The rock-cut tomb and temple façades of the Nabataeans (1st century BC – 2nd century AD): Al-Khazneh, Ad Deir at Petra, Hegra.
note: enwiki: Nabataean architecture; 0 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Early Christian Architecture
defn: The church architecture of the late Roman empire (4th–6th century): basilicas, baptisteries and martyria: Old St Peter's, Santa Sabina, the Mausoleum of Galla Placidia.
aliases: Early Christian art and architecture; Paleochristian architecture
see: K3-10 Ancient Roman Architecture; K4-2 Byzantine Architecture
note: enwiki Early Christian architecture checked: redirects to Early Christian art and architecture; 87 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Byzantine Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Eastern Roman empire (c. 330–1453): domed churches on pendentives and the cross-in-square plan: Hagia Sophia, San Vitale, Ravenna, Hosios Loukas.
see: K4-1 Early Christian Architecture; K2-9 Neo-Byzantine Architecture; K4-3 Serbo-Byzantine Architecture
note: enwiki: Byzantine architecture; 496 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Serbo-Byzantine Architecture
defn: The medieval church architecture of Serbia (12th–15th century) in its Raška, Vardar and Morava schools: Studenica, Gračanica, Ravanica.
note: enwiki: Serbo-Byzantine architecture; 19 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Architecture of Kievan Rus'
defn: The church architecture of Kievan Rus' and its successor principalities (10th–13th century): Saint Sophia Cathedral, Kyiv, Saint Sophia, Novgorod, the Church of the Intercession on the Nerl.
note: enwiki: Architecture in Kievan Rus'; 47 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Armenian Architecture
defn: The stone church architecture of Armenia from the 4th century, with domed central plans and carved khachkars: Etchmiadzin Cathedral, Zvartnots, the Cathedral of the Holy Cross, Aghtamar.
aliases: Architecture of Armenia; Armenian church architecture
see: K4-6 Architecture of Georgia; K4-2 Byzantine Architecture
note: enwiki: Architecture of Armenia; 547 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Architecture of Georgia
defn: The medieval church and fortress architecture of Georgia (Caucasus): Jvari, Svetitskhoveli, Bagrati Cathedral.
note: enwiki: Architecture of Georgia; 10 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Pre-Romanesque Architecture
defn: The architecture of western Europe between the end of Rome and c. 1000: Visigothic, Asturian, Anglo-Saxon, Lombard and Mozarabic churches: Santa María del Naranco, San Juan de Baños, Escomb Church.
see: K4-8 Carolingian Architecture; K4-9 Ottonian Architecture; K4-10 Romanesque Architecture
note: enwiki Pre-Romanesque art and architecture checked (200); 147 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Carolingian Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Carolingian empire (c. 780–900), reviving Roman forms: the Palatine Chapel, Aachen, the Lorsch gatehouse, Germigny-des-Prés.
see: K4-7 Pre-Romanesque Architecture; K4-9 Ottonian Architecture
note: enwiki: Carolingian architecture; 15 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Ottonian Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Ottonian empire (c. 936–1056) leading into Romanesque: St. Michael's Church, Hildesheim, St. Cyriakus, Gernrode.
see: K4-8 Carolingian Architecture; K4-10 Romanesque Architecture
note: enwiki: Ottonian architecture; 6 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Romanesque Architecture
defn: The round-arched, massive-walled architecture of Europe c. 1000–1200, with its regional schools: Speyer Cathedral, Sainte-Foy, Conques, Durham Cathedral, Pisa Cathedral.
see: K4-7 Pre-Romanesque Architecture; T181 Gothic Architecture; K2-8 Romanesque Revival Architecture
note: enwiki: Romanesque architecture; 9766 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Arab-Norman Architecture
defn: The architecture of Norman Sicily (1091–1194) combining Latin, Byzantine and Islamic forms: the Palatine Chapel, Palermo, Monreale Cathedral, the Zisa.
see: K4-10 Romanesque Architecture; K1-3 Fatimid Architecture
note: enwiki: Norman–Arab–Byzantine culture; label as in UNESCO WHS 1487 Arab-Norman Palermo; enwiki Arab-Norman architecture checked: no article; 27 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Moldavian Style
defn: The church architecture of medieval Moldavia (15th–16th century), Gothic-Byzantine in plan with painted exteriors: Voroneț, Sucevița, Putna Monastery.
see: K4-2 Byzantine Architecture; K5-8 Brâncovenesc Style
note: enwiki: Moldavian architectural style; 0 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Tudor Architecture
defn: The English architecture of 1485–1603, late Perpendicular Gothic turning to Renaissance: Hampton Court Palace, King's College Chapel, Hardwick Hall.
see: T182 Renaissance Architecture; K2-7 Tudor Revival Architecture
note: enwiki: Tudor architecture; 133 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Plateresque
defn: The Spanish style of c. 1490–1560 covering façades in fine silversmith-like Renaissance ornament: the University of Salamanca façade, San Esteban, Salamanca, Acolman.
see: T182 Renaissance Architecture; K5-4 Herrerian Style; K5-5 Churrigueresque
note: enwiki: Plateresque; 59 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Manueline
defn: The Portuguese late Gothic style of the reign of Manuel I (1495–1521), with maritime and twisted-rope ornament: Jerónimos Monastery, Belém Tower, the Convent of Christ, Tomar.
note: enwiki: Manueline; 124 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Herrerian Style
defn: The austere classical style of Juan de Herrera for Philip II (from 1567): El Escorial, Valladolid Cathedral, the Archivo de Indias.
note: enwiki: Herrerian style; 38 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Churrigueresque
defn: The late Baroque style of Spain and New Spain (c. 1700–1760) with estípite pilasters and dense ornament: the Sagrario Metropolitano, Mexico City, the Transparente, Toledo.
see: T183 Baroque Architecture; K5-17 Andean Baroque
note: enwiki: Churrigueresque; 23 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Rococo Architecture
defn: The late Baroque architecture and interior style of c. 1730–1770, light, asymmetrical and ornamental: Sanssouci, the Wieskirche, the Amalienburg.
see: T183 Baroque Architecture; T184 Neoclassical Architecture
note: enwiki: Rococo architecture; 144 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Uzorochye
defn: The ornate Muscovite church and palace architecture of the 17th century, with tented roofs, kokoshniki and tilework: the Church of the Nativity in Putinki, the churches of Yaroslavl.
see: K4-4 Architecture of Kievan Rus'; K2-27 Russian Revival Architecture
note: no enwiki article; Russian term attested by the style QID (ru: Узорочье); 78 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Brâncovenesc Style
defn: The Wallachian style of Constantin Brâncoveanu's reign (1688–1714) combining Renaissance, Baroque and Ottoman elements: Horezu Monastery, Mogoșoaia Palace.
see: K4-12 Moldavian Style; K2-29 Romanian Revival Architecture
note: enwiki: Brâncovenesc art; 16 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Palladian Architecture
defn: The architecture derived from Andrea Palladio's villas and treatise, revived in 18th-century Britain, Ireland and America: Villa Rotonda, Chiswick House, Monticello.
see: T182 Renaissance Architecture; K5-10 Georgian Architecture
note: enwiki: Palladian architecture; 191 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Georgian Architecture
defn: The British and colonial American classical architecture of 1714–1830, in brick and stone terraces, houses and churches: the Royal Crescent, Bath, Merrion Square, colonial Williamsburg.
see: K5-9 Palladian Architecture; K5-12 Federal Architecture; K2-21 Colonial Revival Architecture
note: enwiki: Georgian architecture; 1095 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Empire Style
defn: The Napoleonic phase of Neoclassicism (c. 1800–1830), spread across Europe and Russia: the Arc de Triomphe du Carrousel, La Madeleine, the Russian Empire buildings of St Petersburg.
note: enwiki: Empire style; 559 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Federal Architecture
defn: The American classical architecture of c. 1780–1830, after Adam and Palladio: the White House, Massachusetts State House, the Gardner–Pingree House.
see: K5-10 Georgian Architecture; K2-14 Greek Revival Architecture
note: enwiki: Federal architecture; 2833 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Pombaline Style
defn: The rational, earthquake-resistant style of the rebuilding of Lisbon after 1755: the Baixa Pombalina, Praça do Comércio.
note: enwiki: Pombaline style; 5 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Architecture of the Bulgarian Revival
defn: The Bulgarian urban houses, churches and schools of the National Revival (18th–19th century): Plovdiv Old Town, Koprivshtitsa, the Rila Monastery's residential wings.
note: enwiki: Architecture of the Bulgarian Revival; 34 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: American Colonial Architecture
defn: The architecture of the English colonies of North America (17th–18th century): First Period timber houses, saltbox and Cape Cod types, Georgian brick: the Paul Revere House, Westover Plantation.
see: K5-10 Georgian Architecture; K5-20 Dutch Colonial Architecture; K2-21 Colonial Revival Architecture
note: enwiki: American colonial architecture; 361 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Spanish Colonial Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Spanish empire in the Americas and the Philippines (16th–19th century): missions, cathedrals and plazas: the Mission San Xavier del Bac, Cusco Cathedral, the Baroque churches of the Philippines.
see: K5-17 Andean Baroque; K5-5 Churrigueresque; K2-22 Spanish Colonial Revival Architecture
note: enwiki: Spanish colonial architecture; 142 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Andean Baroque
defn: The mestizo Baroque of the colonial Andes (c. 1680–1780) with flat carved Indigenous-inflected ornament: San Lorenzo, Potosí, the Jesuit Church of Arequipa.
see: K5-16 Spanish Colonial Architecture; K5-5 Churrigueresque
note: enwiki: Andean Baroque; 21 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Portuguese Colonial Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Portuguese empire in Brazil, Africa and Asia (16th–19th century): the historic centre of Ouro Preto, Salvador's Pelourinho, the churches of Old Goa.
note: enwiki: Portuguese colonial architecture; 30 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: French Colonial Architecture
defn: The architecture of the French colonies in North America and the Caribbean: raised galleried Creole houses and Quebec stone houses: the Bolduc House, the French Quarter, New Orleans.
note: enwiki: French colonial architecture; 94 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Dutch Colonial Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Dutch colonies (New Netherland, the East Indies, Suriname), with gambrel and stepped-gable roofs: the Jan Martense Schenck House, Dutch colonial houses of Batavia.
see: K5-21 Cape Dutch Architecture; K5-15 American Colonial Architecture
note: enwiki: Dutch colonial architecture; 13 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Cape Dutch Architecture
defn: The whitewashed, thatched, ornate-gabled farmhouses of the Dutch Cape Colony (17th–18th century): Groot Constantia, Vergelegen.
note: enwiki: Cape Dutch architecture; 6 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Arts and Crafts Architecture
defn: The domestic architecture of the Arts and Crafts movement (c. 1860–1920), vernacular materials and honest craftsmanship: the Red House, Voysey's Broadleys, the Gamble House.
aliases: Arts and Crafts movement; Domestic Revival
see: T185 Art Nouveau Architecture; K6-3 Prairie School
note: enwiki: Arts and Crafts movement; 796 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Chicago School
defn: The steel-frame commercial architecture of Chicago (1880s–1910s), the first skyscrapers: the Home Insurance Building, the Monadnock Building, the Carson Pirie Scott Building.
see: K6-3 Prairie School; T186 Modern Architecture
note: enwiki: Chicago school (architecture); 421 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Prairie School
defn: The Midwestern American architecture of Frank Lloyd Wright and his circle (c. 1900–1917), low and horizontal: Robie House, Unity Temple, the Darwin D. Martin House.
see: K6-2 Chicago School; K6-1 Arts and Crafts Architecture
note: enwiki: Prairie School; 628 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Czech Cubism
defn: The Cubist architecture of Bohemia (1910–1925), with faceted crystalline façades and its later rondocubist phase: the House of the Black Madonna, the Kovařovic Villa, the Adria Palace.
see: K6-5 Expressionist Architecture; T185 Art Nouveau Architecture
note: enwiki: Czech Cubism; 44 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Expressionist Architecture
defn: The early 20th-century European architecture of distorted, sculptural and crystalline form, in brick and concrete: the Einstein Tower, the Chilehaus, Het Schip.
see: T186 Modern Architecture; K6-4 Czech Cubism
note: enwiki: Expressionist architecture; 662 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Futurist Architecture
defn: The architecture of speed and the machine announced by Sant'Elia (1914) and its later heirs, from Googie to neo-futurism: Sant'Elia's Città Nuova, the Theme Building, LAX.
see: K6-5 Expressionist Architecture; K6-19 High-tech Architecture
note: enwiki: Futurist architecture; 79 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Art Deco Architecture
defn: The architecture of Art Deco (c. 1920–1940), geometric, stepped and ornamented, with its Streamline Moderne phase: the Chrysler Building, Miami Beach's Art Deco District, Napier.
see: T185 Art Nouveau Architecture; T186 Modern Architecture; K6-14 Stripped Classicism
note: enwiki: Art Deco architecture; 1966 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Bauhaus Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Bauhaus school and its masters (1919–1933) and its diaspora: the Bauhaus Dessau, the Masters' Houses, Tel Aviv's White City.
see: K6-9 International Style; T186 Modern Architecture
note: enwiki: Bauhaus; 53 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: International Style
defn: The modern architecture named by Hitchcock and Johnson (1932): volume rather than mass, regularity, no applied ornament: Villa Savoye, the Barcelona Pavilion, the Seagram Building.
see: K6-8 Bauhaus Architecture; T186 Modern Architecture; K6-18 Mid-Century Modern Architecture
note: enwiki: International Style; 646 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Constructivist Architecture
defn: The Soviet avant-garde architecture of the 1920s–early 1930s: the Shukhov Tower, the Narkomfin Building, the Rusakov Workers' Club.
see: T186 Modern Architecture; K6-15 Stalinist Architecture
note: enwiki: Constructivist architecture; 479 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Reform Architecture
defn: The German-speaking reform movement of c. 1900–1930 that rejected historicism for simple, regional building (Heimatschutz, Um 1800): Paul Schultze-Naumburg's Cecilienhof, Hellerau.
see: T186 Modern Architecture; K6-12 Traditionalist School
note: no enwiki article; attested by the style QID (de: Reformarchitektur); 306 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Traditionalist School
defn: The Dutch traditionalist architecture of c. 1900–1960 in brick and tile, with its Delft and Bossche schools: Granpré Molière's Vreewijk, Dom Hans van der Laan's Roosenberg Abbey.
see: K6-11 Reform Architecture; K6-5 Expressionist Architecture
note: enwiki: Traditionalist School (architecture); 216 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Nordic Classicism
defn: The pared-down classical architecture of Scandinavia and Finland c. 1910–1930: Asplund's Stockholm City Library, the Woodland Chapel, Aalto's early Jyväskylä buildings.
see: K6-14 Stripped Classicism; K6-9 International Style
note: enwiki: Nordic Classicism; 58 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Stripped Classicism
defn: The simplified, unornamented classicism of the 1920s–1940s for government buildings in democracies and dictatorships alike: the Federal Reserve Board Building, the Palais de Chaillot.
see: K6-13 Nordic Classicism; K6-15 Stalinist Architecture; K6-16 Fascist Architecture
note: enwiki: Stripped Classicism; 54 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Stalinist Architecture
defn: The monumental socialist-realist architecture of the USSR and its satellites (1933–1955): the Seven Sisters, the Palace of Culture and Science, Karl-Marx-Allee.
see: K6-10 Constructivist Architecture; K6-14 Stripped Classicism; K6-16 Fascist Architecture
note: enwiki: Stalinist architecture; 667 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Fascist Architecture
defn: The architecture of Fascist Italy (1922–1943), from rationalism to monumental stripped classicism: EUR, Rome, the Casa del Fascio, Como, the Palazzo della Civiltà Italiana.
aliases: Stile Littorio; architecture of the Fascist period
see: K6-17 Nazi Architecture; K6-14 Stripped Classicism; T186 Modern Architecture
note: enwiki: Fascist architecture; 70 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Nazi Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Third Reich (1933–1945), monumental neoclassical for the state and Heimatstil for housing: the Nuremberg Rally Grounds, Tempelhof Airport, the Reich Chancellery.
see: K6-16 Fascist Architecture; K6-15 Stalinist Architecture
note: enwiki: Nazi architecture; 40 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Mid-Century Modern Architecture
defn: The American-led domestic and commercial modernism of c. 1945–1970: post-and-beam houses, glass pavilions and regional variants: the Eames House, the Stahl House, Miami Modern hotels.
see: K6-9 International Style; T187 Brutalist Architecture
note: enwiki: Mid-century modern; 167 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: High-tech Architecture
defn: Late-modern architecture from the 1970s that expresses structure and services as industrial technology: the Centre Pompidou, the Lloyd's Building, HSBC Main Building, Hong Kong.
see: T188 Postmodern Architecture; T190 Contemporary Architecture
note: enwiki: High-tech architecture; 184 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: New Classical Architecture
defn: Contemporary classical and traditional architecture since the 1980s: Poundbury, Robert Adam's Sackler Library, the Schermerhorn Symphony Center.
see: T188 Postmodern Architecture; T184 Neoclassical Architecture
note: enwiki: New Classical architecture; 57 exemplar-tagged buildings incl. kinds

label: Nagara Architecture
defn: The northern Hindu and Jain temple tradition whose sanctum rises in a curvilinear shikhara of stacked courses (latina, shekhari and bhumija forms): Kandariya Mahadeva at Khajuraho, Mahabodhi Temple, Kopeshwar temple, Khidrapur.
aliases: Nagara style;North Indian temple architecture;Indo-Aryan temple style
see: K7-2 Kalinga Architecture; K7-3 Maru-Gurjara Architecture; K7-5 Vesara
note: the generic north-Indian bucket also swept in Buddhist stupas (Sanchi, Dhamek): those go to the Buddhist Architecture leaf

label: Kalinga Architecture
defn: The Odishan temple tradition of the rekha, pidha and khakhara deula with jagamohana halls (7th–13th century): Lingaraja Temple, Konark Sun Temple, Jagannath Temple, Puri.
see: K7-1 Nagara Architecture; K7-7 Bengal Temple Architecture

label: Maru-Gurjara Architecture
defn: The temple tradition of Gujarat and Rajasthan (11th–13th century and its revival) with richly carved marble interiors, especially for Jain patrons: Dilwara temples, Mount Abu, Modhera Sun Temple, Ranakpur.

label: Dravidian Architecture
defn: The southern Hindu temple tradition of stepped pyramidal vimanas, pillared mandapas and monumental gopurams in walled precincts: Shore Temple, Mahabalipuram, Brihadisvara Temple, Thanjavur, Meenakshi Temple, Madurai, Virupaksha Temple, Hampi.
aliases: Dravida style;South Indian temple architecture;Tamil architecture;kovil
note: dynastic schools (Pallava, Chola, Pandya, Vijayanagara, Nayak) are kinds; the dated sub-periods are thin in the candidates (98 of ~16k dated)

label: Vesara
defn: The Deccan temple tradition combining Nagara and Dravidian forms, developed under the Chalukyas and Hoysalas: Pattadakal, Mahadeva Temple, Itagi, Chennakesava Temple, Belur, Hoysaleswara Temple, Halebidu.
see: K7-4 Dravidian Architecture; K7-1 Nagara Architecture

label: Kerala Architecture
defn: The timber-and-laterite building tradition of Kerala with steep tiled and copper roofs: circular and rectangular sreekovil temples, koothambalam theatres, nalukettu houses and palaces: Vadakkunnathan Temple, Padmanabhapuram Palace, Mattancherry Palace.

label: Bengal Temple Architecture
defn: The brick and terracotta temples of Bengal (16th–19th century) whose curved roofs translate the thatched hut: the chala types (do-chala, char-chala, at-chala), jor-bangla and the ratna (pinnacled) types: Jor Bangla Temple, Bishnupur, Rasmancha, Dakshineswar Kali Temple.
aliases: Bengal temple style;terracotta temples of Bengal

label: Buddhist Architecture
defn: The architecture of Buddhism in its South Asian homeland: stupas, chaitya halls and vihara monasteries from the Mauryas to the Palas, and the monasteries of Gandhara: Great Stupa, Sanchi, Dhamek Stupa, Nalanda Mahavihara, Takht-i-Bahi.
see: K7-9 Indian Rock-cut Architecture; K7-10 Sinhalese Architecture; K7-12 Tibetan Buddhist Architecture
note: scoped to South Asia; the Buddhist traditions of East and Southeast Asia are their own leaves (K8, K9)

label: Indian Rock-cut Architecture
defn: Caves, halls and monolithic temples excavated from living rock (3rd century BCE–10th century): Ajanta Caves, Karla chaitya, Kailasa Temple, Ellora, Elephanta Caves.
see: K7-8 Buddhist Architecture; K7-4 Dravidian Architecture

label: Sinhalese Architecture
defn: The Buddhist and royal architecture of Sri Lanka: dagobas, vatadages, image houses and monasteries of Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa, and the timber halls of the Kandyan kingdom: Ruwanweli Maha Seya, Jetavanaramaya, Gal Vihara, Temple of the Tooth.
aliases: architecture of Sri Lanka;Sri Lankan Buddhist architecture
note: attested through the article on the architecture of Sri Lanka (no article under the Sinhalese label)

label: Newar Architecture
defn: The brick-and-timber architecture of the Newars of the Kathmandu valley: multi-roofed pagoda temples, shikhara temples, stupas, bahal courtyards and palace squares with carved struts and windows: Pashupatinath, Nyatapola, Changu Narayan, Swayambhunath.
see: K7-12 Tibetan Buddhist Architecture; K7-1 Nagara Architecture

label: Tibetan Buddhist Architecture
defn: The monastic and palace architecture of Tibet and the Tibetan Buddhist world: battered stone-and-earth walls, flat roofs, gilded roofs, chortens and kumbums: Potala Palace, Jokhang, Drepung, Gyantse Kumbum.
see: K7-13 Dzong Architecture; K7-11 Newar Architecture
note: Himalayan; placed in K7 with Newar and dzong, seam with K8 East Asian (Tibetan temples in China)

label: Dzong Architecture
defn: The fortress-monasteries of Bhutan and Tibet housing civil and monastic administration around a central utse tower: Punakha Dzong, Paro Rinpung Dzong, Trongsa Dzong.

label: Rajput Architecture
defn: The forts, palaces, havelis and cenotaphs of the Rajput kingdoms of Rajasthan and Central India (8th–19th century), with jharokhas and chhatris: Amber Fort, Chittorgarh Fort, Kumbhalgarh, Jaisalmer Fort.
