label: Stepwell
defn: The stepped subterranean wells of western India built as civic and devotional monuments, Hindu and Islamic (vav, baoli): Rani ki vav, Adalaj Stepwell, Chand Baori.

label: Sikh Architecture
defn: The gurdwaras and memorials of the Sikh tradition (17th–19th century) drawing on Mughal and Rajput forms, with fluted domes and gilded upper storeys: Harmandir Sahib, Takht Sri Patna Sahib, Gurdwara Baba Atal.

label: Harappan Architecture
defn: The planned fired-brick cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation (c. 2600–1900 BCE): grid streets, drains, granaries and citadels: Great Bath, Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira.

label: Chinese Architecture
defn: The classical timber-frame tradition of China, with bracket sets (dougong), raised platforms and sweeping tiled roofs, used for palaces, altars, temples, pagodas and gateways and codified in official manuals (Yingzao Fashi): Forbidden City, Temple of Heaven, Foguang Temple, Giant Wild Goose Pagoda.
see: K8-2 Siheyuan; K8-20 Korean Architecture; K8-11 Japanese Buddhist Architecture
note: dynasties (Tang, Song, Liao, Ming, Qing) are period tags; imperial palaces, temples, pagodas and paifang are kinds

label: Siheyuan
defn: The north-Chinese courtyard house of four halls round a central yard, the model of the Beijing hutong: Prince Gong Mansion, Qiao Family Compound.

label: Yaodong
defn: The earth-sheltered cave dwellings of the Loess Plateau, cut into cliffs, sunk round pit courtyards or built as vaults.

label: Hakka Walled Village
defn: The fortified communal dwellings of the Hakka and Minnan of southern China: the earthen tulou of Fujian, weilongwu and walled villages: Tianluokeng tulou cluster, Chengqi Lou.
see: K8-7 Hokkien Architecture; K8-6 Lingnan Architecture

label: Hui-style Architecture
defn: The merchant houses, ancestral halls and memorial arches of Huizhou (southern Anhui), with whitewashed walls, stepped horse-head gables and carved brick, wood and stone: Xidi, Hongcun.

label: Lingnan Architecture
defn: The building tradition of Guangdong and Guangxi: wok-ear gables, ceramic ridge figures, arcaded qilou shophouses and Lingnan gardens: Chen Clan Ancestral Hall, Foshan Ancestral Temple.
see: K8-7 Hokkien Architecture; K8-4 Hakka Walled Village

label: Hokkien Architecture
defn: The Minnan building tradition of southern Fujian, Taiwan and the Hokkien diaspora: swallowtail ridges, red brick and cut-porcelain (jian nian) roof decoration on temples and houses: Bangka Lungshan Temple, Kaiyuan Temple, Quanzhou.
see: K8-6 Lingnan Architecture; K8-4 Hakka Walled Village

label: Sichuanese Architecture
defn: The timber and stilted vernacular of Sichuan and Chongqing (chuan-dou framing, diaojiaolou), with its Song–Yuan temple halls.
note: weakly attested: a Wikidata item with no sitelinks; kept because of its heritage buildings

label: Shikumen
defn: The Shanghai lane-house (lilong) type of the 1860s–1930s joining a Chinese courtyard plan to Western terrace housing behind stone-framed gates: Xintiandi, Tianzifang.

label: Shinto Shrine Architecture
defn: The architecture of Japanese Shinto shrines (jinja) in named styles (zukuri) defined by roof, entrance and plan: Ise Grand Shrine (shinmei), Izumo Taisha (taisha), Kamigamo Shrine (nagare), Nikkō Tōshō-gū (gongen).

label: Japanese Buddhist Architecture
defn: The temple architecture of Japanese Buddhism in its named styles: wayō, daibutsuyō, zenshūyō and the mixed setchūyō, with pagodas, halls, gates and storehouses: Hōryū-ji, Tōdai-ji, Byōdō-in, Engaku-ji Shariden.
see: K8-10 Shinto Shrine Architecture; K8-1 Chinese Architecture
note: Asuka, Nara, Heian, Kamakura, Muromachi and Edo are period tags; the styles are kinds

label: Shinden-zukuri
defn: The Heian aristocratic residence of a main hall facing a south garden and pond, linked to wings by corridors: Kyoto Imperial Palace Shishinden, Byōdō-in (derived).

label: Shoin-zukuri
defn: The warrior-class residential style of the Muromachi to Edo periods with tatami rooms, tokonoma alcove, staggered shelves, built-in desk and sliding fusuma: Ninomaru Palace, Nijō Castle, Kojō-in, Onjō-ji.

label: Sukiya-zukuri
defn: The informal residential and tea-house style derived from the chashitsu, using natural materials and restrained finish: Katsura Imperial Villa, Tai-an, Jo-an.

label: Minka
defn: The vernacular houses of Japan's farmers, craftsmen and merchants: farmhouses (nōka) and townhouses (machiya), in regional types such as gasshō-zukuri and magariya: Shirakawa-gō, Kyoto machiya.

label: Japanese Castle Architecture
defn: The fortified residences of the daimyō (16th–17th century): stone ramparts, moats, gates and the multi-storey tenshu keep: Himeji Castle, Matsumoto Castle, Osaka Castle.

label: Kofun
defn: The mounded tombs of Japan's Kofun period (3rd–7th century), above all the keyhole-shaped zenpō-kōen-fun, often moated and set with haniwa: Daisen Kofun, Mozu-Furuichi kofun group, Ishibutai Kofun.
note: the tomb as monument; the haniwa that stood on them are D (sculpture) or E (ceramics)

label: Ryukyuan Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Ryukyu kingdom (Okinawa): red-tiled gusuku castles and palaces, utaki sacred groves and turtleback and gable-roofed tombs: Shuri Castle, Tamaudun, Nakagusuku Castle.

label: Giyōfū Architecture
defn: The pseudo-Western buildings of early Meiji Japan (1860s–1880s) made by Japanese carpenters imitating Western forms in timber and plaster: Former Kaichi School, Tsukiji Hotel, Former Saiseikan Hospital.

label: Korean Architecture
defn: The timber-frame architecture of Korea's palaces, temples, shrines and fortresses, classified by bracket system (jusimpo, dapo, ikgong) and painted in dancheong: Gyeongbokgung, Bulguksa, Jongmyo, Haeinsa Janggyeong Panjeon.
see: K8-21 Hanok; K8-1 Chinese Architecture; K7-2 Dancheong
note: Three Kingdoms, Silla, Goryeo and Joseon are period tags

label: Hanok
defn: The traditional Korean house with ondol-heated rooms, wooden maru floors and tiled or thatched roofs, set by geomancy: Bukchon Hanok Village, Hahoe Folk Village, Yangdong Village.
note: no input row names it; added as the canonical Korean dwelling tradition

label: Khmer Architecture
defn: The temple-mountains, galleried enclosures and prasat towers of the Khmer empire and its predecessors (7th–13th century) in successive named styles (Sambor Prei Kuk, Preah Ko, Bakheng, Banteay Srei, Baphuon, Angkor Wat, Bayon): Angkor Wat, Banteay Srei, Bayon, Preah Vihear.
see: K9-8 Cham Architecture; K9-6 Thai Architecture

label: Candi Architecture
defn: The Hindu and Buddhist stone temples and stupas of classical Indonesia (7th–15th century), in the Central Javanese (Mataram) and East Javanese (Singhasari, Majapahit) styles and in Sumatra: Borobudur, Prambanan, Candi Penataran, Muara Takus.

label: Balinese Architecture
defn: The Hindu-Balinese building tradition of walled pura temples with split gates (candi bentar), meru towers and pavilions, and compound houses laid out by cosmological axes: Pura Besakih, Pura Taman Ayun, Pura Ulun Danu Bratan.
see: K9-2 Candi Architecture; K9-4 Javanese Traditional House

label: Javanese Traditional House
defn: The timber houses of Java in ranked roof types (joglo, limasan, kampung) with the open pendopo pavilion in front: Kraton Yogyakarta pendopo, Mangkunegaran Palace.

label: Burmese Architecture
defn: The Buddhist architecture of Myanmar: bell-shaped zedi stupas, hollow gu temples, pyatthat spires and teak monasteries, from Pagan to Mandalay: Ananda Temple, Shwezigon, Shwedagon Pagoda, Shwenandaw Monastery.

label: Thai Architecture
defn: The Buddhist and royal architecture of Thailand, in the art-historical styles of Sukhothai, Lanna, Ayutthaya and Rattanakosin: wat compounds with ubosot, vihara, chedi, prang and mondop: Wat Mahathat, Sukhothai, Wat Phra Si Sanphet, Wat Phrathat Doi Suthep, Wat Phra Kaew.
see: K9-1 Khmer Architecture; K9-7 Lao Architecture; K9-5 Burmese Architecture

label: Lao Architecture
defn: The Buddhist architecture of Laos (Lan Xang) in the Luang Prabang, Vientiane and Xieng Khouang temple styles with sweeping multi-tiered roofs and that stupas: Wat Xieng Thong, Pha That Luang, Wat Si Saket.
note: WEAK: no English article on Lao architecture (Architecture of Laos redirects to Culture of Laos); attested through UNESCO Town of Luang Prabang, which describes the traditional Lao temple architecture

label: Cham Architecture
defn: The brick tower-temples (kalan) of the Champa kingdoms in central and southern Vietnam (7th–15th century) in successive styles (Mỹ Sơn E1, Đồng Dương, Tháp Mắm): Mỹ Sơn, Po Nagar, Po Klong Garai.
see: K9-1 Khmer Architecture; K9-9 Vietnamese Architecture

label: Vietnamese Architecture
defn: The timber architecture of Vietnam's pagodas (chùa), communal houses (đình), citadels and imperial tombs, from the Lý to the Nguyễn: One Pillar Pagoda, Temple of Literature, Thiên Mụ Pagoda, Imperial City of Huế.
see: K9-8 Cham Architecture; K8-1 Chinese Architecture

label: Batak Architecture
defn: The saddle-roofed timber houses (rumah adat) and granaries of the Batak peoples of North Sumatra, raised on piles and carved and painted with gorga ornament.

label: Bahay Kubo
defn: The Philippine nipa hut: a stilted house of bamboo and timber with a thatched nipa roof, the base type of lowland Filipino vernacular.

label: Bahay na Bato
defn: The Spanish-colonial Filipino town house (18th–19th century) with a stone lower storey and a timber upper storey with capiz-shell sliding windows: Vigan, Casa Manila.

label: Sino-Portuguese Architecture
defn: The shophouses and mansions of Phuket, Penang and the Straits Settlements (late 19th–early 20th century) mixing Hokkien plans with European façades.

label: Aksumite Architecture
defn: The stone architecture of the Aksumite kingdom (1st–7th century) with its 'monkey-head' timber-and-rubble walls, palaces and carved monolithic stelae: Northern Stelae Field, Aksum, Dungur palace, Debre Damo.
note: the title is a redirect to Architecture of Ethiopia (section on Aksumite architecture)

label: Ethiopian Rock-hewn Churches
defn: The monolithic and semi-monolithic churches carved from rock in Ethiopia (10th–13th century and later): Bete Giyorgis, Lalibela, Bete Medhane Alem, Abuna Yemata Guh.
aliases: rock-hewn churches of Lalibela;Tigray rock churches
see: K10-1 Aksumite Architecture; K10-3 Gondarine Architecture

label: Gondarine Architecture
defn: The castle-palaces and churches of the Gondar period (17th–18th century), with battlemented towers and domes: Fasil Ghebbi, Fasilides' Bath, Debre Berhan Selassie.
note: attested through the type site; no article under the style name

label: Nubian Pyramids
defn: The steep pyramids, temples and palaces of the Kushite kingdoms of Napata and Meroë (8th century BCE–4th century CE): Meroë, Jebel Barkal, El-Kurru, Musawwarat es-Sufra.

label: Great Zimbabwe
defn: The dry-stone architecture of the Zimbabwe culture (11th–19th century): mortarless granite enclosures, coursed walls with chevron and chequer friezes: Great Zimbabwe, Khami, Mapungubwe, Naletale.
note: label is the type site; the culture's other sites (Khami, Naletale, Mapungubwe) are kinds

label: Ksar
defn: The fortified earthen and stone villages, granaries (agadir, ghorfa) and kasbahs of the Amazigh and Saharan world: Aït Benhaddou, Ksar of Ouadane, Ksar Ouled Soltane, Ghardaïa (M'zab).

label: Hausa Architecture
defn: The earthen architecture of the Hausa city-states of northern Nigeria and Niger: domed and vaulted mud houses and palaces with relief façades (zanko pinnacles): Gidan Rumfa, Kano, Zaria Friday Mosque.

label: Maya Architecture
defn: The stone architecture of the Maya (c. 1000 BCE–1500 CE): stepped pyramid-temples, palaces with corbel vaults, ballcourts and stelae plazas, in the regional styles Petén, Usumacinta, Río Bec, Chenes and Puuc: Tikal Temple I, Temple of the Inscriptions, Palenque, Uxmal, Chichen Itza.
see: K11-2 Mesoamerican Architecture; K11-3 Aztec Architecture

label: Mesoamerican Architecture
defn: The monumental architecture of non-Maya Mesoamerica: Olmec mounds, the talud-tablero platforms of Teotihuacan, Zapotec and Mixtec Oaxaca, Classic Veracruz and Toltec Tula: Pyramid of the Sun, Monte Albán, Mitla, Pyramid of the Niches, El Tajín.
see: K11-1 Maya Architecture; K11-3 Aztec Architecture

label: Aztec Architecture
defn: The architecture of the Mexica and their Late Postclassic neighbours (14th–16th century): twin-temple pyramids, palaces and causeway cities: Templo Mayor, Tenayuca, Santa Cecilia Acatitlan, Malinalco.

label: Inca Architecture
defn: The fitted-masonry architecture of Tawantinsuyu (15th–16th century): ashlar and polygonal walls, trapezoidal doorways and niches, terraces, roads and tambos: Machu Picchu, Sacsayhuamán, Coricancha, Ollantaytambo.

label: Andean Architecture
defn: The monumental architecture of the Andes before the Inca: Caral's platform mounds, Chavín's galleried temple, Moche adobe huacas, Tiwanaku's stone platforms, Wari administrative centres, Chimú Chan Chan and Chachapoya Kuélap.
note: WEAK: no English article titled Andean architecture for the pre-Inca building traditions; attested through the Andean civilizations article; cultures are kinds

label: Ancestral Puebloan Architecture
defn: The masonry and adobe great houses, cliff dwellings, kivas and terraced pueblos of the Ancestral Puebloans and their descendants in the US Southwest: Pueblo Bonito, Chaco Canyon, Cliff Palace, Mesa Verde, Taos Pueblo.

label: Mound Builders
defn: The earthen platform mounds, effigy mounds and geometric earthworks of the Eastern Woodlands (Archaic to Mississippian, c. 3500 BCE–1600 CE): Poverty Point, Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks, Monks Mound, Cahokia, Serpent Mound.

label: Wharenui
defn: The carved Māori meeting house on the marae, its frame read as the body of an ancestor: Te Hau ki Tūranga, Te Tokanganui-a-Noho, Rauru.
note: no input row; added as the user-named Oceanic meeting-house tradition

label: Fale
defn: The Samoan open-sided house with a domed thatched roof on posts, including the round fale tele guest house.
note: no input row; Pacific meeting-house tradition

label: Maneaba
defn: The great community meeting house of Kiribati and Tuvalu, a vast thatched roof on low posts.
note: no input row; Pacific meeting-house tradition

label: Haus Tambaran
defn: The spirit and men's houses of the Sepik region of Papua New Guinea with soaring painted gable façades.
note: no input row; Pacific meeting-house tradition

label: Marae
defn: The stone-paved ceremonial platforms and courts of East Polynesia, including the image ahu of Rapa Nui with their moai: Taputapuātea, Ahu Tongariki, Ahu Tahai.

label: Nan Madol
defn: The basalt-prism megalithic architecture of the Saudeleur polity on Pohnpei (c. 1180–1628) and Leluh on Kosrae: artificial islets of stacked columnar basalt.
note: label is the type site; stands for the Micronesian basalt megalithic tradition

label: Chilotan Architecture
defn: The shingled timber architecture of the Chiloé archipelago, above all the Jesuit-founded wooden churches built by local boatwrights (18th–19th century): Church of Castro, Church of Achao, palafitos of Castro.
aliases: Chiloé School of religious wooden architecture

label: Gongbi
defn: The meticulous, finely outlined and coloured manner of Chinese court and academy painting from the Tang and Song: Emperor Huizong's Auspicious Cranes, Zhang Zeduan's Along the River during the Qingming Festival.
note: fallback for East Asian painters born before 1200 with no school (court/professional painting)

label: Northern Landscape Style
defn: The monumental landscape painting of the Five Dynasties and Northern Song: Fan Kuan's Travelers among Mountains and Streams, Guan Tong's Waiting for the Ferry.

label: Literati Painting
defn: Scholar-amateur painting of China (wenrenhua) and its Korean and Japanese reflexes, valuing brushwork, poetry and calligraphy over likeness: Ni Zan's Rongxi Studio, Huang Gongwang's Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains, Dong Qichang's landscapes.
note: labelled as the brief asks; attested by Southern School (Q1142000), the literati-painting lineage; Four Wangs a kind

label: Zhe School
defn: The professional Ming school of landscape continuing Southern Song Ma–Xia painting (15th–16th century): Dai Jin's Returning Home Late from a Spring Outing, Wu Wei's figures.
note: no members yet; brief-named school

label: Wu School
defn: The Ming literati school of Suzhou (15th–16th century) around Shen Zhou and Wen Zhengming: Shen Zhou's Lofty Mount Lu, Wen Zhengming's Old Trees by a Cold Waterfall.
note: no members yet; brief-named school

label: Shanghai School
defn: The commercial-literati painting of late Qing Shanghai, bold in colour and subject: Ren Bonian's portraits, Wu Changshuo's flowers.

label: Lingnan School
defn: The Cantonese school (early 20th century) of the Gao brothers and Chen Shuren that joined Chinese brushwork with Japanese and Western realism: Gao Jianfu's Flying in the Rain, Zhao Shao'ang's birds.
note: Three Masters of Lingnan a kind

label: Yamato-e
defn: The classical Japanese narrative and court painting style from the Heian period, continued by the Tosa school: the Tale of Genji scrolls, the Shigisan engi emaki, Tosa Mitsuoki's Quail and Millet.
note: Tosa school and Fujiwara no Takanobu's nise-e are kinds

label: Kanō School
defn: The hereditary school of Japanese official painting (15th–19th century) joining Chinese ink and Yamato-e colour: Kanō Eitoku's Cypress Trees, Kanō Tan'yū's Nijō Castle screens.

label: Rinpa School
defn: The decorative Japanese school of Sōtatsu, Kōrin and Hōitsu (17th–19th century): Sōtatsu's Wind God and Thunder God, Kōrin's Irises.
note: no members yet; brief-named school

label: Nanga
defn: Japanese literati painting (bunjinga) of the later Edo period and its Meiji continuation: Ike no Taiga and Yosa Buson's Ten Conveniences and Ten Pleasures, Uragami Gyokudō's Frozen Clouds.

label: Maruyama–Shijō School
defn: The naturalistic Kyoto painting of Maruyama Ōkyo and Matsumura Goshun (from the 1770s) and its modern heirs: Ōkyo's Pine Trees in Snow, Goshun's Woodcutters and Fishermen.
note: Maruyama school (Q11394770) and Shijō school (Q3577704) merged

label: Nihonga
defn: Modern Japanese-style painting (from the 1880s) in mineral pigments and ink on silk and paper: Hishida Shunsō's Fallen Leaves, Yokoyama Taikan's works, Uemura Shōen's Flame.

label: Palaeologan Renaissance
defn: Late Byzantine painting (1261–1453), classicising and intensely expressive in icons and frescoes: the Chora Church frescoes, Theophanes the Greek's icons.

label: Russian Icons
defn: Icon painting of Rus' and Muscovy and its schools (Novgorod, Moscow, Vologda, Stroganov): Rublev's Trinity, Dionisius's Ferapontov icons.
note: icon painting of Vologda a kind

label: Romanesque Painting
defn: Panel, book and wall painting of Latin Europe in the 11th–12th centuries, with flat, linear, hieratic figures: the Master of Pedret, painted altar frontals of Catalonia, the Registrum Gregorii.
note: period-style home for European painters born before 1200; Ottonian illumination kept as a kind

label: Gothic Painting
defn: Painting in Latin Europe from the 13th to the late 14th century, from Italo-Byzantine panel crosses to the narrative altarpieces of Giotto and his followers: Coppo di Marcovaldo's crucifixes, Giotto's Ognissanti Madonna, Catalan Gothic retables.
note: Gothic art (Q46825) merged

label: Sienese School
defn: The school of painting of Siena, 13th–15th century, with its gold grounds, lyrical line and colour: Duccio's Maestà, Simone Martini's Annunciation, Lorenzetti's Allegory of Good Government.

label: International Gothic
defn: The courtly late Gothic style shared by painters across Europe c. 1375–1425, elegant, decorative and richly detailed: the Wilton Diptych, Gentile da Fabriano's Adoration of the Magi, the Très Riches Heures.
see: T18 Gothic Painting;T21 Early Netherlandish Painting
note: International Gothic art in Italy (Q3773652) merged

label: Early Netherlandish Painting
defn: Oil painting of the Burgundian and Habsburg Netherlands in the 15th and early 16th centuries, with minute naturalism and luminous glazes: the Ghent Altarpiece, the Arnolfini Portrait, Rogier van der Weyden's Descent from the Cross.

label: Italian Renaissance Painting
defn: Painting in Italy c. 1400–1530, from the perspective and naturalism of the Florentine Early Renaissance to the High Renaissance: Masaccio's Trinity, Piero della Francesca's Flagellation, Leonardo's Last Supper, Raphael's School of Athens.
see: T23 Venetian School;T25 Mannerism;T24 Northern Renaissance
note: phases (Early, High) and city schools (Florentine, Umbrian, Veronese, Ferrarese, Mantuan) are kinds

label: Venetian School
defn: The painting of Venice and its terraferma from the Bellini to the 18th century, built on colour and light: Giovanni Bellini's San Zaccaria Altarpiece, Giorgione's Tempest, Titian's Assumption, Veronese's Wedding at Cana.

label: Northern Renaissance
defn: The Renaissance north of the Alps (German lands, the Low Countries, France, England), c. 1490–1580: Dürer's Self-Portrait of 1500, the Isenheim Altarpiece, Holbein's Ambassadors, Bruegel's Hunters in the Snow.
aliases: German Renaissance;Dutch and Flemish Renaissance painting;French Renaissance
note: regional names (German, French, Dutch and Flemish Renaissance) are kinds; holds German, French, British and Central European painters born 1400–1564 and Netherlandish painters born 1500–1564 with no movement

label: Mannerism
defn: The artificial, elongated and complex style that followed the High Renaissance, c. 1520–1600: Pontormo's Deposition, Parmigianino's Madonna with the Long Neck, Bronzino's Allegory with Venus and Cupid.
see: T26 School of Fontainebleau;T27 Baroque Painting

label: School of Fontainebleau
defn: The Mannerist decoration and painting of the French court at Fontainebleau, led by Rosso and Primaticcio (c. 1530–1610): the Galerie François I, Gabrielle d'Estrées and One of Her Sisters.

label: Baroque Painting
defn: European painting of the 17th and early 18th centuries, dramatic in light, movement and emotion, from Rome to Madrid and the colonial Americas: Rubens's Elevation of the Cross, Velázquez's Las Meninas, Pietro da Cortona's Barberini ceiling.
see: T28 Caravaggisti;T29 Flemish Baroque Painting;T30 Dutch Golden Age Painting;T31 Rococo
note: Baroque (Q37853) merged; colonial Andean schools (Cusco, Quito, Potosí) kept as kinds

label: Caravaggisti
defn: Followers of Caravaggio's dramatic tenebrism and naturalism across Europe, c. 1600–1640: Gentileschi's Judith Slaying Holofernes, Ter Brugghen's Calling of Saint Matthew, Valentin de Boulogne's Concert.
note: Utrecht Caravaggism a kind

label: Flemish Baroque Painting
defn: Painting of the Southern Netherlands c. 1585–1700 around Rubens, van Dyck and Jordaens: Rubens's Descent from the Cross, van Dyck's Charles I at the Hunt, Snyders's market stalls.
see: T27 Baroque Painting;T30 Dutch Golden Age Painting

label: Dutch Golden Age Painting
defn: Painting of the Dutch Republic in the 17th century, its genres sold on an open market: Rembrandt's Night Watch, Vermeer's View of Delft, Ruisdael's Jewish Cemetery, Heda's breakfast pieces.
see: T29 Flemish Baroque Painting;T27 Baroque Painting
note: Delft school and fijnschilders are kinds

label: Rococo
defn: The light, ornamental, intimate style of the 18th century, from the French fêtes galantes to Venetian ceilings: Watteau's Pilgrimage to Cythera, Fragonard's The Swing, Tiepolo's Würzburg ceiling.

label: Neoclassicism
defn: Painting of the later 18th and early 19th century modelled on antiquity, severe in line and moral in subject: David's Oath of the Horatii, Mengs's Parnassus, Ingres's Grande Odalisque.

label: Romanticism
defn: Painting c. 1780–1850 that put feeling, the sublime and the imagination before rule: Friedrich's Wanderer above the Sea of Fog, Géricault's Raft of the Medusa, Delacroix's Liberty Leading the People, Turner's Slave Ship.
see: T32 Neoclassicism;T40 Academic Art;T34 Nazarene Movement
note: Romantic painting (Q3088366) merged

label: Nazarene Movement
defn: German Romantic painters in Rome (from 1809) who revived the religious art of Dürer and early Raphael: Overbeck's Italia and Germania, the Casa Bartholdy frescoes.
note: Italian Purismo kept as a kind

label: Danish Golden Age
defn: Danish painting of the first half of the 19th century, around Eckersberg and his pupils: Købke's View of Lake Sortedam, Eckersberg's views of Rome.

label: Düsseldorf School of Painting
defn: Painters trained at the Düsseldorf Academy c. 1819–1918, known for detailed landscapes and history scenes: Achenbach's seascapes, Leutze's Washington Crossing the Delaware.

label: Barbizon School
defn: French landscape painters working from nature in the forest of Fontainebleau c. 1830–1870: Rousseau's Forest of Fontainebleau, Millet's The Gleaners, Corot's Souvenir de Mortefontaine.
note: Groupe de Marlotte a kind

label: Hudson River School
defn: American Romantic landscape painting c. 1825–1875: Cole's The Oxbow, Church's Heart of the Andes, Bierstadt's Rocky Mountains.

label: Norwich School of Painters
defn: The regional landscape school of Norwich (1803–1833) around John Crome and John Sell Cotman: Crome's Mousehold Heath, Cotman's Greta Bridge.

label: Academic Art
defn: Painting shaped by the European academies and their Salons in the 19th century, finished, idealising and hierarchical in subject: Cabanel's Birth of Venus, Bouguereau's Nymphs and Satyr, Gérôme's Pollice Verso.
note: period-style home for European-lineage painters born 1815–1859 with no movement

label: Neo-Grec
defn: A mid-19th-century French current of small-scale, archaeologically detailed antique genre scenes: Gérôme's Cock Fight, Hamon's My Sister Is Not In.
note: neo-Pompeian (Q19953536) merged

label: Realism
defn: The mid-19th-century movement that painted contemporary life and labour without idealisation: Courbet's A Burial at Ornans, Millet's The Angelus, Repin's Barge Haulers on the Volga.
note: French Realism (Q2642826) merged; Peredvizhniki and Belgian landscape schools are kinds

label: Costumbrismo
defn: Spanish and Latin American painting of local customs, types and manners in the 19th century: Bécquer's Andalusian scenes, Pancho Fierro's Lima watercolours.

label: Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood
defn: The English brotherhood (1848) and its circle that painted with the detail and colour of art before Raphael: Millais's Ophelia, Rossetti's Beata Beatrix, Hunt's The Light of the World.
note: kept as a leaf: the group names the movement

label: Hague School
defn: Dutch painters working in The Hague c. 1860–1900 in grey-toned realist landscape and genre: Mesdag's Panorama, Mauve's Morning Ride on the Beach.
note: Laren School a kind

label: Macchiaioli
defn: Tuscan painters of the 1850s–1870s who built pictures from patches (macchie) of light and shade: Fattori's The Rotonda di Palmieri, Lega's The Visit.

label: Naturalism
defn: Late-19th-century plein-air painting of rural and working life with photographic truth: Bastien-Lepage's Haymaking, Stanhope Forbes's A Fish Sale on a Cornish Beach, the Skagen Painters.
note: art colonies (Newlyn, Skagen, Étaples, Concarneau, Nagybánya ...) are kinds

label: Munich School
defn: Painters trained at the Munich Academy c. 1850–1914 in dark, painterly realism: Leibl's Three Women in Church, Gyzis's works, Chase's early portraits.

label: Impressionism
defn: The French movement of the 1860s–1880s that painted modern life and light in broken colour outdoors, and its national offshoots: Monet's Impression, Sunrise, Renoir's Bal du moulin de la Galette, Morisot's The Cradle.
note: national and regional Impressionisms (American, Californian, Heidelberg School, German, Amsterdam) and Secessions are kinds

label: Neo-Impressionism
defn: The systematic colour-division of Seurat and Signac from 1886 and its Italian divisionist branch: Seurat's A Sunday on La Grande Jatte, Signac's Portrait of Félix Fénéon.
note: pointillism (Q200034) merged

label: Post-Impressionism
defn: Painting after Impressionism c. 1886–1905 that turned colour and form to structure and expression: Cézanne's Mont Sainte-Victoire, Van Gogh's Starry Night, Gauguin's Vision after the Sermon.
note: Les Nabis, Bloomsbury Group, Scottish Colourists and intimism are kinds

label: Pont-Aven School
defn: Painters around Gauguin and Émile Bernard in Brittany from 1886, flat colour and bounding line (synthetism, cloisonnism): Bernard's Breton Women in the Meadow, Sérusier's The Talisman.
note: synthetism and cloisonnism are kinds

label: Symbolism
defn: Late-19th-century painting of dream, myth and inner states: Moreau's The Apparition, Redon's The Cyclops, Khnopff's I Lock My Door Upon Myself.
see: T44 Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood;T168 Art Nouveau;T54 Aestheticism
note: Russian symbolism, Mir iskusstva, Young Poland and the Rose+Croix salons are kinds

label: Aestheticism
defn: The British "art for art's sake" painting of the 1860s–1890s: Whistler's Symphony in White, Leighton's Flaming June, Albert Moore's Midsummer.

label: Tonalism
defn: American (and Australian) landscape painting c. 1880–1915 in muted, atmospheric tones: Inness's Home of the Heron, Dewing's The Recitation.
note: Australian Tonalism a kind

label: Luminism
defn: American landscape painting c. 1850–1875 of calm, hidden-brushwork light: Fitz Henry Lane's Owl's Head, Heade's Approaching Thunder Storm.

label: Glasgow School
defn: The Glasgow Boys (c. 1880–1900), Scottish painters of plein-air naturalism and decorative colour: Guthrie's A Highland Funeral, Henry and Hornel's The Druids.

label: Expressionism
defn: Painting from c. 1905 that distorted colour and form for emotional force, centred in Germany and Austria: Kirchner's Street, Berlin, Kokoschka's The Bride of the Wind, Marc's Blue Horse.
note: Die Brücke, Der Blaue Reiter circles, Secessions and German Expressionism are kinds

label: Fauvism
defn: The French painting of pure, arbitrary colour around Matisse and Derain, 1904–1908: Matisse's Woman with a Hat, Derain's Charing Cross Bridge.
note: Brabant fauvism a kind

label: Cubism
defn: The movement of Picasso and Braque (from 1907) that fractured objects into planes and multiple viewpoints, with its Salon Cubist and Section d'Or circles: Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, Braque's Violin and Candlestick, Gris's Portrait of Picasso.
note: Salon Cubism, Section d'Or, Purism, post-cubism are kinds

label: Futurism
defn: The Italian movement (1909) celebrating speed, machines and the city, and its Russian Cubo-Futurist branch: Boccioni's The City Rises, Balla's Dynamism of a Dog on a Leash, Severini's Armoured Train.
note: aeropittura, Russian Futurism, Cubo-Futurism, Rayonism are kinds

label: Orphism
defn: Abstract painting of prismatic colour around Robert and Sonia Delaunay and Kupka, c. 1912: Robert Delaunay's Simultaneous Windows, Kupka's Amorpha.
note: Synchromism and simultanism are kinds

label: Vorticism
defn: The British avant-garde of 1914–1915 around Wyndham Lewis and the magazine BLAST: Bomberg's The Mud Bath, Lewis's The Crowd.

label: Suprematism
defn: Malevich's abstraction of pure geometric forms from 1915: Black Square, Suprematist Composition: White on White.

label: Constructivism
defn: The Russian movement from c. 1915 of art as construction and production, and its international heirs: Tatlin's Monument to the Third International, Rodchenko's Pure Colours, El Lissitzky's Proun.
see: T64 Suprematism;T66 De Stijl;T89 Concrete Art
note: Universal Constructivism (Torres-García) a kind

label: De Stijl
defn: The Dutch movement (1917) of Neoplasticism, reducing art to primaries and the right angle: Mondrian's Composition with Red, Blue and Yellow, van Doesburg's Counter-Composition.
note: neoplasticism (Q845421) merged

label: Dada
defn: The anti-art movement born in Zurich in 1916 and spread to Berlin, Paris and New York: Duchamp's Fountain, Höch's Cut with the Kitchen Knife, Arp's collages.
note: Incoherents (proto-Dada) a kind

label: Surrealism
defn: The movement launched by Breton in 1924 that painted dream and the unconscious: Dalí's The Persistence of Memory, Magritte's The Treachery of Images, Ernst's Europe after the Rain.
see: T67 Dada;T69 Metaphysical Painting;T71 Magic Realism
note: Belgian surrealism, post-surrealism, Fantastic Realism are kinds

label: Metaphysical Painting
defn: Giorgio de Chirico's and Carrà's painting of uncanny piazzas and mannequins, 1910–1920: The Disquieting Muses, Mystery and Melancholy of a Street.

label: New Objectivity
defn: The sober, sharp-focus realism of Weimar Germany in the 1920s: Dix's Portrait of Sylvia von Harden, Grosz's Pillars of Society, Schad's Self-Portrait with Model.
note: Q59818567 merged

label: Magic Realism
defn: Realist painting of the 1920s–1950s that makes the everyday strange: Carel Willink's Wilma, Pyke Koch's Shooting Gallery, Ivan Albright's The Picture of Dorian Gray.

label: Precisionism
defn: American painting of the 1920s–1930s rendering industry and the city in crisp geometric planes: Sheeler's American Landscape, Demuth's My Egypt.

label: Regionalism
defn: American painting of the 1930s of the rural Midwest: Wood's American Gothic, Benton's America Today, Curry's Tragic Prelude.
note: American scene painting a kind

label: Ashcan School
defn: New York realist painters of the early 20th century who depicted the city's streets and poor: Bellows's Stag at Sharkey's, Sloan's McSorley's Bar.

label: Social Realism
defn: Politically engaged realist painting of the 1920s–1940s on labour and poverty: Ben Shahn's The Passion of Sacco and Vanzetti, Isabel Bishop's working women.
see: T76 Socialist Realism;T73 Regionalism;T191 Mexican Muralism
note: Italian neorealism in painting a kind

label: Socialist Realism
defn: The official style of the Soviet Union from 1932 and of the socialist states: Gerasimov's Lenin on the Tribune, Deineka's Defence of Petrograd.
note: Leningrad School, Leipzig School and socialist realism in France are kinds

label: Harlem Renaissance
defn: The flowering of African-American art in the 1920s–1930s centred in Harlem: Aaron Douglas's Aspects of Negro Life, Archibald Motley's Nightlife, Augusta Savage's The Harp.
note: New Negro Movement (Q104010227) merged

label: School of Paris
defn: The international, often émigré artists working in Paris c. 1900–1940 outside a single movement: Modigliani's Jeanne Hébuterne, Chagall's I and the Village, Soutine's Carcass of Beef.

label: Scuola Romana
defn: Roman painters of the 1920s–1930s around Scipione and Mafai, expressionist in colour against the classicising Novecento: Mafai's Demolitions, Scipione's Cardinal Decano.

label: Neo-Romanticism
defn: Figurative painting of the 1930s–1950s (Berman, Tchelitchew; the British Neo-Romantics) reviving Romantic landscape and mood: Paul Nash's Totes Meer, Sutherland's Entrance to a Lane.

label: Naïve Art
defn: Painting by artists without academic training, flat, detailed and frontal: Henri Rousseau's The Dream, Séraphine Louis's Tree of Paradise, Ivan Generalić's Hlebine paintings.
see: T82 Art Brut;A6 Folk & Popular Painting

label: Art Brut
defn: Dubuffet's "raw art" of outsiders, the untrained and the institutionalised, and its successor outsider art: Adolf Wölfli's illustrated books, Aloïse Corbaz's theatres.
note: art brut Q57174052 and Art outsider Q16303875 merged

label: Abstract Expressionism
defn: The New York painting of the 1940s–1950s, gestural or field-based: Pollock's Autumn Rhythm, de Kooning's Woman I, Kline's Chief.
see: T84 Color Field;Art Informel;T85 Lyrical Abstraction
note: action painting and the New York School are kinds

label: Color Field
defn: Abstraction of large expanses of flat or stained colour from the late 1940s: Rothko's No. 61 (Rust and Blue), Frankenthaler's Mountains and Sea, Newman's Vir Heroicus Sublimis.
note: Washington Color School and Post-painterly Abstraction are kinds

label: Lyrical Abstraction
defn: Post-war gestural abstraction in Paris (abstraction lyrique) and its American 1960s sense: Georges Mathieu's Capetians Everywhere, Zao Wou-Ki's large canvases.

label: Informalism
defn: European post-war abstraction of matter, sign and gesture (art informel, tachisme, matter painting): Fautrier's Hostages, Wols's It's All Over, Tàpies's matter paintings.
note: Tachisme, Matterism, Movimento Spaziale are kinds

label: COBRA
defn: The Copenhagen–Brussels–Amsterdam movement (1948–1951) of spontaneous, childlike expressionist painting: Appel's Questioning Children, Jorn's Letter to My Son.

label: Hard-edge Painting
defn: Abstraction of crisp-edged flat colour areas from the late 1950s: Ellsworth Kelly's Red Blue Green, Karl Benjamin's compositions.
see: T84 Color Field;T89 Concrete Art;T90 Op Art
note: Les Plasticiens a kind

label: Concrete Art
defn: Geometric abstraction built from pure plastic means, after van Doesburg's 1930 manifesto, in Switzerland, Italy and Latin America: Max Bill's Endless Ribbon, Lygia Clark's Bichos, Tomás Maldonado's works.
see: T66 De Stijl;T65 Constructivism;T90 Op Art
note: Movimento Arte Concreta, Madí, neo-concrete movement, Art Concret group are kinds

label: Op Art
defn: Abstraction of the 1960s exploiting optical effects: Bridget Riley's Movement in Squares, Vasarely's Vega series.
note: Nouvelle tendance a kind

label: Pop Art
defn: Art of the late 1950s–1960s drawn from mass media, advertising and consumer goods: Warhol's Campbell's Soup Cans, Lichtenstein's Whaam!, Hamilton's Just What Is It ....
note: neo-pop, capitalist realism and Figuration narrative are kinds

label: Neo-Dada
defn: American art of the late 1950s reviving Dada assemblage and found imagery: Rauschenberg's Monogram, Johns's Flag.

label: Nouveau Réalisme
defn: The French movement founded in 1960 around Restany, appropriating the real (décollage, accumulation, wrapping): Arman's Accumulations, Yves Klein's Anthropometries, Villeglé's torn posters.
note: the Affichistes a kind

label: Funk Art
defn: Irreverent figurative art of the San Francisco Bay Area in the 1960s, often in ceramics: Robert Arneson's self-portrait busts, Roy De Forest's paintings.
see: T91 Pop Art;T95 Bay Area Figurative Movement

label: Bay Area Figurative Movement
defn: San Francisco painters of the 1950s–1960s who returned from abstraction to the figure: Diebenkorn's Cityscape I, David Park's Four Men.

label: Northwest School
defn: Painters of the Pacific Northwest in the 1930s–1950s, mystical and Asian-influenced: Mark Tobey's white writing, Morris Graves's Blind Bird.

label: Pattern and Decoration
defn: The American movement of the mid-1970s that reclaimed ornament, textile and craft: Miriam Schapiro's femmages, Robert Kushner's costumes.

label: Photorealism
defn: Painting from the late 1960s that reproduces photographs with exacting fidelity: Richard Estes's storefronts, Chuck Close's Big Self-Portrait.
note: hyperrealism (Q749832, gathering reference) merged

label: Neo-figurative
defn: The return to the figure in 1960s Latin America and Spain (Otra Figuración): Jorge de la Vega's works, Luis Felipe Noé's Introduction to Hope.
note: New Figuration (Q368002) a kind

label: Neo-Expressionism
defn: Figurative, expressive painting of the late 1970s–1980s: Baselitz's upside-down figures, Kiefer's Margarethe, Basquiat's Untitled (Skull).
note: national branches (Neue Wilde, Transavantgarde, Figuration Libre) and Bad Painting are kinds

label: Lettrism
defn: Isidore Isou's movement (from 1945) of letters and signs as the material of poetry and painting: Isou's hypergraphic novels, Lemaître's works.
note: Letterist International and Situationist International are kinds

label: Black Arts Movement
defn: The African-American art movement of 1965–1975 tied to Black Power (AfriCOBRA, the Wall of Respect): Jeff Donaldson's Wives of Shango, Wadsworth Jarrell's Revolutionary.
see: T77 Harlem Renaissance;T103 British Black Arts Movement

label: British Black Arts Movement
defn: Black British artists of the 1980s (the BLK Art Group) addressing race and diaspora: Lubaina Himid's A Fashionable Marriage, Keith Piper's works.

label: Lowbrow
defn: Californian pop-surrealist painting from the late 1970s rooted in comics, hot-rod and tattoo culture: Robert Williams's paintings, Mark Ryden's The Meat Show.
note: gathering contemporary reference

label: Mission School
defn: San Francisco artists of the 1990s working from street, folk and graffiti culture: Barry McGee's installations, Margaret Kilgallen's murals.
note: gathering contemporary reference

label: Stuckism
defn: The figurative painting movement founded in London in 1999 against conceptual art: Charles Thomson's Sir Nicholas Serota Makes an Acquisitions Decision.
note: gathering contemporary reference

label: Superflat
defn: Takashi Murakami's Japanese postmodern movement (2000) of flat anime and print-derived imagery: Murakami's Tan Tan Bo, Aya Takano's paintings.
note: gathering contemporary reference

label: Hurufiyya Movement
defn: Modern art of the Arab world and Iran (from the 1950s) that uses Arabic letters as abstract form: Madiha Omar's works, Shakir Hassan Al Said's The Contemplative Dimension, Parviz Tanavoli's Heech.
note: Saqqa-khaneh school a kind

label: Dakar School
defn: Senegalese painting of the 1960s–1970s fostered by Senghor's Négritude policy: Papa Ibra Tall's tapestries, Iba N'Diaye's works.

label: Yōga
defn: Japanese painting in Western oil technique from the Meiji period: Kuroda Seiki's Lakeside, Takahashi Yuichi's Salmon, Kishida Ryūsei's Reiko.

label: Bengal School of Art
defn: The Indian nationalist painting movement of Abanindranath Tagore and his pupils (c. 1900–1940) reviving Mughal and Ajanta idioms: Abanindranath Tagore's Bharat Mata, Nandalal Bose's Haripura posters.
note: period-style home for South Asian painters born 1850–1899

label: Modern Art
defn: The period style of painters born c. 1860–1944 working outside a recorded movement, across the global lineages of easel painting: academic-trained modern portraitists, independent landscape painters, national modernisms.
note: period-style leaf (brief); exhibition societies and groups of this generation are kinds

label: Contemporary Art
defn: The period style of painters born from 1945, working after modernism in global, plural practices: post-colonial figurative painting, new abstraction.
note: period-style leaf (brief); contemporary art (Q186030) movement row itself is a tag

label: Old Master Drawing
defn: European drawing before c. 1800 as preparatory study and finished work, in metalpoint, chalk, pen and wash: Leonardo's Vitruvian Man, Dürer's Praying Hands, Rembrandt's landscape drawings.
note: label qualified by medium; attested via Old Master

label: Illustration
defn: Drawing made for books, periodicals, posters and caricature from the 18th century to the present: Gillray's caricatures, Tenniel's Alice illustrations, Saul Steinberg's New Yorker covers.
note: period-style home for draughtsmen born 1750–1849 and from 1900

label: Golden Age of Illustration
defn: Book and magazine illustration c. 1880–1920, when colour printing made illustrators celebrities: Arthur Rackham's Peter Pan, Howard Pyle's pirates, Edmund Dulac's Arabian Nights.
note: Brandywine School a kind

label: Ligne Claire
defn: The clear-line drawing style of Hergé and the Brussels school of Franco-Belgian comics: The Adventures of Tintin, Blake and Mortimer.
note: School of Brussels, atom style and the Flemish school are kinds

label: Marcinelle School
defn: The dynamic, rounded Franco-Belgian comics style of Spirou magazine (Jijé, Franquin, Morris): Spirou et Fantasio, Lucky Luke, Gaston.

label: Manga
defn: Japanese comics and their drawn idiom from the 20th century: Tezuka's Astro Boy, Oda's One Piece, Takeuchi's Sailor Moon.
note: may belong to a comics tab; rule sends Japanese draughtsmen born from 1850 here (Chinese and Korean illustrators go to T118)

label: Old Master Print
defn: Western printmaking before c. 1830 in woodcut, engraving, etching and mezzotint: Dürer's Melencolia I, Rembrandt's Hundred Guilder Print, Piranesi's Carceri.
see: T124 Etching Revival;T117 Old Master Drawing

label: Etching Revival
defn: The re-emergence of etching as an original art c. 1850–1930 in France, Britain and the United States: Whistler's Thames Set, Méryon's Eaux-fortes sur Paris, Seymour Haden's landscapes.

label: Modern Printmaking
defn: Printmaking by artists born c. 1880–1944: the expressionist woodcut, the artist's lithograph and the screenprint: Kollwitz's War cycle, Picasso's Vollard Suite.
note: label qualified by medium; attested via modern art

label: Contemporary Printmaking
defn: Printmaking by artists born from 1945 across print and multiple practices.
note: label qualified by medium; attested via contemporary art

label: Ukiyo-e
defn: Japanese woodblock prints and paintings of the floating world (17th–19th century): Hokusai's Great Wave, Hiroshige's Fifty-three Stations, Utamaro's beauties.
note: Utagawa school a kind

label: Shin-hanga
defn: The 20th-century Japanese revival of ukiyo-e production by publisher Watanabe Shōzaburō: Kawase Hasui's landscapes, Hashiguchi Goyō's beauties.

label: Sōsaku-hanga
defn: Japanese "creative prints" (from 1904) designed, carved and printed by the artist: Onchi Kōshirō's abstractions, Munakata Shikō's Buddhist prints.
note: period-style home for East Asian printmakers born 1850–1944

label: Chinese Calligraphy
defn: The art of writing Chinese characters with the brush, in seal, clerical, regular, running and cursive scripts: Wang Xizhi's Lantingji Xu, Huaisu's Autobiography, Mi Fu's Poems Written on a Boat on the Wu River.
note: rule sends Chinese and Korean book-arts artists here; Japanese go to T131, Ottoman to C1-3, Persian to C1-4

label: Japanese Calligraphy
defn: Shodō: the Japanese art of the brush in kanji and kana, with its court lineages (Sesonji-ryū) and Zen bokuseki: Ono no Michikaze's works, Fujiwara no Yukinari's Hakubunshū.
note: Sesonji-ryū a kind

label: Western Calligraphy
defn: The art of Latin-script writing, from Renaissance chancery hands and writing masters to modern lettering: Arrighi's La Operina, Palatino's writing book.

label: Type Design
defn: The design of typefaces and lettering for print and screen since the 19th century: Johnston's Underground typeface, Frutiger's Univers, Miedinger's Helvetica.
note: placed in C1 as lettering; owner may prefer a design sub-family (see notes)

label: Gothic Book Illustration
defn: The illumination of Gothic manuscripts (13th–15th century), from Paris workshops to the Books of Hours: Jean Pucelle's Hours of Jeanne d'Évreux, the Douce Apocalypse, the Bedford Hours.

label: Ghent-Bruges School
defn: Flemish manuscript illumination c. 1475–1560 with illusionistic borders: the Grimani Breviary, Simon Bening's Da Costa Hours.
see: T134 Gothic Book Illustration;T21 Early Netherlandish Painting

label: Archaic Greek Sculpture
defn: Greek sculpture c. 650–480 BC: kouroi, korai and temple pediments: the New York Kouros, the Peplos Kore, the Aegina pediments.
note: School of Chios a kind

label: Classical Greek Sculpture
defn: Greek sculpture c. 480–323 BC from the Severe Style to Praxiteles and Lysippos: the Riace bronzes, the Parthenon marbles, Polykleitos's Doryphoros.
see: T136 Archaic Greek Sculpture;T138 Hellenistic Sculpture
note: art of Classical Greece (Q16064885) merged; severe style a kind

label: Hellenistic Sculpture
defn: Greek sculpture 323–31 BC, theatrical and realistic: the Pergamon Altar, the Winged Victory of Samothrace, the Laocoön.
see: T137 Classical Greek Sculpture;T139 Roman Sculpture
note: Hellenistic art (Q221375) merged

label: Romanesque Sculpture
defn: Carved portals, capitals and church furnishings of the 11th–12th centuries: Gislebertus's Last Judgement at Autun, Wiligelmo's Modena reliefs, the Pórtico de la Gloria.

label: Gothic Sculpture
defn: Sculpture of the Gothic cathedrals and their workshops (c. 1140–1500): the Chartres Royal Portal, the Naumburg donor figures, Giovanni Pisano's pulpits.

label: Renaissance Sculpture
defn: European sculpture c. 1400–1560 reviving antique form: Donatello's David, Ghiberti's Gates of Paradise, Michelangelo's David.
note: Mannerist sculptors included

label: Baroque Sculpture
defn: Sculpture of the 17th and early 18th centuries, dynamic and theatrical: Bernini's Ecstasy of Saint Teresa, the Fontana dei Quattro Fiumi, Gregorio Fernández's pasos.
note: Rococo sculptors included

label: Neoclassical Sculpture
defn: Sculpture c. 1750–1840 on antique models in white marble: Canova's Psyche Revived by Cupid's Kiss, Thorvaldsen's Jason, Houdon's Voltaire.

label: Academic Sculpture
defn: Salon and public-monument sculpture of the 19th-century academies, Romantic to Beaux-Arts: Rude's La Marseillaise, Carpeaux's The Dance, Bartholdi's Statue of Liberty.
see: T144 Neoclassical Sculpture;T148 Modern Sculpture;T146 New Sculpture
note: label qualified by medium; attested via academic art

label: New Sculpture
defn: The British movement (1880s–1910s) of naturalistic, symbolist bronze sculpture: Leighton's Athlete Wrestling with a Python, Gilbert's Eros.

label: Animalier School
defn: 19th-century French sculpture of animals in small bronzes: Barye's Lion Crushing a Serpent, Mêne's hunting groups.
note: gathering reference movement

label: Modern Sculpture
defn: Sculpture by artists born c. 1850–1944, from Rodin to abstraction, assemblage and constructed sculpture: Rodin's The Thinker, Brâncuși's Bird in Space, Hepworth's Single Form.

label: Contemporary Sculpture
defn: Sculpture by artists born from 1945, object, figure and installation-based.
note: label qualified by medium; attested via contemporary art

label: Kinetic Art
defn: Sculpture that moves or appears to move, from Calder's mobiles to the ZERO group: Calder's Lobster Trap and Fish Tail, Tinguely's Homage to New York.
note: ZERO a kind

label: Minimalism
defn: American sculpture of the 1960s of industrial, serial, geometric units: Judd's Untitled stacks, Carl Andre's Equivalent VIII, Dan Flavin's fluorescent works.
note: Finish Fetish a kind

label: Postminimalism
defn: Sculpture after Minimalism (late 1960s) of process, materials and the body: Eva Hesse's Contingent, Serra's Splash Piece.
note: process art a kind

label: Kei School
defn: The Japanese Buddhist sculptors' lineage of Unkei and Kaikei (Kamakura period), realistic in joined-wood technique: the Tōdai-ji Niō, Unkei's Muchaku.
note: Kamakura-period Japanese sculptors only; earlier Japanese busshi go to east_asia:L21, Chinese and Korean sculptors to east_asia:L19/L20

label: Mosan Art
defn: Romanesque goldsmiths' work and enamel of the Meuse valley (11th–13th century): Nicholas of Verdun's Klosterneuburg Altar, the Stavelot Triptych.
note: period-style home for European decorative artists born before 1250

label: Quilts of Gee's Bend
defn: Quilts made by the women of Gee's Bend, Alabama, since the 19th century: Annie Mae Young's work-clothes quilts, Mary Lee Bendolph's quilts.
note: single row; check against a North America slice

label: International Gothic (decorative arts)
defn: Courtly late Gothic goldsmiths' work, tapestry and glass (c. 1250–1450): the Goldenes Rössl, the Apocalypse Tapestry of Angers.
note: label qualified by medium

label: Mannerism (decorative arts)
defn: Renaissance and Mannerist decorative arts and ornament (c. 1450–1600): Cellini's Salt Cellar, Jamnitzer's goldsmiths' work, Pannemaker's tapestries.
note: label qualified by medium

label: Louis XIV Style
defn: French court decorative arts c. 1660–1715 under Le Brun: Boulle marquetry, Gobelins tapestries, Versailles silver furniture.

label: Louis XV Style
defn: The Rococo decorative arts of France c. 1715–1760: Cressent's commodes, Meissonnier's ornament, Vincennes-Sèvres porcelain.
see: T161 Louis XIV Style;T163 Louis XVI Style

label: Louis XVI Style
defn: Early neoclassical decorative arts in France c. 1760–1790: Riesener's furniture, Marie-Antoinette's boudoir at Fontainebleau.
see: T162 Louis XV Style;T164 Empire Style

label: Empire Style
defn: Napoleonic neoclassical design c. 1800–1830: Percier and Fontaine's Malmaison, Jacob-Desmalter's furniture.

label: Biedermeier
defn: Central European design and domestic culture 1815–1848, simple and comfortable, and its painting of bourgeois life: Danhauser furniture, Waldmüller's genre scenes.
see: T164 Empire Style;T166 Victorian Decorative Arts
note: movement placed in design; Biedermeier painters go to their period leaf with the tag

label: Victorian Decorative Arts
defn: British decorative arts 1837–1901, historicist and industrial: Pugin's Gothic Revival furniture, Minton majolica.

label: Arts and Crafts Movement
defn: The reform of design and craft after Ruskin and Morris (1860s–1920s): Morris & Co. wallpapers, Ashbee's silver, Stickley's Craftsman furniture.
note: American Craftsman a kind

label: Art Nouveau
defn: The international style of organic line and ornament c. 1890–1910 across design, architecture and painting: Gallé's glass, Mucha's posters, Horta's Hôtel Tassel, Klimt's Beethoven Frieze.
see: T169 Art Deco;T185 Art Nouveau Architecture;T53 Symbolism
note: movement placed in design; Art Nouveau painters go to their period leaf with the tag; Catalan modernisme, Vienna Secession, École de Nancy are kinds

label: Art Deco
defn: The streamlined geometric luxury style of the 1920s–1930s: Ruhlmann's furniture, Lalique glass, Cassandre's posters, the Chrysler Building.
note: Streamline Moderne a kind

label: Bauhaus
defn: The German school of art and design (1919–1933) and its functional modernism: Breuer's Wassily Chair, Brandt's tea infuser, Albers's weavings.
see: T169 Art Deco;T172 Mid-Century Modern;T65 Constructivism

label: Mingei
defn: The Japanese folk-craft movement (1926) of Yanagi Sōetsu, Hamada and Kawai: Hamada Shōji's stoneware, Serizawa Keisuke's stencil dyeing.
see: T167 Arts and Crafts Movement;E3 Stoneware
note: material families mixed (ceramics dominant); placed in I3 pending a design sub-family

label: Mid-Century Modern
defn: Modern design c. 1933–1965: the Eames Lounge Chair, Arne Jacobsen's Egg chair, Castiglioni lamps.
note: period-style home for designers born 1910–1944

label: Contemporary Design
defn: Design by makers born from 1945: product, furniture, fashion and graphic design.
note: label qualified by medium; attested via contemporary art

label: Early Photography
defn: Photography of the daguerreotype, calotype and wet-collodion decades (1839–c. 1880): Talbot's The Open Door, Nadar's portraits, Cameron's portraits.
note: label attested by museum essay title, not an encyclopedia entry

label: Pictorialism
defn: The first international art-photography movement (1880s–1920s), soft-focus and hand-worked: Steichen's The Pond—Moonlight, Käsebier's Blessed Art Thou among Women.
note: Photo-Secession and Le Groupe des XV are kinds

label: Straight Photography
defn: Sharp-focus, unmanipulated modernist photography from the 1910s (Group f/64): Strand's Wall Street, Weston's Pepper No. 30, Adams's Moonrise, Hernandez.

label: New Vision
defn: The experimental photography of the 1920s–1930s (Neues Sehen) of angles, close-ups and photograms: Moholy-Nagy's photograms, Rodchenko's Pioneer Girl.
note: Shinkō shashin, Zen'ei shashin and Fotoform are kinds

label: Humanistic Photography
defn: French post-war photography of everyday life and its dignity: Doisneau's Kiss by the Hôtel de Ville, Willy Ronis's Le Petit Parisien.

label: Documentary Photography
defn: Photography that records people, places and events for social or historical purpose, including photojournalism: Lange's Migrant Mother, Evans's Let Us Now Praise Famous Men, Salgado's Workers.
note: photojournalism and war photography are kinds

label: Contemporary Photography
defn: Photography by artists born from 1945, staged, documentary and conceptual.
note: label qualified by medium; attested via contemporary art

label: Gothic Architecture
defn: Medieval European architecture of the pointed arch, rib vault and flying buttress (c. 1140–1520): Chartres Cathedral, Sainte-Chapelle, Cologne Cathedral.

label: Renaissance Architecture
defn: European architecture c. 1400–1600 reviving classical orders: Brunelleschi's Duomo dome, Bramante's Tempietto, Palladio's Villa Rotonda.

label: Baroque Architecture
defn: European and colonial architecture c. 1600–1750 of movement and spatial drama: Borromini's San Carlo, Versailles, Melk Abbey.
note: Dutch Baroque architecture a kind

label: Neoclassical Architecture
defn: Architecture c. 1750–1850 on Greek and Roman models: the Panthéon, Paris, the British Museum, the Brandenburg Gate.
note: Neoclassical architecture in Russia a kind

label: Art Nouveau Architecture
defn: Architecture of the Art Nouveau c. 1890–1914: Horta's Hôtel Tassel, Guimard's Métro entrances, Gaudí's Casa Batlló.

label: Modern Architecture
defn: Architecture of the modern movement (c. 1900–1975): functionalism, the International Style and their regional forms: Villa Savoye, the Barcelona Pavilion, Fallingwater.
note: Neues Bauen, functionalism, rationalism, Amsterdam School, Metabolism, high-tech, organic and expressionist architecture are kinds

label: Brutalist Architecture
defn: Modernist architecture of the 1950s–1970s in exposed concrete and massive forms: Unité d'Habitation, the Barbican Estate, Boston City Hall.

label: Postmodern Architecture
defn: Architecture from the 1960s–1990s returning to ornament, history and irony: Venturi's Vanna Venturi House, Graves's Portland Building, Stirling's Neue Staatsgalerie.

label: Deconstructivism
defn: Architecture from the 1980s of fragmented, non-rectilinear forms: Gehry's Guggenheim Bilbao, Libeskind's Jewish Museum Berlin, Hadid's Vitra Fire Station.
note: gathering contemporary reference

label: Contemporary Architecture
defn: Architecture by architects born from 1945, in plural idioms from parametric design to vernacular-sustainable building: Kéré's Gando school, SANAA's Rolex Learning Center.

label: Street Art
defn: Unsanctioned and commissioned art in public space from the 1970s: graffiti writing, stencil, paste-up and mural: Banksy's Girl with Balloon, Os Gêmeos's murals, JR's Women Are Heroes.
note: gathering contemporary reference

label: Installation Art
defn: Art that makes or transforms a space to be entered or experienced, from the 1960s: Kabakov's The Man Who Flew into Space, Kusama's Infinity Mirror Rooms.
note: period-style home for installation, performance and conceptual artists; Light and Space, Mono-ha and relational art are kinds

label: Conceptual Art
defn: Art since the mid-1960s in which the idea is the work: Kosuth's One and Three Chairs, Sol LeWitt's Wall Drawings, On Kawara's Date Paintings.
note: Art & Language, Moscow Conceptualists, signalism and neo-conceptual art are kinds

label: Fluxus
defn: The international intermedia network of the 1960s around George Maciunas: event scores, actions and multiples: Yoko Ono's Cut Piece, Fluxkits.
see: T194 Conceptual Art;T196 Mail Art;T200 Performance Art
note: Zaj a kind

label: Mail Art
defn: Art sent and exchanged through the postal system from the 1960s (Ray Johnson's New York Correspondence School): Johnson's moticos, artistamps.

label: Arte Povera
defn: The Italian movement (1967) of "poor" materials and process: Pistoletto's Venus of the Rags, Merz's igloos, Kounellis's live horses.

label: Land Art
defn: Art made in and of the landscape from the late 1960s: Smithson's Spiral Jetty, De Maria's Lightning Field, Goldsworthy's works.
note: environmental art a kind

label: Viennese Actionism
defn: The radical Austrian performance movement of the 1960s: Nitsch's Orgien Mysterien Theater, Schwarzkogler's actions.

label: Performance Art
defn: Art made by the artist's live action before an audience, from the 1960s: Abramović's Rhythm 0, Beuys's I Like America and America Likes Me.
note: body art a kind

label: Video Art
defn: Art made with video from the mid-1960s: Nam June Paik's TV Buddha, Bill Viola's The Crossing, Joan Jonas's Vertical Roll.
note: period-style home for video and digital artists born before 1945

label: New Media Art
defn: Art made with digital, networked and computational technologies: Cory Arcangel's Super Mario Clouds, Rafael Lozano-Hemmer's Pulse Room.
note: digital, internet, post-internet, interactive and bio art are kinds; period-style home from 1945

label: Hispano-Flemish Style
defn: Fifteenth-century painting of Castile and Aragon shaped by Early Netherlandish oil technique and realism, under the patronage of Isabella I: Bartolomé Bermejo's Saint Michael Triumphant, Fernando Gallego's Pietà, Pedro Berruguete's altarpieces.
see: T21 Early Netherlandish Painting;T24 Northern Renaissance
note: added for Iberian painters born 1400–1499 (country rule); the article names Gallego, Bermejo, Berruguete, Juan de Flandes

label: Ink Wash Painting
defn: Monochrome ink painting of the Zen monasteries of Muromachi Japan (suibokuga), after Song and Yuan models: Mokuan Reien's Four Sleepers, Josetsu's Catching a Catfish with a Gourd, Sesshū's Landscape of the Four Seasons.
see: T3 Literati Painting;T9 Kanō School;T11 Nanga
note: Suibokuga and Sumi-e redirect to Ink wash painting; used for Japanese painters born 1300–1499 with no school

label: Dansaekhwa
defn: The Korean monochrome painting movement of the 1970s: Park Seo-bo's Ecriture, Yun Hyong-keun's Umber-Blue, Chung Sang-hwa's grids, Ha Chong-hyun's Conjunction.
see: T193 Installation Art (Mono-ha kind);T84 Color Field
note: members placed by name where the enwiki article names them (Park Seo-bo, Yun Hyong-keun, Chung Sang-hwa, Chung Chang-sup, Ha Chong-hyun, Lee Ufan, Kim Tschang-yeul)
